Choose Earned and possible points when every point has equal value. The calculator’s mode links select a method; enter your own scores after opening it.

table.caption: Choose the method that matches the way your course is graded
rows: One row per category; leave ungraded scores blank
Score percentage, then weight on each line
Earned points, then possible points on each line
Assessment grade and weight; check the letter mapping

links.label: Enter course categories and what-if scores
Enter weighted letter or percentage assessments

sections.title: Worked example: current grade with an unfinished final
paragraphs: Suppose homework is worth 20% of a course, the midterm 30%, a project 25%, and the final exam 25%. Your completed scores are 88%, 75%, and 92%. Those categories contribute 17.6 + 22.5 + 23 = 63.1 course percentage points. Because they cover 75% of the course, your current average is 63.1 ÷ 0.75 = 84.1333%, or about 84.13%.

Enter these four categories, leave the final’s Current score blank, and clear the example What-if score values. The current result describes completed work. The 63.1 course points are not the current average, and 84.13% is not yet a final course grade.

table.caption: Three completed categories and one ungraded final

sections.title: Keep a blank score, a zero and a what-if score separate
paragraphs: For the same example, a blank final score leaves the current average at 84.13%. Entering an actual zero on the final makes all 100% of the course graded and reduces the course grade to 63.1%. A missing grade and an earned zero therefore answer different questions.

To explore an 80% final without changing the current record, put 80 in the final’s What-if score. It adds 80 × 0.25 = 20 course points, producing a projected course grade of 83.1%. A what-if entry replaces that row’s current score in the projection; it does not add a second assessment or change the current result.

A projection covering less than 100% is an average of the entered scores. Add the missing categories and their planned scores before treating it as a whole-course projection. Category weights may total less than 100% while a course is being set up, but they cannot exceed 100% in this mode.

sections.title: Why averaging assignment percentages can give the wrong answer
paragraphs: Two assessments scored 18 out of 20 and 42 out of 60 give a total of 60 out of 80: 75%. Averaging their percentages, 90% and 70%, gives 80%, which incorrectly treats the 20-point and 60-point assessments as equally important in a points-based course.

If those two assessments belong to a category worth 25% of the course, first obtain the 75% category average, then enter one category row with score 75 and weight 25. Its contribution is 18.75 course points. Do not give each assignment the full 25% category weight. This two-step method assumes the assignments are combined by points within that category.

table.caption: Points-based assessments are weighted by their possible points

links.label: Calculate the category average from points

sections.title: Translate letter grades only with an explicit scoring convention
paragraphs: A letter does not identify one exact percentage. In Weighted letter or percentage assessments, the editable starting example represents A as 95 and B as 85. With A worth 40 and B worth 60, the weighted result is (95 × 40 + 85 × 60) ÷ 100 = 89%. Changing the representative values changes that estimate.

Use actual percentage scores when available. Otherwise, confirm the representative scores with your instructor. These input mappings are not letter-grade cutoffs, so the calculator does not infer a final letter from the weighted average. Grade points such as A = 4 belong in GPA calculations, not in a percentage score field.

links.label: Check or edit representative letter scores
Calculate GPA from course grades and credits

sections.title: Find the final-exam score needed for a target grade
paragraphs: In the four-category example, an 85% final course target requires another 85 − 63.1 = 21.9 course points. The final is worth 25%, so its required score is 21.9 ÷ 0.25 = 87.6%. A perfect final would produce 88.1% overall under these weights.

Open the Final Exam Grade Calculator and enter the unrounded current average 84.1333333333, target 85, and final weight 25. Use the completed-work average, not the 63.1 course points. The dedicated calculator checks whether a target is possible within the entered scoring assumptions.

links.label: Read a full final-exam planning example

sections.title: Check dropped work, extra credit and rounding before relying on a result
paragraphs: Apply any drop-lowest, replacement-exam, late-penalty or category-specific rule before entering the retained scores or category averages. These modes do not infer those rules from an assessment name. The points method accepts earned points above possible points for an extra-credit scenario, but whether those points count is determined by your course. Category current and what-if scores are limited to 0–100%.

Keep unrounded averages while calculating and apply the instructor’s rounding rule at the end. A displayed 89.5% is not automatically an A or a passing result. The worked numbers on this page are illustrative; the syllabus determines category weights, letter boundaries and which work counts.

faqs.question: How do I calculate my current grade before the final exam?
faqs.answer: Multiply each graded category score by its course weight, add the contributions, then divide by the graded share of the course. Leave the ungraded final blank in Category weights & what-if grades; do not enter zero unless it is an actual zero.

faqs.question: What if my grade weights add up to less than 100%?
faqs.answer: The included scores are normalized over their entered weights. That is an average for the work included, not a complete final course grade. A whole-course projection needs categories and projected scores covering 100%.

faqs.question: Should missing assignments be blank or zero?
faqs.answer: Use a blank current score for ungraded work in Category weights & what-if grades. Enter zero for work that your gradebook actually counts as a zero. An instructor may treat missing work as zero, so follow the course policy.

faqs.question: Can I mix letter grades and percentages?
faqs.answer: Yes, in Weighted letter or percentage assessments. Letter inputs use editable representative percentages. Those values are examples rather than universal school cutoffs; use the original numeric scores when available.

faqs.question: How do I calculate a grade from points earned?
faqs.answer: Add all earned points, divide by all possible points, and multiply by 100. For 18/20 and 42/60, the combined result is 60/80 = 75%. A simple average of the two percentages would be incorrect for that points-based system.

faqs.question: Can I see how a future assignment changes my grade?
faqs.answer: Enter a what-if score in the category row to compare a projection while keeping the current grade separate. For a single assignment inside a category, first recalculate that category’s average and use the new average as the what-if category score.

faqs.question: Does this calculate the final score I need to pass?
faqs.answer: Use the linked Final Exam Grade Calculator with your current completed-work average, desired overall grade and remaining assessment weight. It calculates the required score; your course defines the pass boundary.

faqs.question: Does the calculator automatically drop the lowest grade?
faqs.answer: No. Apply the syllabus rule to the correct category first and enter the resulting average or retained points. Dropping an assessment with a different weight can change the answer differently from dropping the lowest percentage.

tip-calculator.description: Calculate a tip from a chosen percentage and divide the bill plus tip evenly among a selected number of people.

faqs.question: Is the tip calculated before or after tax?
faqs.answer: It uses the amount entered. If you use a pre-tax subtotal, remember that the calculated combined total also excludes the tax.

faqs.question: Does splitting the bill change the tip?
faqs.answer: No. The tip is calculated once, then the bill plus tip is divided equally.

faqs.question: Can I use a currency other than dollars?
faqs.answer: The arithmetic works for any consistent currency. Treat the output amounts as that currency; the tool does not convert exchange rates.

faqs.question: What if a service charge is already included?
faqs.answer: Review the receipt and decide whether an additional gratuity is appropriate. The calculator does not automatically detect or deduct service charges.

faqs.question: Why do rounded shares sometimes miss the total?
faqs.answer: Division can produce fractions of the smallest payment unit. Assign the remaining cent or equivalent to one participant when collecting payment.

sections.title: Calculate the tip and an equal bill split
paragraphs: Enter the bill amount you want to use as the tipping base, your chosen percentage, and the number of people sharing it. The result separates the tip, the combined total, and each person’s equal share. A tip percentage is a choice; this tool does not infer a local custom from your currency or location.

sections.title: Worked example: a 120 bill shared by three people
paragraphs: At 18%, the tip is 120 × 0.18 = 21.60. The combined bill is 141.60, and dividing by three gives 47.20 each. Calculate the tip once on the whole bill before dividing it.

table.caption: Compare chosen tip rates on the same 120 bill

sections.title: Choose a consistent base for tax and service charges
paragraphs: The percentage applies to exactly the amount entered. If you enter a pre-tax subtotal, the output total also excludes that tax; add the tax separately when settling the payment. Entering a tax-inclusive total includes it in both the percentage base and the amount split.
Check the receipt for an existing gratuity or service charge before choosing an additional tip. The calculator does not distinguish mandatory charges from voluntary gratuities.

sections.title: Equal shares, unequal orders and rounding
paragraphs: An equal split assumes everyone shares the same cost, regardless of what each person ordered. Use an expense splitter to allocate different paid amounts or settle several purchases.
Currency amounts may round to cents. For a 10.00 total divided three ways, three displayed shares of 3.33 leave one cent unpaid; assign that remainder to one payment rather than changing the bill.

links.label: Split several expenses and settle balances

tip-calculator.seoTitle: Tip Calculator: Tip Percentage & Bill Split

fuel-cost-calculator.description: Estimate trip fuel and cost using metric, US or independently selected units for distance, fuel economy and pump price.

faqs.question: Does the calculation include the return trip?
faqs.answer: Only if you include that distance in the input. Double an identical one-way distance for a simple return-trip estimate.

faqs.question: Can I mix kilometers and miles per gallon?
faqs.answer: Yes. Use the independent-units mode and select the correct unit for each input.

faqs.question: Why is Imperial mpg different from US mpg?
faqs.answer: An Imperial gallon is larger than a US gallon. Identify the gallon standard before comparing economy figures.

faqs.question: Does selecting USD or GBP convert prices?
faqs.answer: No. Currency is a label. Enter the price in the currency you want the cost to use.

faqs.question: Are tolls and parking included?
faqs.answer: No. The result estimates fuel only; add other travel expenses separately.

sections.title: Choose units that match your route and pump price
paragraphs: Metric trip uses kilometers, liters per 100 km and price per liter. US trip uses miles, US miles per gallon and price per US gallon. Choose independent units when, for example, your distance is in miles but your fuel consumption is in L/100 km.
Enter the full distance you intend to drive, including a return leg if applicable. The calculator estimates fuel spending from your assumptions; it does not obtain live pump prices or traffic.

sections.title: Worked example: 500 km at 7 L/100 km
paragraphs: Fuel needed = 500 × 7 / 100 = 35 liters. At 1.50 per liter, the cost is 52.50. If the 500 km is only the outward journey and the return is identical, 1,000 km needs 70 liters and costs 105.00.

table.caption: Sensitivity to fuel consumption at the same distance and price

sections.title: US mpg, Imperial mpg and L/100 km
paragraphs: Miles per gallon measures distance from one gallon; L/100 km measures fuel needed for a fixed distance. Higher mpg and lower L/100 km indicate lower consumption. A US gallon and an Imperial gallon have different volumes, so the same mpg number cannot be swapped between them.

In US mode, 300 miles at 30 mpg needs 10 US gallons. At 3.50 per gallon the cost is 35.00. Selecting a currency label in independent-units mode does not change the numeric pump price or apply an exchange rate.

sections.title: Make a useful trip budget
paragraphs: Use measured economy from comparable driving when available. Compare a lower- and higher-consumption scenario for traffic, hills, load or weather instead of treating one estimate as guaranteed.

Fuel is only one travel cost. Tolls, parking, vehicle wear and accommodation are outside this calculation. A shared-trip budget can divide the estimated cost, but the calculator does not determine a reimbursement rate.

fuel-cost-calculator.seoTitle: Fuel Cost Calculator: Trip Distance & Fuel Economy

gas-mileage-calculator.description: Measure observed fuel economy from distance and fuel used, or compare odometer readings and fuel cost with consistent fill-up assumptions.

faqs.question: Should I use fuel added or fuel consumed?
faqs.answer: Use fuel consumed over the measured distance. Fuel added approximates that quantity when both endpoints have comparable tank fill levels.

faqs.question: Can I average two mpg results?
faqs.answer: Use total miles divided by total gallons. A simple mean is only equivalent under specific weighting conditions, such as equal fuel amounts.

faqs.question: Is 30 mpg the same for US and UK figures?
faqs.answer: No. US and Imperial gallons differ. This calculator’s US mode uses US gallons.

faqs.question: Why does lower L/100 km mean better economy?
faqs.answer: It means less fuel is used to cover the same 100 km. MPG instead rises when the vehicle covers more distance per gallon.

faqs.question: Does a single poor result prove the car needs repair?
faqs.answer: No. Measurement variation and driving conditions affect individual trips. Compare consistent observations before drawing conclusions.

sections.title: Measure fuel economy from the same trip interval
paragraphs: Enter distance and fuel used for the same interval. US fuel economy reports miles per US gallon, metric consumption uses liters per 100 km, and odometer mode derives miles from two readings and adds fuel-cost metrics.

For a full-to-full comparison, note the odometer when filling, drive, then record the fuel added at the next comparable fill level. A partial refill alone does not reveal all fuel consumed since a previous full tank.

sections.title: Worked example: 300 miles on 10 US gallons
paragraphs: Fuel economy is 300 / 10 = 30 US mpg. This is approximately 7.84 L/100 km. With odometer readings of 10,000 and 10,300 miles and a price of 3.50 per US gallon, fuel cost is 35.00, or about 0.1167 per mile.

sections.title: Average multiple fill-ups with totals
paragraphs: Add the distances and fuel amounts, then divide totals. An unweighted average of mpg figures can overstate or understate the combined result when the trips use different quantities of fuel.

table.caption: Why averaging the displayed mpg is misleading

sections.title: Interpret changes before assuming a vehicle problem
paragraphs: A lower mpg or higher L/100 km means more fuel per distance. Compare similar routes and several fill-ups because tank fill variation, idling, load and conditions affect the measurement. The result alone does not diagnose a mechanical fault.

Odometer mode assumes the displayed distance is accurate. A different tire circumference can affect distance readings; a nominal tire comparison illustrates the direction of that effect but does not calibrate the vehicle.

links.label: Estimate fuel cost for your next trip

gas-mileage-calculator.seoTitle: Gas Mileage Calculator: MPG & Liters per 100 km

horsepower-calculator.description: Calculate power from torque or work, and convert mechanical, metric, electric and boiler horsepower with explicit unit definitions.

faqs.question: Can torque alone tell me horsepower?
faqs.answer: No. Rotational speed is also required. Use torque measured at the same RPM used in the calculation.

faqs.question: Why is the familiar formula divided by about 5,252?
faqs.answer: That factor converts lb-ft and revolutions per minute into mechanical horsepower. It changes when different torque or power units are used.

faqs.question: Is metric horsepower the same as mechanical horsepower?
faqs.answer: No. Metric horsepower is 735.49875 W, while mechanical horsepower is about 745.699872 W.

faqs.question: Does work divided by time give peak power?
faqs.answer: It gives average power over the entered interval. It does not reveal an unmeasured peak within that interval.

faqs.question: Can I convert wheel horsepower directly to crank horsepower?
faqs.answer: Not without an appropriate loss model or measurements. The calculator does not assume a universal drivetrain-loss percentage.

sections.title: Match the power method to the measurements you have
paragraphs: Torque & RPM calculates rotational power from a torque measured at the same rotational speed. Force, distance & time calculates average mechanical power for a constant force acting along the displacement. Power unit converter changes the unit of an already known power value.
These methods share the concept of energy transfer per time, but their inputs are not interchangeable. Torque alone cannot establish power without rotational speed.

links.label: Power as work per unit time

sections.title: Worked torque example at one operating point
paragraphs: With 300 lb-ft of torque at 5,000 rpm, mechanical horsepower is approximately 300 × 5,000 / 5,252.113122 = 285.60 hp. Use the torque at 5,000 rpm, not a peak torque measured at some other speed.
Changing either input changes the result proportionally. This is a power calculation at one operating point, not a reconstructed engine power curve.

table.caption: Constant entered torque at different speeds

sections.title: Work and time provide a separate route to power
paragraphs: A parallel force of 1,000 N acting through 20 m does 20,000 J of work. If that work takes 10 seconds, the average power is 2,000 W, or 2 kW. The force-through-distance mode does not include an unknown angle between force and motion.
Use the measured-work method to select independent force, distance and time units. A force perpendicular to displacement does not do the same work as the parallel-force model.

links.label: Select force, distance and time units

sections.title: Mechanical, metric and boiler horsepower are different units
paragraphs: A mechanical horsepower is approximately 745.699872 W; metric horsepower is 735.49875 W. The difference is small enough to overlook but large enough to affect a comparison. Boiler horsepower is a separate heat-rate convention and is not an engine-output synonym.
Select the exact definition in the converter. A bare “hp” value from another source should be interpreted using that source’s unit convention before comparison.

sections.title: Do not equate crank, wheel and rated input power
paragraphs: A measurement at the crankshaft and a measurement at the wheels describe different locations in a drivetrain. This calculator does not infer drivetrain losses, accessory loads, efficiency or correction standards.
For a constant-power energy estimate, multiply power by time in compatible units. For quarter-mile empirical estimates, use Engine Horsepower and read its separate assumptions.

horsepower-calculator.seoTitle: Horsepower Calculator: Torque, Work & Power Units

engine-horsepower-calculator.description: Calculate power from torque and RPM, or explore empirical quarter-mile horsepower estimates from elapsed time or measured trap speed.

faqs.question: Is the result crank horsepower or wheel horsepower?
faqs.answer: The torque calculation reflects where the torque was measured. The empirical quarter-mile estimate does not independently establish exact crank or wheel power.

faqs.question: Should reaction time be included?
faqs.answer: No. Use the run’s elapsed time excluding reaction time in the elapsed-time model.

faqs.question: Can I use average speed instead of trap speed?
faqs.answer: No. The trap-speed coefficient assumes the measured end-of-run speed, not distance divided by elapsed time.

faqs.question: Which vehicle weight should I enter?
faqs.answer: Use the total race weight corresponding to the run, including the relevant carried load, with the selected mass unit.

faqs.question: Why do the elapsed-time and trap-speed methods disagree?
faqs.answer: They approximate performance through different measurements and can respond differently to launch, traction, drag and conditions. Neither is a substitute for a direct power measurement.

sections.title: Separate measured torque power from a performance estimate
paragraphs: Torque & RPM uses a physical relationship at a measured operating point. Quarter-mile performance estimate uses historical empirical formulas based on total race weight and either elapsed time or trap speed. The two methods answer different questions.
Use torque from the same RPM as the speed input. For the quarter-mile method, include the total mass represented by the run rather than an unrelated advertised empty-vehicle weight.

sections.title: Check power at the same torque and RPM
paragraphs: An entered 300 lb-ft at 5,000 rpm corresponds to approximately 285.60 mechanical horsepower. Substituting the engine’s maximum torque from another RPM would not reproduce the power at 5,000 rpm.
A power curve can be built only from corresponding torque/speed pairs across the operating range. One pair gives one point; it does not identify the maximum power automatically.

links.label: Review mechanical power and unit conversions

sections.title: Work through the quarter-mile model’s two inputs
paragraphs: For a 3,200 lb race weight and elapsed time of 11.65 seconds, the implemented elapsed-time formula gives 3,200 × (5.825/11.65)³ = 400 hp. The trap-speed formula with 117 mph gives 3,200 × (117/234)³ = 400 hp.
These deliberately chosen numbers demonstrate the two formulas. They do not establish that every 400 hp vehicle will produce either track result.

table.caption: Two illustrative empirical inputs at the same race weight

sections.title: Use elapsed time and trap speed as distinct measurements
paragraphs: Elapsed time in this model excludes reaction time. Trap speed is the reported speed near the end of the run, not the average speed calculated by dividing a quarter mile by total elapsed time. Substituting one for the other changes the meaning of the equation.
Traction, launch, aerodynamic drag, gearing and conditions can affect a real run. The empirical estimate does not isolate each of these effects or certify exact wheel or crankshaft power.

sections.title: Understand the model’s sensitivity before comparing vehicles
paragraphs: Both quarter-mile formulas use a cube: the time estimate varies with the inverse cube of elapsed time, while the speed estimate varies with the cube of trap speed. A small measurement change can therefore produce a larger percentage change in estimated horsepower.

Compare runs using consistent weight and timing conventions. Treat the result as an approximate performance-based estimate, and use appropriate measurements when an exact engine-output figure is required.

engine-horsepower-calculator.seoTitle: Engine Horsepower Calculator: Torque & Quarter Mile

tire-size-calculator.description: Compare nominal tire dimensions and speedometer effects, or estimate the aspect ratio needed for a different rim at the same diameter.

faqs.question: Is the aspect ratio a measurement in millimeters?
faqs.answer: No. It is sidewall height as a percentage of nominal tire width.

faqs.question: Will a larger tire make the speedometer read lower?
faqs.answer: Relative to an unchanged original calibration, a larger rolling circumference produces a higher actual speed for the same indicated speed. This tool estimates that using nominal diameter.

faqs.question: Does equal diameter guarantee fit?
faqs.answer: No. Width, rim compatibility, clearance, load and speed ratings, and vehicle requirements still need checking.

faqs.question: Why is the target aspect ratio not available in shops?
faqs.answer: The calculation solves a continuous equation; manufactured sizes come in selected combinations.

faqs.question: Can I use either mph or km/h for indicated speed?
faqs.answer: Yes. Enter the speed number and interpret the modeled result in the same speed unit.

sections.title: Read a tire size before comparing alternatives
paragraphs: In 205/55R16, 205 is nominal section width in millimeters, 55 is sidewall height as a percentage of that width, R identifies radial construction, and 16 is rim diameter in inches. The 55 is not a sidewall measurement in millimeters.

Compare two written sizes, inspect one tire’s nominal dimensions, or solve for the aspect ratio that would preserve diameter on another rim. An exact calculated aspect ratio need not be a commercially available size.

sections.title: Worked example: 205/55R16 versus 225/45R17
paragraphs: The first sidewall is 205 × 0.55 = 112.75 mm. Its diameter is 16 × 25.4 + 2 × 112.75 = 631.9 mm. The second size has a 101.25 mm sidewall and a 634.3 mm diameter.
The new nominal diameter is about 0.38% larger. At an indicated 60 speed units, the diameter-ratio model gives about 60.23 in those same units, assuming the original calibration was exact.

table.caption: Nominal dimensions from the size code

sections.title: Understand speedometer and circumference effects
paragraphs: Circumference is π × diameter, so the circumference ratio equals the diameter ratio. A larger circumference travels farther per wheel revolution. The model therefore increases road speed relative to the original indication.
Real rolling circumference depends on the tire model, load, inflation, wear and construction. Nominal arithmetic cannot establish the exact speedometer or odometer error.

sections.title: Check fit separately from matching diameter
paragraphs: Matching diameter does not establish rim-width compatibility, clearance, load capacity, speed rating or manufacturer approval. Compare the vehicle requirements and the tire maker’s specifications for the particular product. There is no universal percentage difference that makes every replacement suitable.

tire-size-calculator.seoTitle: Tire Size Calculator: Dimensions & Speed Comparison

square-footage-calculator.description: Calculate square footage for floors, rooms and other shapes. Enter mixed units, set a quantity and estimate material cost from a price per square foot.

faqs.question: How do I calculate square footage?
faqs.answer: Multiply length by width in feet for a rectangle. Use a matching shape formula for nonrectangular areas and keep all pieces in the same area unit.

faqs.question: How do I enter feet and inches?
faqs.answer: Convert to decimal feet or total inches in a mode supporting the selected unit. Ten feet six inches is 10.5 ft or 126 in.

faqs.question: Can I calculate an L-shaped room?
faqs.answer: Split it into nonoverlapping rectangles and add their areas, or subtract a rectangular cutout from the enclosing rectangle.

faqs.question: Does square footage include flooring waste?
faqs.answer: The geometric area does not itself include cutting or purchasing allowances. Apply those separately in the relevant material calculator.

faqs.question: Is a square foot the same as a linear foot?
faqs.answer: No. Square feet measure area; linear feet measure length. A width is needed to connect them.

faqs.question: Can I use this for an official property area?
faqs.answer: The arithmetic can support your measurement, but the applicable reporting standard determines which boundaries and spaces count.

sections.title: Breaking a floor plan into measurable shapes
paragraphs: For an irregular floor plan, divide the area into shapes supported by the calculator and avoid counting overlaps twice. Check whether measurements refer to the interior area or a different boundary. The mixed-unit and cost modes help convert dimensions and apply an entered area price. Material quantities can still require allowances beyond the geometric floor area.

sections.title: Mixed units and irregular-room measurements
paragraphs: A rectangular section 3 ft long and 24 in wide has width 2 ft and area 6 ft². At a price of 2.50 per square foot, the area cost is 15 in the selected currency. Choose each dimension’s actual unit in the mixed-unit mode, and select the unit used by the material price separately.

For an L-shaped room, divide it into nonoverlapping rectangles, calculate each area using the same area unit, and add them. Subtract openings or cutouts instead of counting them twice. Enter feet and inches as decimal feet or as total inches: 10 ft 6 in is 10.5 ft or 126 in, not 10.6 ft.

sections.title: Worked L-shaped floor plan without double-counting
paragraphs: Divide an L-shaped room into a 12 ft × 10 ft rectangle and a separate 6 ft × 4 ft rectangle that does not overlap it. Their areas are 120 and 24 ft², for a combined 144 ft². If the plan instead uses a 12 ft × 14 ft outer rectangle with a 6 ft × 4 ft cutout, subtract 24 from 168 to obtain the same 144 ft².
Keep a sketch showing which boundaries belong to each section. Adding two rectangles that overlap at a corner counts the shared floor twice.

table.caption: Two ways to account for the same L-shaped area

sections.title: Use area pricing rather than a linear-foot price
paragraphs: At an illustrative 2.50 per square foot, 144 ft² has an area-based cost of 360. If the quoted price is per square meter, select that price unit in the mixed-unit mode; do not multiply it directly by a square-foot total.

A linear-foot price cannot be converted into an area price without a width or another stated product convention. Likewise, room area alone does not calculate perimeter trim, labor, waste or package rounding.

links.label: Choose the area unit used by the price

sections.title: Match the measured boundary to the purpose
paragraphs: Interior usable floor area, external building footprint and an area reported under a listing or appraisal standard can differ. This calculator evaluates the geometry you enter; it does not determine which boundary a reporting standard requires.

For circular sections use diameter when the field asks for diameter. Entering a radius in that field makes the calculated area one quarter of the intended area. Use the Area Calculator for further shape-specific formulas and examples.

links.label: Review shape diagrams and area formulas

square-footage-calculator.seoTitle: Square Footage Calculator: Area, Quantity & Cost

concrete-calculator.description: Estimate concrete for slabs, columns, tubes, solid stairs or curb-and-gutter sections, with mixed units, allowance and volume-based pricing.

faqs.question: Why must slab thickness be converted from inches?
faqs.answer: Length and width in feet require thickness in feet before multiplication. Divide inches by 12 to obtain cubic feet, then divide by 27 for cubic yards.

faqs.question: Does the answer already include extra material?
faqs.answer: Read the selected mode and allowance field. Mixed-unit mode shows net and ordered quantities separately.

faqs.question: How much extra concrete should I add?
faqs.answer: The percentage is an input, not a universal recommendation. Use the project’s tolerances, site conditions and supplier’s ordering guidance.

faqs.question: Can I calculate a hollow round column?
faqs.answer: Yes. Use the tube geometry with both outer and inner diameters and the relevant height.

faqs.question: Does the stair estimate include empty space beneath the stairs?
faqs.answer: It models a solid block to ground, including the stated platform. It is not a suspended-stair slab model.

faqs.question: Can I convert volume into bags by dividing by bag weight?
faqs.answer: No. Use the product’s mixed-volume yield per bag. Weight alone does not specify that yield.

sections.title: Separating concrete volume from an order quantity
paragraphs: Select the shape that matches the slab, column, footing, or stairs, and check each thickness and depth unit carefully. The geometric volume describes the idealized form. Use the supported quantity and cost inputs to explore an allowance or price, while keeping those assumptions explicit. Site irregularities and supplier ordering increments can make the delivered amount differ from the geometric estimate.

sections.title: Slab volume example: feet, inches, and cubic yards
paragraphs: For a slab 20 ft long, 10 ft wide, and 4 in thick, convert thickness to feet first: 4 ÷ 12 = 1/3 ft. Net volume is 20 × 10 × 1/3 = 66.67 ft³, or 66.67 ÷ 27 ≈ 2.47 yd³. An entered 10% extra allowance raises the modeled quantity to about 2.72 yd³; that percentage is an example assumption, not a universal ordering recommendation.

Use the mixed-unit mode when individual dimensions use different units, and check whether pricing applies to net volume or volume including the allowance. Enter the overall diameter for a round column, not its radius. A hollow column requires both outer and inner diameters.

sections.title: Compare net volume, allowance and quantity explicitly
paragraphs: For the 20 ft × 10 ft × 4 in slab example, net volume is 200/81 ≈ 2.4691 yd³. An entered 10% allowance multiplies it by 1.10, producing approximately 2.7160 yd³. Two identical slabs double both quantities; do not also double a dimension unless the geometry itself is twice as large.

table.caption: Same slab under chosen ordering assumptions

links.label: Set quantity, allowance and the price basis

sections.title: Use the actual cross-section for columns, tubes and stairs
paragraphs: A round column uses π times radius squared times height. A hollow tube subtracts the inner circular area before multiplying by height; its inner diameter must be smaller than the outer diameter. A solid-stair calculation assumes material extends to the ground under the steps.

The stair mode includes the top platform at full height. It does not describe a thin suspended stair slab or a structure with voids unless those are modeled separately. For a curb, keep exposed gutter width separate from curb width as the field labels specify.

sections.title: Convert volume into product quantities using stated yield
paragraphs: Bag mass is not the same as the volume of mixed concrete it produces. Use the manufacturer’s stated yield for the particular mix when translating a volume into bags, and round the final bag count up. Product yields and uneven substrate can change the practical order.
The calculator does not select concrete strength, reinforcement, subbase or structural dimensions. Keep those design decisions separate from the volume and cost arithmetic.

links.label: QUIKRETE product coverage and yield calculations

mulch-calculator.description: Estimate mulch volume and cost from bed dimensions or a known area, with depth and editable bulk-density assumptions.

faqs.question: How do I calculate mulch in cubic yards?
faqs.answer: Multiply area in square feet by depth in inches, then divide by 12 and by 27.

faqs.question: How many 2 ft³ bags cover 200 ft² at 3 inches?
faqs.answer: The geometric volume is 50 ft³, so 25 such bags cover that modeled volume before any allowance.

faqs.question: Should each bed be rounded to bags separately?
faqs.answer: Combine volumes first if the same product can be shared between beds. Separate rounding can increase the total unnecessarily.

faqs.question: Is the displayed depth a planting recommendation?
faqs.answer: No. It is an input assumption. Choose a suitable depth for the planting, material and site using relevant guidance.

faqs.question: Why does the weight change when density changes?
faqs.answer: Mass is volume times density. Moisture and compaction can change bulk density without changing your measured bed dimensions.

faqs.question: Can I enter a known area instead of length and width?
faqs.answer: Yes. Use Known area or the appropriate purchasing input and enter the area unit explicitly.

sections.title: Turning bed area and depth into mulch volume
paragraphs: Mulch volume depends on both the bed area and the intended layer depth. A common mistake is to mix a depth in inches with area measurements in feet without conversion. Use the bag and cost mode to connect volume with the package size being purchased. The estimate assumes the entered bed dimensions and layer depth, which can differ from settled material on site.

sections.title: From bed measurements to cubic yards or bags
paragraphs: A 20 ft × 10 ft bed at a uniform 3 in depth covers 200 ft² and needs 200 × 3 ÷ 12 = 50 ft³, equivalent to about 1.85 yd³. If each bag supplies 2 ft³, the same net volume is 25 bags before any entered allowance. Use the purchasing mode to combine nonoverlapping beds and round the combined bag count.

Depth must use the unit shown beside its input. Enter 3 inches as 3 with inches selected, rather than entering 3 feet. Weight additionally depends on your supplied bulk density; changing density changes the weight estimate without changing the bed volume.

sections.title: See how an entered depth changes the material quantity
paragraphs: For a 200 ft² bed, each inch of depth adds 200/12 ≈ 16.67 ft³. A two-inch layer therefore needs half as much geometric volume as a four-inch layer. The depth in this comparison is a chosen input, not a recommendation for every planting or mulch product.

table.caption: Volume and two-cubic-foot bags for a 200 ft² bed, before allowance

sections.title: Combine beds before rounding the bag count
paragraphs: If two separate beds require 1.2 bags each, buying for them separately rounds to 2 + 2 = 4 bags. Combining their material requirement gives 2.4 bags and rounds to 3 when the same product can be shared. Purchasing mode applies rounding after combining the entered beds.
Select the actual bag volume and price basis. A price per bag, cubic yard or unit of mass must match the selected unit; the same number entered under a different basis changes the estimate.

links.label: Combine beds and compare bag or bulk costs

sections.title: Separate geometric depth from settlement and delivery weight
paragraphs: Uniform area times depth is an idealized volume. Existing mulch, uneven ground, settlement and the material’s moisture can affect the delivered or retained layer. Estimate separate sections when depths differ rather than using one depth without considering its area weighting.
Weight requires a matching bulk-density assumption. The volume calculation can remain unchanged while a wetter or more compacted material produces a different mass estimate.

mulch-calculator.seoTitle: Mulch Calculator: Bed Volume, Bags & Material Cost

gravel-calculator.description: Estimate gravel volume, weight and cost for rectangular or circular beds, including bag counts from entered density and bag weight.

faqs.question: Does gravel weight follow directly from area?
faqs.answer: No. Area and depth give volume, then bulk density converts that volume into mass.

faqs.question: How many pounds are in a cubic yard of gravel?
faqs.answer: It depends on the product and its condition. Enter the supplier’s bulk density rather than assuming one universal value.

faqs.question: Is a ton the same as a tonne?
faqs.answer: No. A US short ton is 2,000 lb, while a tonne is 1,000 kg. Select the unit matching the quote.

faqs.question: Does the calculator apply compaction automatically?
faqs.answer: No. The chosen geometry and any explicit allowance define the modeled quantity. Check the material’s placed and delivered states separately.

faqs.question: Can I calculate a round bed?
faqs.answer: Yes. Use the circular option with diameter and depth, keeping the diameter distinct from radius.

faqs.question: Why is the bag cost higher than exact-volume cost?
faqs.answer: Bag purchasing rounds up to complete bags. The cost then applies to the rounded purchase quantity.

sections.title: Using a material density for gravel estimates
paragraphs: A gravel volume estimate comes from the bed shape and depth, while a mass estimate also depends on the entered material density. Keep these quantities separate when comparing a supplier's price by volume with a price by weight. Bag sizes and cost assumptions should match the product being considered. Compaction and irregular ground can change the amount needed in practice.

sections.title: Circular-bed example with whole-bag ordering
paragraphs: A circular bed with a 10 ft diameter and a 3 in depth has radius 5 ft and volume π × 5² × 0.25 ≈ 19.63 ft³, or 0.73 yd³. With an illustrative bulk density of 2,800 lb/yd³, the modeled weight is about 2,036.22 lb. Dividing by 50 lb per bag and rounding up gives 41 bags; at 5 per bag, the cost is 205 in the selected currency.

The density and bag size in this example are inputs, not specifications for every gravel product. Use your supplier’s stated material information, and keep the quantity and price basis consistent when comparing bulk volume, bulk weight, and bags.

sections.title: Connect bed volume with a chosen bulk density
paragraphs: A 10 ft × 10 ft rectangular bed at 3 inches depth contains 25 ft³, or approximately 0.9259 yd³. With an illustrative density of 2,800 lb/yd³, the estimated mass is 2,592.59 lb. That is about 1.2963 US short tons, using 2,000 lb per short ton.
The density is part of the estimate. Use the supplier’s value for the particular material and state rather than treating this example as a universal gravel specification.

table.caption: One rectangular-bed example before allowance

sections.title: Compare supplier units before comparing prices
paragraphs: A quotation per cubic yard and a quotation per ton cannot be compared directly without a density assumption. A tonne, a US short ton and a long ton also have different masses. Purchasing mode lets you select the relevant volume, mass and bag units.
Round bag counts after combining compatible beds. Whole-bag purchasing can produce excess material beyond the exact calculated mass or volume, and the bag-price total follows the rounded count.

sections.title: Account for the state represented by the volume
paragraphs: Loose, placed and compacted material may occupy different volumes. The geometric bed calculation does not predict a compaction factor automatically. Keep any entered allowance explicit and check whether the supplied density describes loose or compacted material.
For an uneven bed, split it into sections with representative depths. A single maximum depth applied to the whole area can substantially overstate the material needed.

gravel-calculator.seoTitle: Gravel Calculator: Volume, Weight, Bags & Cost

tile-calculator.description: Estimate tile quantities, boxes and cost using area or layout assumptions, with grout gaps and an allowance for cuts and waste.

faqs.question: Does an area estimate include edge cuts?
faqs.answer: It models coverage and the entered allowance. It does not optimize cut reuse or every laying pattern.

faqs.question: Why do the grid and area estimates differ?
faqs.answer: Grid mode rounds each direction to whole tile positions; area mode estimates coverage from the repeating module.

faqs.question: How do I calculate boxes?
faqs.answer: Divide the required tile count by tiles per box and round up. For 132 tiles in boxes of eight, buy 17 boxes under that example.

faqs.question: Does grout spacing affect the estimate?
faqs.answer: Yes in the procurement model. It changes the tile-and-joint module or the rectangular grid spacing.

faqs.question: Is a 10% allowance always appropriate?
faqs.answer: No. It is an example input. Layout, cuts, breakage and product requirements determine the allowance for the actual project.

faqs.question: Does the cost include installation?
faqs.answer: Only the selected material price basis is calculated. Add labor and other project costs separately.

sections.title: Separating covered area from tile layout
paragraphs: An area-based tile estimate describes coverage, while the layout mode accounts for the entered tile dimensions and arrangement assumptions. Check whether gaps, waste, box quantities, and prices are included in the selected fields. Rounding to whole boxes can increase the purchase quantity above the exact coverage. Edge cuts and an unusual room outline can require a separate layout review.

sections.title: Tile count example and the effect of box rounding
paragraphs: A 12 ft × 10 ft room covers 120 ft². A 12 in × 12 in tile covers 1 ft², so the basic area estimate needs 120 tiles before allowance. With an entered 10% allowance, the result is 132 tiles; at 3 per tile, the material cost is 396 in the selected currency.

The procurement mode can account for grout joints and compare area-based counting with a rectangular grid. Buying by the box rounds up again after the tile estimate, so purchased tile area may exceed the modeled need. Actual patterns, edge cuts, breakage, and irregular rooms can change the order quantity.

sections.title: Work through a whole-box purchase
paragraphs: The 132-tile example requires 17 boxes when each box contains eight tiles: 132/8 = 16.5, rounded up. The purchase supplies 136 tiles, four more than the allowance-adjusted tile requirement. At 24 per box, the modeled box cost is 408.
The extra four tiles come from packaging, separately from the entered 10% allowance. Keep those sources of surplus distinct when comparing quantities.

table.caption: Coverage, allowance and packaging are separate stages

sections.title: Choose an area estimate or a rectangular grid
paragraphs: Area estimation divides coverage by the effective tile-and-joint module. Rectangular grid counting rounds the number of tiles along each direction before multiplying. A room that needs partial edge tiles can therefore produce a different count from its area-only estimate.
A grid count does not optimize reuse of every offcut or model every laying pattern. Compare the model with the actual starting point, tile orientation and room boundary before ordering.

links.label: Choose the layout and purchase basis

sections.title: Use consistent dimensions for tiles and grout joints
paragraphs: Enter the actual tile size and the selected joint size in the unit shown. A 300 mm tile is 0.3 m, not 300 m; an incorrect unit can overwhelm every later allowance calculation. The same principle applies when entering a room area directly.
Labor, adhesive, grout quantity, substrate preparation and trim are separate costs unless explicitly represented by an input. The tile material total does not estimate an entire installed project.

tile-calculator.seoTitle: Tile Calculator: Tile Count, Boxes & Cost

roofing-calculator.description: Estimate roof surface from footprint, pitch or angle, then calculate allowance, area cost or whole material packages from coverage.

faqs.question: What is a roofing square?
faqs.answer: It is an area unit of 100 square feet. It is not a 100-foot-long side or a single bundle.

faqs.question: Does 6:12 mean six degrees?
faqs.answer: No. It is a rise-to-run ratio. Its angle from horizontal is about 26.565 degrees.

faqs.question: Should I use footprint or roof surface area?
faqs.answer: Use projected footprint for a pitch-adjusted calculation. Use measured sloped surface area directly in the material-packaging mode.

faqs.question: Do I add overhangs twice for both roof sides?
faqs.answer: For a rectangular footprint, a uniform overhang extends both ends of each dimension. Do not add it again if the measured dimensions already include it.

faqs.question: How many bundles are in a square?
faqs.answer: That depends on the product’s installed coverage. Enter the actual packages-per-square or coverage-per-package value.

faqs.question: Can a single pitch calculate a complex roof?
faqs.answer: Only for sections that match that slope assumption. Measure separate slopes and shapes, then combine their surface areas.

sections.title: Distinguishing roof footprint from sloped area
paragraphs: A roof's horizontal footprint is different from the surface area on a slope. Choose a footprint-and-pitch mode when that is the information available, or the measured-area mode when the roof surface is already known. Check how overhangs and package coverage are entered. The estimate models the chosen geometry and does not assess structural condition or installation requirements.

sections.title: Pitch, projected area, and roofing squares
paragraphs: A 6:12 pitch rises 6 units for every 12 horizontal units. For a 40 ft × 30 ft horizontal footprint that already includes overhangs, the slope factor is √(1 + (6/12)²) ≈ 1.118. Modeled roof surface is 1,200 × 1.118 ≈ 1,341.64 ft². An entered 10% allowance gives about 1,475.80 ft², or 14.76 roofing squares of 100 ft² each.

That calculation assumes a consistent slope across the modeled roof. Calculate sections with different pitches separately. Package ordering starts with roof surface area and the product’s installed coverage, not the horizontal footprint; the calculator rounds packages up to whole units.

sections.title: Check pitch and angle as two descriptions of the same slope
paragraphs: A 6:12 rise-to-run ratio has tangent 6/12, so the angle is approximately 26.565°. It is not a six-degree roof. The slope factor is √(1 + (6/12)²), equivalently 1/cos(angle), when the angle is measured from horizontal.
Use projected horizontal dimensions in a footprint method. If you already measured the sloped surface, applying the slope factor again would overstate the area.

table.caption: Slope factors for illustrative rise-per-12 inputs

sections.title: Include overhangs once in the projected dimensions
paragraphs: For a 40 ft by 30 ft rectangle with a uniform 1 ft overhang on all four sides, the projected dimensions become 42 ft by 32 ft, giving 1,344 ft² before the slope factor. If the supplied plan dimensions already include those edges, do not add them again.
The area-angle mode accepts explicit rectangular overhangs or a known projected area. A known projected area should already include the relevant overhangs.

sections.title: Round packages from their installed coverage
paragraphs: For 1,500 ft² of measured roof surface, an entered 10% allowance produces 1,650 ft², or 16.5 roofing squares. If a product uses three packages per square, 49.5 rounds to 50 packages. At 40 per package, the material total is 2,000.
Use the product’s installed coverage rather than its unfolded dimensions. Complex sections, valleys, dormers and courses need a measured takeoff; one rectangular slope does not describe every roof.

roofing-calculator.seoTitle: Roofing Calculator: Roof Area, Pitch & Material Cost

stair-calculator.description: Explore straight-stair geometry, standard or flush mounting and headroom using finished-floor dimensions and explicit layout assumptions.

faqs.question: Why are there fewer treads than risers?
faqs.answer: The standard modeled layout uses the upper floor as the final landing, so N risers correspond to N−1 regular treads.

faqs.question: How is the number of risers selected?
faqs.answer: Basic mode divides total rise by the entered preferred maximum and rounds the count up, then redistributes the total rise evenly.

faqs.question: Does increasing riser count increase the stair length?
faqs.answer: With a fixed tread run and one-fewer-tread layout, more risers generally add tread positions and increase total horizontal run.

faqs.question: Should total rise include floor finishes?
faqs.answer: Use the finished-floor reference required by the layout model and account consistently for finish levels.

faqs.question: Does the calculator provide a stringer cutting plan?
faqs.answer: No. It models geometry, including selected mounting and headroom relationships, rather than a complete structural design.

faqs.question: Are the default dimensions legal building-code limits?
faqs.answer: No. They are example inputs. Verify the applicable requirements for the location and intended staircase separately.

sections.title: Checking stair geometry against the intended layout
paragraphs: Total rise, tread dimensions, and the number of risers work together to determine a stair layout. Review whether the upper floor acts as the final landing in the selected mode. Mounting and headroom inputs add geometric constraints but do not establish compliance with every building requirement. Verify the actual layout and applicable local rules before using an estimate for construction.

sections.title: Relating risers, treads, and total run
paragraphs: With a total rise of 108 in and a preferred maximum riser of 7.75 in, the basic mode rounds 108 ÷ 7.75 up to 14 risers. Each riser is then 108 ÷ 14 ≈ 7.71 in. The standard layout has 13 treads; a 10 in tread run gives 130 in of total horizontal run.

The preferred maximum and tread size are your assumptions, not a statement of local requirements. The layout mode distinguishes standard and flush mounting and uses finished-floor measurements. Its headroom model does not supply a structural stringer design or certify a staircase.

sections.title: Compare alternative riser counts before fixing the run
paragraphs: For a total rise of 108 inches, 14 risers give approximately 7.7143 inches each; 15 risers give 7.2 inches each. Under the stated one-fewer-tread layout, those choices produce 13 or 14 treads. With a 10-inch tread run, their total runs are 130 and 140 inches.
Changing the count therefore changes both vertical spacing and required horizontal space. The example values are geometry assumptions, not local construction limits.

table.caption: Riser count and footprint for a 108-inch rise

sections.title: Measure total rise between finished floor levels
paragraphs: Floor finishes and tread thickness affect the relationship between the rough structure and the walking surface. The layout mode uses finished-floor geometry and distinguishes standard from flush mounting. Use the diagram and field definitions consistently.
A total-rise measurement taken before floor finishes are accounted for can change the final first or last step. The calculator does not survey the site or choose construction tolerances.

sections.title: Read headroom as a geometric constraint
paragraphs: In the layout model, headroom depends on the floor opening, mounting offset, riser-to-run ratio and floor thickness. For standard mounting with a 7-inch rise, 10-inch run, 130-inch opening and 6-inch floor thickness, the model gives 130 × 7/10 − 6 = 85 inches.
Flush mounting uses a different offset, so copying a standard-mount result into a flush layout changes the geometry. This model is not a structural stringer cutting plan or a compliance certificate.

stair-calculator.seoTitle: Stair Calculator: Rise, Run, Treads & Headroom

btu-calculator.description: Estimate room cooling needs, or compare steady heating loss and cooling heat gains using US county temperatures and assembly references.

faqs.question: Is BTU the same as BTU/h?
faqs.answer: No. BTU measures energy; BTU/h measures the rate of heat transfer.

faqs.question: Does the room table account for high ceilings?
faqs.answer: Its reference assumes an 8-foot ceiling. The calculator does not add an unsupported ceiling multiplier.

faqs.question: What is the difference between U and UA?
faqs.answer: U is heat transfer per unit area per temperature difference. UA includes the exposed area, summed over the relevant surfaces.

faqs.question: Can I enter a blower-door ACH50 value as operating air changes?
faqs.answer: No. The pressure-test result describes different conditions and needs an appropriate conversion or assessment before use.

faqs.question: Does the heat-loss result specify an air conditioner size?
faqs.answer: No. Steady heating loss, cooling gains and equipment selection are different calculations. Review the mode’s assumptions and obtain a complete design where needed.

sections.title: Choose cooling capacity, heat energy or heat loss
paragraphs: Room cooling estimates BTU per hour from a floor-area reference and its listed adjustments. Heat-energy mode calculates the energy to change a mass’s temperature. The building and envelope modes estimate steady heat transfer from geometry, thermal properties and temperature difference.
BTU is energy; BTU/h is a rate. A cooling-capacity number does not by itself tell you electricity consumption, because equipment efficiency and operating time also matter.

sections.title: Worked room-cooling example
paragraphs: For a 300 ft² room with typical sun, two occupants and no kitchen, the room table returns a 7,000 BTU/h baseline. Choosing very sunny conditions increases that baseline by 10%, to 7,700 BTU/h. A third occupant adds another 600 BTU/h under this reference method.
The table assumes an 8-foot ceiling. Shared range endpoints use the lower capacity row here. The method does not invent an extra height multiplier or account for every building feature.

sections.title: Heat-energy example: warming a known mass
paragraphs: In heat-energy mode, a 2 kg mass with specific heat 1,000 J/(kg·K) and a 10 °C increase requires Q = 2 × 1,000 × 10 = 20,000 J. This assumes constant specific heat and no phase change. A 10 °C temperature difference is 10 K, while a 10 °F difference is only about 5.56 K.

When using volume and density, the tool first calculates mass. Heating air, water and another material requires different density and specific-heat inputs. Use properties appropriate to the modeled substance and conditions.

sections.title: Understand the envelope heat-loss inputs
paragraphs: UA combines exposed surface area with thermal transmittance. It is not a U-value for one square meter. Enter total UA when already known, or calculate it from individual exposed surfaces in component mode. Operating air changes per hour describes ventilation and infiltration during use; a pressure-test ACH50 number is not directly interchangeable.

A 50 m³ space, UA of 100 W/K, 0.5 air changes per hour, air heat capacity of 1,207 J/(m³·K), and a 20 °C inside–outside difference gives about 2,167.64 W of modeled sensible heating loss. Of this, 2,000 W is envelope transmission and about 167.64 W is air exchange.

sections.title: Interpret the result before choosing equipment
paragraphs: A floor-area reference and a steady envelope calculation answer different questions. They need not return the same capacity. The cooling design mode reports a heat-gain subtotal from the entered terms; it is not a time-dependent design peak.

The advanced modes do not perform a complete Manual J calculation. Solar timing, moisture loads, ducts, warm-up, equipment performance and local design requirements can matter. Their assumptions and reference dates remain visible in the calculator.

btu-calculator.seoTitle: BTU Calculator: Room Cooling & Heat Transfer

electricity-calculator.description: Estimate appliance energy use and cost from wattage, operating time and tariff, with an optional average-load factor.

faqs.question: What is the difference between kW and kWh?
faqs.answer: kW is power; kWh is energy. Multiply kW by operating hours to obtain kWh.

faqs.question: Should I enter cents or whole currency units?
faqs.answer: Use currency units per kWh, such as 0.16 for 16 cents. The tool multiplies the number directly.

faqs.question: How do I model a device that cycles on and off?
faqs.answer: Use an average load factor over the full observation period, or full-power hours without a second duty-cycle reduction.

faqs.question: Does this calculate my whole electricity bill?
faqs.answer: No. It estimates the entered device’s energy charge at one rate and excludes other billing components.

faqs.question: Can I compare two appliances?
faqs.answer: Calculate each using comparable hours and rates. Use measured average input power where available rather than assuming both run at their nameplate maximum.

sections.title: Estimate appliance energy use and its variable cost
paragraphs: Enter power in watts, hours used per day, number of days and the price per kilowatt-hour. For equipment that does not draw its full rated power continuously, use load-factor mode with total operating hours and an estimated average percentage of rated power.
A kilowatt is a rate of energy use; a kilowatt-hour is an amount of energy. A 1 kW appliance running for one hour uses 1 kWh. Do not enter the monthly kWh from a bill into the watts field.

sections.title: Worked example: a 1,000 W appliance
paragraphs: At 4 hours per day for 30 days, energy is 1,000 / 1,000 × 4 × 30 = 120 kWh. At 0.16 per kWh the energy charge is 19.20.

table.caption: Same operating time and tariff, different average power

sections.title: Use load factor without counting downtime twice
paragraphs: For a 1,000 W device available for 120 hours at an estimated 50% average load, load-factor mode gives 60 kWh and 9.60 at the same rate. If your 120 hours already represents only full-power running time, a further duty-cycle reduction would undercount consumption.

Rated input power can differ from measured average power. Refrigeration, heating and variable-speed devices change their draw during operation. Use a suitable meter or documented consumption figure when a more reliable estimate is needed.

sections.title: Why this result may differ from your utility bill
paragraphs: The output covers energy multiplied by one unit price. Fixed account fees, demand charges, time-of-use prices, taxes and tiered rates are not automatically modeled. For multiple prices, calculate each portion separately and add the charges.
Treat the currency consistently. An entered rate of 0.16 means 0.16 currency units per kWh; entering 16 when you mean 16 cents makes the estimated charge 100 times too large.

electricity-calculator.seoTitle: Electricity Cost Calculator: Watts, kWh & Usage

ohms-law-calculator.description: Solve voltage, current, resistance and power from two supported known quantities in a DC or purely resistive model.

faqs.question: How many values do I need?
faqs.answer: Choose one of the six supported pairs and enter two positive known quantities.

faqs.question: Can I enter milliamps and kilohms?
faqs.answer: Yes. Use measurement-units mode and choose the units for both inputs.

faqs.question: Is the result valid for every electrical component?
faqs.answer: No. The equations describe an ideal resistive load, not all nonlinear or reactive components.

faqs.question: Does a 2 A power supply force 2 A through a resistor?
faqs.answer: No. Its rating describes capacity. The actual current depends on the circuit and operating voltage.

faqs.question: Is the computed power a recommended resistor wattage?
faqs.answer: No. It is modeled dissipation. Component selection also requires suitable ratings and operating-temperature considerations.

sections.title: Solve voltage, current, resistance and power from two values
paragraphs: Choose the pair you know, then enter those two quantities in the displayed order. The base mode uses volts, amperes, ohms and watts. The measurement-units mode lets you choose prefixes for each input and output. All pairs describe the same ideal resistive load.
Voltage is measured across the load; current flows through it. Do not combine a supply’s maximum current rating with a load voltage as if that rating were the actual current draw.

sections.title: Worked example: 12 V across a 6 Ω resistor
paragraphs: Select voltage and resistance, then enter 12 V and 6 Ω. Current is I = V/R = 2 A. Power is P = VI = 24 W. This is the power dissipated by the modeled resistor, not a recommended component rating.

table.caption: Equivalent known pairs for this same operating point

sections.title: Convert prefixes before comparing results
paragraphs: A milliampere is 0.001 A and a kilohm is 1,000 Ω. For example, 5 V across 1 kΩ gives 5 mA and 0.025 W, or 25 mW. Entering 1 as ohms instead of kilohms would produce a very different current.
The formula family is V = IR, P = VI, P = I²R and P = V²/R. Two positive quantities determine the remaining two in this model.

sections.title: Recognize where the resistor model stops
paragraphs: The calculation assumes a resistive relationship at the operating point. It does not model diode behavior, a motor’s changing load, capacitor transients or AC phase relationships. Real power in a general AC circuit is not simply RMS voltage multiplied by RMS current without considering power factor.
Power dissipation alone does not select a safe component or wire. Temperature, component ratings and the complete circuit still matter.

ohms-law-calculator.seoTitle: Ohm’s Law Calculator: Voltage, Current & Resistance

resistor-calculator.description: Find series or parallel resistance, decode supported color bands, or estimate conductor resistance from dimensions and conductivity.

faqs.question: Why is parallel resistance smaller than each resistor?
faqs.answer: Each added branch offers another current path. Conductances add, so the equivalent resistance decreases for positive finite resistances.

faqs.question: What does gold mean on a four-band resistor?
faqs.answer: In the tolerance position it means ±5%; in a multiplier position gold has a different role. Interpret it using the selected band layout.

faqs.question: Does tolerance tell me the exact resistance?
faqs.answer: No. It gives a range around the nominal value. Measure the component appropriately to determine its actual resistance.

faqs.question: Can I calculate a mixed series-parallel circuit?
faqs.answer: Reduce the network in stages where its connections permit, then use each equivalent value in the next stage.

faqs.question: Which wire diameter should I enter?
faqs.answer: The conducting material’s diameter. Insulation does not contribute to the electrical cross-sectional area in this model.

sections.title: Choose a resistor calculation
paragraphs: Use the network mode for a list of resistances in series or parallel. Use color bands to decode a resistor’s nominal value and tolerance. The conductor mode instead calculates resistance from length, diameter and conductivity. These inputs describe different physical problems.

sections.title: Worked example: series versus parallel
paragraphs: Two resistors of 100 Ω and 200 Ω have a series equivalent of 300 Ω. In parallel, 1/R = 1/100 + 1/200, so R is approximately 66.67 Ω. A parallel equivalent of positive resistors is less than the smallest individual resistance.

table.caption: Example two-resistor networks

sections.title: Read significant digits, multiplier and tolerance
paragraphs: For a four-band yellow–violet–red–gold resistor, yellow and violet give 47, red multiplies by 100, and gold indicates ±5%. The nominal value is 4,700 Ω, with a tolerance interval of 4,465–4,935 Ω. Tolerance describes the allowed interval, not a measured value.

Three-band mode uses two digits and no tolerance band; five- and six-band modes use three significant digits. In six-band mode, the extra band specifies a temperature-coefficient class. Count the bands before assigning their roles.

sections.title: Calculate the resistance of a conductor
paragraphs: The conductor model uses R = L/(σA), where σ is conductivity and A is the circular cross-section from the entered diameter. Use the metal conductor diameter rather than the cable’s outer insulation diameter.

At fixed material and length, doubling diameter makes area four times larger and resistance one quarter as large. Doubling length doubles resistance. Conductivity must be appropriate to the material and temperature.

sections.title: Check the circuit before using the equivalent value
paragraphs: The list mode assumes every listed component is in one series chain or across the same two nodes in parallel. A mixed network needs reduction in stages. Color codes and a nominal equivalent do not determine power ratings, fault behavior or actual measured resistance.

links.label: Calculate current and power for a resistive load

resistor-calculator.seoTitle: Resistor Calculator: Color Bands, Series & Parallel

voltage-drop-calculator.description: Estimate DC or simplified AC voltage drop from conductor data, or convert AWG and kcmil sizes to nominal wire geometry.

faqs.question: Should length include the return conductor?
faqs.answer: The length field is one-way. The applicable circuit factor already accounts for the return path or balanced three-phase geometry.

faqs.question: Why does a larger conductor reduce DC drop?
faqs.answer: At the same material, temperature and length, resistance varies inversely with cross-sectional area.

faqs.question: Can I enter resistance per kilometer?
faqs.answer: Yes in impedance mode. Select the matching coefficient unit; do not enter an Ω/km number as Ω/m.

faqs.question: Does the result tell me the correct wire size?
faqs.answer: It compares modeled voltage drop. Ampacity, protection, installation conditions and applicable rules must also be checked.

faqs.question: Is the NEC mode based on current local code?
faqs.answer: It is explicitly a 2017 reference-table calculation. It does not establish which edition or requirements apply to your installation.

sections.title: Choose a model that matches the circuit
paragraphs: The basic DC mode estimates loop resistance from material, temperature, conductor area and one-way length. The impedance mode accepts per-length resistance/reactance or an effective longitudinal coefficient for the selected circuit. Wire-gauge mode adds AWG and area conversions. The NEC reference mode uses a specifically dated table with stated conditions.
Use source voltage appropriate to the selected system. The balanced three-phase model reports line-to-line drop; it is not an unbalanced-network or motor-starting simulation.

sections.title: Worked DC example: a 12 V load on copper cable
paragraphs: For 10 A, 10 m one-way length, 2.5 mm² copper and 20 °C, the tool uses resistivity 0.017241 Ω·mm²/m. Loop resistance is 2 × 0.017241 × 10 / 2.5 = 0.137928 Ω. Voltage drop is 1.37928 V, or 11.494% of 12 V, leaving 10.62072 V in the model.
The factor of two accounts for outgoing and return conductors. Entering 20 m into the one-way field for that same circuit would double-count its length.

table.caption: Effect of conductor area with the other example inputs unchanged

sections.title: Keep per-length impedance units consistent
paragraphs: A value in Ω/km differs by a factor of 1,000 from the same number in Ω/m. Select the unit matching your source data. Resistance and reactance must refer to the same length basis and appropriate operating conditions.

For an entered DC resistance of 0.01 Ω/m, a one-way length of 30 m and current of 10 A, drop is 2 × 10 × 30 × 0.01 = 6 V. Parallel-conductor count assumes equal sharing in the modeled arrangement, not arbitrary additional wires.

sections.title: Use the dated reference table within its conditions
paragraphs: The 2017 NEC option is a reference calculation for the listed material, size and conduit under its stated 75 °C, 60 Hz and conductor-arrangement assumptions. It is not a lookup of today’s local electrical requirements. Nominal AWG geometry is also different from the outside diameter of an insulated cable.

sections.title: Voltage drop is only one part of conductor selection
paragraphs: A small calculated drop does not establish ampacity, protection, installation suitability or code compliance. Higher conductor temperature changes resistance, and connectors or other circuit elements may add losses. Use actual cable data and the applicable design requirements for an installation.

voltage-drop-calculator.seoTitle: Voltage Drop Calculator: DC, AC & Wire Sizes

wind-chill-calculator.description: Calculate National Weather Service wind chill for temperatures at or below 50°F and wind speeds above 3 mph.

faqs.question: Should I enter actual temperature or feels-like temperature?
faqs.answer: Enter actual air temperature. Wind chill is the output of combining it with wind speed.

faqs.question: Can I use Celsius and kilometers per hour?
faqs.answer: Yes. Select those units in measurement-units mode.

faqs.question: Why does the tool reject warm or calm conditions?
faqs.answer: The NWS equation used here is defined for temperatures at or below 50 °F and winds above 3 mph.

faqs.question: Can wind chill make water pipes colder than the air?
faqs.answer: Wind alone speeds cooling toward the air temperature; the wind-chill index is not the final temperature of an unheated pipe.

faqs.question: Does this tell me how long I can stay outside safely?
faqs.answer: No. It does not model clothing, wetness, personal factors or a safe duration of exposure.

sections.title: Calculate wind chill from air temperature and wind
paragraphs: Enter measured air temperature and wind speed, not an existing feels-like temperature. The basic mode uses °F and mph. The measurement-units mode converts Celsius, Fahrenheit or Kelvin and supported wind units before applying the same NWS equation.

The equation applies at or below 50 °F with wind above 3 mph. Converting the input units does not extend that domain. A rejected result outside it is not an indication that all outdoor conditions are safe.

sections.title: Worked example: 20 °F with a 10 mph wind
paragraphs: Using T = 20 and V = 10 in 35.74 + 0.6215T − 35.75V^0.16 + 0.4275TV^0.16 gives a wind chill of approximately 8.85 °F. The air itself is still 20 °F; the index represents the modeled cooling effect on exposed skin.

With the air temperature held at 20 °F, changing wind from 5 to 10 to 20 mph produces approximately 12.98, 8.85 and 4.24 °F respectively. This illustrates why the wind speed needs to match the conditions being evaluated.

sections.title: Distinguish wind chill from an object’s temperature
paragraphs: Wind accelerates heat loss toward the actual air temperature. It does not make an unheated object settle at the lower wind-chill number solely through that effect. Do not use wind chill as the air-temperature input for a building heat-loss calculation.

sections.title: Interpret the index within its assumptions
paragraphs: The NWS index is based on exposed-skin cooling and assumes no warming effect from sunshine. Clothing, wetness, activity, exposure duration and individual circumstances are not entered here. Use local forecasts and cold-weather guidance when planning exposure; this tool does not calculate a personal safe exposure time.

links.label: NWS explanation and limits of wind chill

wind-chill-calculator.seoTitle: Wind Chill Calculator: Air Temperature & Wind Speed

heat-index-calculator.description: Estimate NWS apparent heat from air temperature and humidity, or infer humidity from a supplied dew point.

faqs.question: Does heat index change the actual air temperature?
faqs.answer: No. It expresses a modeled apparent temperature from air temperature and humidity.

faqs.question: Does this include direct sunlight?
faqs.answer: No. The index assumes shade and light wind. Direct sunlight can increase heat stress.

faqs.question: Can I calculate it from dew point?
faqs.answer: Yes. Use the dew-point mode and enter its temperatures in °C.

faqs.question: Why can the result differ slightly from a weather chart?
faqs.answer: Charts round values, while this method evaluates the equations and applicable adjustments. Different input observations can also explain differences.

faqs.question: Is heat index the same as WBGT?
faqs.answer: No. WBGT uses additional environmental information and is not interchangeable with heat index.

sections.title: Choose humidity or dew point as your second input
paragraphs: The NWS mode takes air temperature in °F and relative humidity as a percentage. The dew-point mode takes air temperature and dew point in °C, estimates relative humidity, then applies the heat-index method. Dew point cannot exceed air temperature for the supported conditions.
Use observations from the same time and place. An afternoon temperature paired with a morning humidity reading may describe a combination that never occurred.

sections.title: Worked example: 90 °F and 70% humidity
paragraphs: The NWS calculation gives approximately 105.92 °F at 90 °F and 70% relative humidity. At the same temperature with 50% humidity, the result is about 94.60 °F. The thermometer has not changed; the modeled apparent heat has.
Enter 70 for 70%, not 0.70. Check whether a humidity observation is relative humidity: dew point is a temperature and belongs in the other mode.

sections.title: Why the calculator uses more than one equation
paragraphs: The method first evaluates the NWS simple estimate. It uses the Rothfusz regression when the screening result reaches the relevant threshold, with the specified low- or high-humidity adjustments where applicable. Applying the full regression blindly to every temperature can produce misleading values.
The dew-point pathway adds an approximation: relative humidity is inferred through the Magnus relationship before heat index is calculated. Slight differences from a chart can also reflect rounding.

sections.title: Heat index, shade and outdoor activity
paragraphs: Heat index assumes shade and light wind. Direct sunshine, exertion, clothing and other conditions affect actual heat stress. A number from this calculator is not a forecast, a diagnosis or permission to continue an activity.

Wet-bulb globe temperature and heat index are different measures. WBGT incorporates additional environmental factors and may be used in work or sport guidance; do not treat a heat-index value as a WBGT reading.

links.label: NWS comparison of heat assessment tools
Calculate dew point from temperature and humidity

dew-point-calculator.description: Estimate dew point, relative humidity or air temperature with the liquid-water Magnus approximation and explicit input ranges.

faqs.question: Can dew point exceed air temperature?
faqs.answer: Not for the nonsupersaturated conditions supported here. Check units and measurements if it appears to do so.

faqs.question: What does 100% relative humidity mean in this model?
faqs.answer: Air temperature and dew point are equal.

faqs.question: Why can the same humidity percentage feel different on different days?
faqs.answer: Relative humidity depends on temperature. The same percentage at a higher temperature can correspond to more water vapor and a higher dew point.

faqs.question: Is dew point the same as frost point?
faqs.answer: No. Saturation over liquid water and over ice use different relationships.

faqs.question: Can I find humidity from dew point?
faqs.answer: Yes. In inverse mode, select humidity and enter air temperature and dew point.

sections.title: Calculate dew point or solve the inverse relationship
