That is a total cash-flow comparison; it is not a declaration that every entered charge belongs in a legally disclosed APR. Fee classification and disclosure rules depend on the transaction and jurisdiction.

sections.title: Compare offers at the same usable borrowing amount
paragraphs: Two offers with the same note principal can provide different amounts of usable cash. Compare proceeds, repayment term, scheduled payments, fees and any separate insurance together. A lower monthly payment caused by a longer term may increase the total amount paid.

links.label: Include origination fees and monthly insurance

sections.title: Understanding the cash cost of a personal loan
paragraphs: The amount financed and the cash you receive can differ when a personal loan includes an origination fee or insurance. Use the fee and cash-cost mode to separate those amounts. Compare the payment with the total borrowing cost, and keep the repayment term the same when evaluating offers. The lender's fee treatment matters as much as the advertised rate.

personal-loan-calculator.seoTitle: Personal Loan Calculator: Payments, Fees & Total Cost

boat-loan-calculator.description: Estimate fixed monthly boat-loan payments, interest and payoff timing, including optional extra payments toward principal.

faqs.question: Does the payment include the cost of owning a boat?
faqs.answer: No. Storage, insurance, maintenance, fuel and registration are separate from the principal-and-interest loan estimate.

faqs.question: What changes if I make extra principal payments?
faqs.answer: The modeled balance falls faster, reducing later interest and shortening repayment. Contractual prepayment charges are not automatically included.

faqs.question: Can I calculate a boat price from a monthly budget?
faqs.answer: Yes. Select the reverse-price method and enter the payment budget, financing term, rate and applicable down-payment, trade and tax assumptions.

faqs.question: Where do maintenance and mooring fees go?
faqs.answer: They are separate operating costs. They are not part of principal and interest unless a specific cost is actually financed.

faqs.question: What if the trade-in loan exceeds its value?
faqs.answer: Enter the value and debt separately. The unpaid difference increases the amount that must be funded.

faqs.question: Does a longer boat loan save money?
faqs.answer: It can lower the installment while increasing total interest at the same rate. Compare total payments and the outstanding balance, not just the monthly amount.

sections.title: Separate the boat price from the amount financed
paragraphs: For a straightforward installment calculation, enter the financed balance after the down payment and any trade credit. The price-budget method can also include trade debt, rebates, taxes and fees. A boat’s purchase price is not automatically its loan principal, especially when an existing loan must be paid off.

sections.title: Worked boat-financing example
paragraphs: Financing 30,000 at an assumed 7% annual interest rate over ten years gives a monthly payment of about 348.33 and full-term interest of about 11,799.05 before separate fees. Set extra payment to zero to reproduce the base schedule. The example isolates financing; it does not include docking, storage, fuel, insurance or maintenance.

table.caption: Loan cash flow versus ongoing boat costs

sections.title: Account for a trade with debt attached
paragraphs: If a trade is valued at 8,000 and its payoff is 10,000, it brings 2,000 of negative equity before taxes and fees. Enter both figures in the price-budget method. Subtracting the trade value while forgetting its debt understates the new financing requirement.

sections.title: Use a payment budget without mistaking it for a price quote
paragraphs: The reverse-price method solves the largest modeled selling price consistent with your entered payment, term and tax treatment. It does not obtain a lender offer, value the boat or decide which taxes apply. Keep all ownership costs outside the financing payment when setting a household budget.

links.label: Solve for boat price from a payment budget
Check the rest of the household budget

sections.title: Setting a boat purchase budget
paragraphs: Start with either the boat price you are considering or the payment you can set aside each month. A down payment reduces the financed balance, but extending the term can make a more expensive boat appear affordable on a monthly basis. Check the resulting price and total interest together. Ongoing ownership expenses need a separate budget beyond the financing calculation.

boat-loan-calculator.seoTitle: Boat Loan Calculator: Payments, Interest & Price Budget

business-loan-calculator.description: Compare business-loan payment schedules and compounding frequencies, with optional extra principal and modeled upfront financing fees.

faqs.question: Can I compare monthly and less frequent business-loan payments?
faqs.answer: Yes. The frequency mode supports separate compounding and payment schedules, provided the term contains a whole number of payments.

faqs.question: Is the result a business-loan approval or legal APR disclosure?
faqs.answer: No. It models entered cash flows; underwriting, variable pricing, security requirements and jurisdiction-specific APR rules are outside its scope.

faqs.question: Can I use this for a revolving credit line?
faqs.answer: The term-loan schedule assumes a starting balance and regular payments. Changing draws and available credit require a separate revolving-balance model.

faqs.question: Does the calculated payment include tax savings?
faqs.answer: No. It calculates financing cash flows. Business tax treatment depends on the transaction and applicable rules.

faqs.question: Why enter compounding and payment frequency separately?
faqs.answer: Interest may be quoted with one compounding convention while payments occur at another interval. The frequency method converts between them.

faqs.question: Is this a lender approval or affordability result?
faqs.answer: No. The payment does not assess trading history, collateral, coverage ratios, guarantees or lender underwriting.

sections.title: Match debt service to the business cash-flow schedule
paragraphs: A term loan has a specified repayment schedule. Enter its principal, rate and term to estimate installments. For contracts paid weekly, quarterly or on another regular interval, use the frequency method and enter compounding separately. A revolving line with changing draws does not behave like a fully funded fixed-balance term loan.

sections.title: Worked equipment-loan example
paragraphs: A 50,000 equipment loan at 6% for five years has a monthly installment of approximately 966.64. Twelve such installments require roughly 11,599.68 in annual debt service. Full-term interest is about 7,998.40 before fees. The equipment’s purchase price, tax deductions and resale value are separate from this repayment arithmetic.

table.caption: Five-year fixed-rate business-loan scenario

sections.title: Check cash received when a lender charges an upfront fee
paragraphs: In the frequency method, an upfront fee reduces net proceeds used to estimate the financing rate but does not lower the contractual principal repaid. A fee paid outside the loan also uses working capital at closing. Compare the funds available for the business project with the repayment obligation it creates.

sections.title: A payment result is not a debt-service-coverage assessment
paragraphs: The calculator does not forecast sales, margins or seasonality. Add the payment to a cash-flow forecast and check low-revenue months, existing obligations and timing of customer receipts. A business can show an annual profit while lacking cash on a particular payment date.

sections.title: Matching business loan payments to cash flow
paragraphs: Match the payment frequency to the schedule in the proposed business loan agreement. A monthly payment cannot be compared directly with a weekly payment without also considering how many payments occur. Review total repayment and the timing of installments alongside your expected business cash flow. The calculation models the entered loan terms; it does not forecast revenue available to make those payments.

business-loan-calculator.seoTitle: Business Loan Calculator: Payments, Fees & Interest

home-equity-loan-calculator.description: Estimate a home-equity loan payment and available borrowing capacity from property value, existing debt and a chosen combined LTV limit.

faqs.question: How is additional borrowing capacity estimated?
faqs.answer: Multiply home value by the maximum combined loan-to-value ratio, then subtract existing secured debt. The result cannot be less than zero.

faqs.question: Does available equity guarantee I can borrow that amount?
faqs.answer: No. The capacity model does not assess credit, income, property valuation or lender eligibility requirements.

faqs.question: Is home equity the same as borrowing capacity?
faqs.answer: No. Equity is home value minus secured debt. Borrowing capacity also applies the chosen combined loan-to-value limit.

faqs.question: Does the existing-debt input include only the first mortgage?
faqs.answer: Use the secured debt relevant to the lender’s combined-LTV assessment, including other applicable liens. The calculator cannot determine which obligations a lender includes.

faqs.question: Why is net cash lower than additional borrowing?
faqs.answer: The capacity method subtracts the closing fees you entered. Other costs or payoff requirements may reduce available cash further.

faqs.question: Can I estimate payments after finding capacity?
faqs.answer: Yes. Use the loan method with the amount you actually plan to borrow, the quoted rate and the repayment term.

sections.title: Answer borrowing capacity and repayment as separate questions
paragraphs: The capacity method estimates additional secured borrowing from a home value, existing debt and a chosen maximum combined loan-to-value ratio. The loan method estimates payments on the amount actually borrowed. A mathematical capacity is not a commitment that a lender will offer that amount.

sections.title: Worked home-equity capacity example
paragraphs: For a home worth 400,000, existing secured debt of 250,000 and an assumed combined LTV cap of 80%, total modeled secured debt can be 320,000. Subtract the existing 250,000 to obtain 70,000 of additional capacity. If closing fees of 2,000 are paid from those funds, net cash is 68,000.

table.caption: From property value to potential cash

sections.title: Do not confuse total equity with usable borrowing
paragraphs: The example has 150,000 of value above existing debt, but the assumed LTV cap leaves 80,000 of value unborrowed. Changing the property valuation or cap can materially change capacity. Include other debt secured on the property when constructing the existing-debt input.

sections.title: Compare a fixed home-equity loan with a HELOC
paragraphs: An amortizing loan normally models a funded amount repaid over a term. The HELOC calculator separates an interest-only draw period from later repayment under its stated constant-balance assumptions. Compare the payment structure and costs instead of treating both products as identical.

sections.title: Separating available equity from the loan payment
paragraphs: Available home equity and an affordable home-equity loan are different questions. The equity worksheet uses the property value, existing debt, and entered lending limit to estimate capacity. The payment mode then models repayment on a chosen amount. A change in the property-value estimate can change available equity without changing your income or the cash available for monthly payments.

home-equity-loan-calculator.seoTitle: Home Equity Loan Calculator: Payments & Borrowing Limit

payment-calculator.description: Find the payment for a fixed-rate loan or estimate payoff time from a monthly payment amount you choose.

faqs.question: Should I enter a repayment term or a payment amount?
faqs.answer: Use Loan & schedule when the term is known. Use Fixed-payment payoff when you want to test a chosen monthly payment.

faqs.question: Why must the chosen payment exceed monthly interest?
faqs.answer: Otherwise the payment does not reduce principal, so this fixed-rate model cannot reach a finite payoff date.

faqs.question: Which method should I choose if I know my monthly budget?
faqs.answer: Choose the payoff method. It solves the number of installments from the balance, interest rate and monthly payment.

faqs.question: Why can a longer term reduce the payment but increase cost?
faqs.answer: Principal is spread across more installments, while interest continues over more periods. Compare total interest with the monthly amount.

faqs.question: Can I enter a zero interest rate?
faqs.answer: Yes. The payment becomes the principal divided by the number of installments. Any fees remain a separate consideration.

faqs.question: Is the displayed payment a lender quote?
faqs.answer: No. It is an estimate based on your inputs and the stated monthly repayment model, without underwriting or live interest-rate pricing.

sections.title: Solve either the payment or the repayment time
paragraphs: Use the loan method when you know the principal, interest rate and intended term. Use the payoff method when a monthly budget is known and you want the number of installments. Do not enter a payment from one term while interpreting a result from another; they answer different planning questions.

sections.title: Worked payment example: 10,000 over three years
paragraphs: For a 10,000 principal at 8% annual interest over three years, with no extra payment, the monthly installment is about 313.36. The 36 payments total about 11,281.09, including 1,281.09 of interest. At 0%, the same principal and term would require approximately 277.78 per month.

table.caption: Effect of interest on the same repayment target

sections.title: Make the payment interval agree with the rate interval
paragraphs: The ordinary form calculates monthly payments using annual rate divided by twelve. If a contract uses a different compounding convention or payment interval, use the Loan Calculator’s frequency method. Multiplying a monthly payment by twelve gives annual debt service, not an independently calculated annual-payment contract.

sections.title: Compare the total obligation as well as the installment
paragraphs: A payment estimate excludes charges that have not been included in principal or modeled separately. Before choosing between scenarios, compare usable loan proceeds, fees, term, payment and total interest. The result cannot determine approval or whether the payment fits your other expenses.

links.label: Find repayment time from a fixed payment

sections.title: Choosing a payment or a payoff target
paragraphs: Use the scheduled-loan mode when the amount, rate, and term are known. Use fixed-payment payoff when you want to see what a chosen payment does to an existing balance. Check whether that payment covers accruing interest and reduces principal. A payment that looks manageable today may extend repayment considerably, so review the payoff duration as well as the installment amount.

For a $10,000 loan at an 8% nominal annual rate over 3 years, Loan & schedule uses 36 monthly payments and a monthly rate of 0.08 / 12. The calculated payment is about $313.36 before fees. The schedule totals about $1,281.09 of interest using unrounded calculations; a lender that rounds each installment or accrues interest daily can produce a different final payment.

payment-calculator.seoTitle: Payment Calculator: Loan Payments & Payoff Time

repayment-calculator.description: Plan fixed-rate debt repayment by term or payment budget, with a schedule showing the balance, interest and final installment.

faqs.question: Why is the last repayment sometimes smaller?
faqs.answer: Once the remaining balance and interest are below the normal payment, the model reduces the final installment to the amount due.

faqs.question: Does the repayment estimate include new borrowing?
faqs.answer: No. It assumes a fixed starting balance and rate, with no new charges or late fees during the schedule.

faqs.question: Why must my payment exceed monthly interest?
faqs.answer: Only the amount remaining after interest reduces principal. If no principal is repaid, the starting balance cannot reach zero under a constant-rate model.

faqs.question: Does the result assume I stop adding to the balance?
faqs.answer: Yes. It models repayment of the entered debt without new borrowing or purchases.

faqs.question: Why does the installment count round upward?
faqs.answer: A partial final installment still occurs in a payment period. The model reports the number of actual payment periods needed.

faqs.question: How do I model a 400 total payment when 300 is required?
faqs.answer: Enter payment 300 and extra 100, or payment 400 and extra zero. Entering 400 plus 100 would model a 500 total.

sections.title: Find how long a fixed payment takes to clear a balance
paragraphs: Enter the current balance, annual interest rate and the amount you can pay each month. Add any recurring extra separately. The model accrues monthly interest, applies the payment, and reduces the final installment when less than a full payment remains. It assumes no new borrowing.

sections.title: Worked repayment budget: 300 versus 400 per month
paragraphs: For 6,000 at 12% annual interest, a 300 monthly payment takes 23 installments and produces approximately 728.09 of interest. Raising the total payment to 400 reduces that to 17 installments and about 533.65 of interest. Both scenarios start with the same debt and rate.

table.caption: A higher payment changes time and interest together

sections.title: Recognize when a payment cannot amortize the debt
paragraphs: At 12% on a 6,000 balance, first-month interest is 60. A payment of 60 only covers that interest under the model; less than 60 does not even do that. A finite payoff requires the payment to exceed interest. The calculator rejects a non-amortizing payment instead of displaying an invented payoff date.

sections.title: Use a statement balance and avoid double-counting the extra
paragraphs: If the selected payment is already your full planned amount, leave extra payment at zero. If it is the contractual installment, enter an additional recurring amount separately. For changing interest rates, new purchases or several debts, use a model that represents those cash flows rather than assuming this single-balance schedule will match them.

links.label: Find a payment for a chosen term

sections.title: Planning a repayment schedule
paragraphs: A repayment plan depends on how much is owed, how interest is charged, and how much is paid each period. Compare a fixed term with a fixed payment to see which constraint fits your question. Keep any extra payments separate from the regular installment. The schedule assumes the entered terms continue, so a variable rate or missed payment can change the outcome.

For a $10,000 balance at 8% with a fixed $300 monthly payment, the model reaches payoff in 38 installments and charges about $1,346.95 in interest. Keeping the regular payment at $300 and adding $100 each month reduces this to 28 installments and about $976.04 in interest: 10 fewer installments and $370.91 less interest. Both scenarios include a smaller final installment and assume no new borrowing or fees.

repayment-calculator.seoTitle: Repayment Calculator: Payoff Time & Interest Schedule

mortgage-payoff-calculator.description: Estimate mortgage payoff and interest, infer a remaining balance from loan history, or compare an accelerated biweekly scenario.

faqs.question: Should I enter the original loan amount or the remaining balance?
faqs.answer: Use the remaining balance in the standard payoff modes. Accelerated biweekly with balance inference can also start from original terms and completed payments, or a known payment and remaining term.

faqs.question: Can I use my full escrow-inclusive mortgage payment?
faqs.answer: Use principal and interest only. Taxes, insurance and other escrow charges do not reduce mortgage principal.

faqs.question: Does the biweekly result reproduce my lender’s exact payment dates?
faqs.answer: No. It models 26 equal interest periods per year and half the contractual monthly payment. Actual collection dates, fees and principal-credit timing depend on the lender.

faqs.question: Should I include escrow in the monthly payment?
faqs.answer: No. Use the principal-and-interest payment for payoff arithmetic. Escrow for taxes and insurance does not reduce the mortgage balance.

faqs.question: Can the result use my original loan terms?
faqs.answer: The inferred methods can estimate a balance from original terms or a known payment. Past extras, missed payments or changes to the contract can make that estimate differ from your statement.

faqs.question: Why is the final payment lower than the selected amount?
faqs.answer: The model stops when principal and accrued interest are paid. It does not collect an unnecessary full installment after the debt is nearly cleared.

faqs.question: Will paying early eliminate property tax and insurance?
faqs.answer: No. Those are ongoing ownership costs. Early payoff removes the loan obligation, not all costs of owning the home.

sections.title: Use the current balance for an existing mortgage
paragraphs: A payoff calculation starts with what remains owed today, rather than the original purchase price. In the known-payment method, enter the current principal, annual rate, scheduled principal-and-interest payment and extra monthly principal. Do not include escrow for taxes or insurance in the payment available to repay the loan.

sections.title: Worked payoff comparison: adding 200 a month
paragraphs: A current balance of 120,000 at 6%, paid at 1,000 per month, takes 184 monthly installments in this model and incurs about 63,716.42 of future interest. Adding 200 per month shortens payoff to 139 installments with approximately 46,770.94 of interest. The final installment is smaller than a full payment.

table.caption: Same balance and rate, different principal-paydown budget

sections.title: Distinguish a lump sum, a monthly extra and a biweekly schedule
paragraphs: A one-time principal payment changes the balance once. A monthly extra recurs until payoff, and a biweekly arrangement changes payment frequency. The dated-extra-payment method can combine monthly, annual and one-time entries. Avoid entering the same extra money in more than one place.

sections.title: Check the lender’s posting and payoff rules
paragraphs: The modeled savings assume extras reach principal as specified. Servicer timing, fees and prepayment restrictions can affect the real result. An inferred current balance assumes the entered original payments were made as scheduled; use the current statement balance when past extra payments or missed payments make that inference unsuitable.

sections.title: Evaluating an earlier mortgage payoff
paragraphs: Compare the baseline mortgage with the extra-payment scenario using the same starting balance and interest rate. Calendar-based extras let you represent payments when they occur, while the balance-inference option estimates a balance from the stated loan history. Review both the interest saved and the earlier payoff date. An inferred balance should be checked against a current lender statement before use.

mortgage-payoff-calculator.seoTitle: Mortgage Payoff Calculator: Extra Payments & Interest Saved

credit-card-calculator.description: Estimate payoff time or a target payment for a credit-card balance using a fixed rate and no new purchases.

faqs.question: Does this reproduce a credit-card statement exactly?
faqs.answer: No. It uses a monthly fixed-rate model. Daily balance methods, changing APRs, fees and issuer minimum-payment rules can differ.

faqs.question: What happens if I keep making new purchases?
faqs.answer: New charges are not modeled. The estimated payoff time assumes the starting balance receives no additional borrowing.

faqs.question: Does this follow my card’s changing minimum payment?
faqs.answer: The single-balance form uses the fixed payment you enter. Your issuer’s minimum may change with the balance or include fees and interest.

faqs.question: Does it include new purchases?
faqs.answer: No. The estimate assumes the entered balance is being paid down without new spending.

faqs.question: Can a promotional rate be assumed for the whole payoff?
faqs.answer: Only if that is the scenario you intend. A promotion that ends before payoff requires the later rate and timing to be considered separately.

faqs.question: Why is my statement interest different?
faqs.answer: Daily balances, the billing-cycle length, payment posting, multiple rates, fees and grace-period rules can differ from this simplified monthly model.

sections.title: Estimate payoff for one balance with no new spending
paragraphs: Use the current balance, the applicable annual rate and a fixed monthly payment. This page’s single-balance method is useful for exploring a repayment budget; it does not model the changing minimum-payment formula on every card. The fixed-term method instead finds a monthly amount for a target repayment period.

sections.title: Worked credit-card payoff example
paragraphs: A balance of 2,400 at 18%, paid at 150 each month, takes 19 installments under the monthly model. Estimated interest is 365.17. First-month interest is 2,400 × 0.18 ÷ 12 = 36, leaving 114 for principal. This example assumes no fees, no rate change and no new purchases.

table.caption: Beginning of the illustrative card repayment

sections.title: Why the result can differ from the next card statement
paragraphs: Many issuers use a daily balance method, and different balance types can carry different rates. Statement dates, payment dates, promotional periods and grace-period treatment can therefore change actual interest. The calculator’s annual-rate-divided-by-twelve model is a planning approximation, not a reconstruction of the issuer’s ledger.

sections.title: Separate one-card analysis from several-card priorities
paragraphs: For several cards, a combined total and average rate can hide important differences. Use the dedicated payoff planner to retain each balance, rate and minimum. Preserve the overall repayment budget when comparing strategies, and confirm account-specific terms before treating an estimate as a payment instruction.

sections.title: Why a fixed card payment matters
paragraphs: A credit-card balance can take much longer to repay when the payment only slightly exceeds the interest charged. The fixed-payment mode helps you compare larger regular payments on the same balance. This projection assumes the modeled balance and rate, rather than reproducing every issuer's statement rules. New purchases, changing rates, or additional fees can alter the actual payoff path.

In the opening example, a $5,000 balance at 20% has about $83.33 of first-month interest in this monthly model. A $200 payment therefore reduces the balance by about $116.67 in that first month. With the same payment and no new charges, payoff takes 33 installments and about $1,522.10 in total interest. The final installment is smaller; your issuer may use daily balances and different payment rules.

credit-card-calculator.seoTitle: Credit Card Calculator: Payment & Payoff Time

auto-loan-calculator.description: Calculate auto-loan payments and price budgets with trade debt, rebates, fees and scoped US state tax treatment.

faqs.question: How does an outstanding trade-in loan affect financing?
faqs.answer: Trade-in value reduces the amount financed, while debt still owed on that vehicle is added back to the financing calculation.

faqs.question: Does the calculator choose my local vehicle sales-tax rules?
faqs.answer: The US state worksheet supports selected state presets and explains their scope after you choose a state. It does not look up local rates or confirm transaction eligibility. Enter your applicable rate, verified taxable-base assumptions, or actual quoted tax amount. The other modes use the trade-in and rebate treatment you enter.

faqs.question: How do I enter a trade with an existing loan?
faqs.answer: Enter both its trade value and the payoff amount. The calculator credits the value and adds the debt that still needs to be settled.

faqs.question: Does the down payment always reduce taxable price?
faqs.answer: No universal rule is assumed. Tax treatment depends on the transaction and jurisdiction; use the applicable tax settings or an actual quoted tax amount.

faqs.question: Can I work backward from a monthly payment?
faqs.answer: Yes. Select the reverse-price method and enter the term, rate, down payment and applicable trade, rebate, fee and tax assumptions.

faqs.question: Is the payment the complete monthly cost of driving?
faqs.answer: No. It covers the modeled financing. Insurance, fuel, maintenance and other operating costs belong in a separate budget.

sections.title: Reconcile the amount financed before comparing payments
paragraphs: Start with vehicle price, then subtract cash down, trade value and eligible rebate; add the amount owed on the trade plus financed tax and fees. A trade with an outstanding loan is not simply a discount. The selected sales-tax treatment must match the transaction rather than a national assumption.

sections.title: Worked car-financing example with tax and fees
paragraphs: For a 30,000 vehicle, 5,000 down, no trade or rebate, 6% sales tax and 500 in financed fees, the loan principal is 27,300. At 6% for five years, the monthly payment is about 527.79. The tax percentage is an illustrative input, not a rate inferred from your location.

table.caption: Build the financed amount before amortizing it

sections.title: Use the reverse-price and tax methods for more specific questions
paragraphs: The reverse-price method solves a purchase price from a payment budget and the entered costs. The state-tax financing method offers scoped source notes and manual or quoted-tax inputs. Choosing a state is not the same as knowing the local rate, taxable base or eligibility for a trade deduction.

sections.title: Compare a car’s cost beyond the advertised installment
paragraphs: Keep the term and amount financed visible when comparing offers. A smaller installment may reflect a longer repayment period, a larger down payment or different fees. Fuel, insurance, repairs, registration and depreciation are separate ownership considerations.

links.label: Solve for price from a payment budget
Compare cash back with a promotional rate

sections.title: Looking beyond the vehicle's monthly payment
paragraphs: Compare the vehicle price, down payment, trade-in treatment, fees, and financing term together. A longer term can lower the monthly payment while increasing total interest. The payment-budget mode works backward from an installment you choose. For tax comparisons, select the applicable supported state treatment and review its notes; a vehicle's advertised price alone does not capture the financed amount.

auto-loan-calculator.seoTitle: Auto Loan Calculator: Payments, Trade-In & Vehicle Budget

cash-back-or-low-interest-calculator.description: Compare a vehicle rebate with promotional financing, recalculating taxes, financed costs and total cash for each offer.

faqs.question: How are the rebate and low-rate offers compared?
faqs.answer: The comparison adds the down payment and scheduled loan payments for each offer over its entered term.

faqs.question: Does the cheaper offer remain cheaper after early payoff?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. The main comparison assumes scheduled repayment and excludes taxes, fees, early payoff and eligibility differences.

faqs.question: Does cash back always beat a lower rate?
faqs.answer: No. The outcome depends on rebate size, interest rates, amount financed and repayment term. Compare total cash paid under the same assumptions.

faqs.question: Are taxes included in the simple comparison?
faqs.answer: No. Use the expanded financing method or add verified tax and fee differences to the comparison.

faqs.question: Can I combine both offers?
faqs.answer: The basic comparison treats them as alternatives. If a lender allows both together, enter that actual combination in the Auto Loan Calculator.

faqs.question: Why might an early payoff change which offer costs less?
faqs.answer: Early payoff reduces the interest paid over time, while a rebate reduces principal at purchase. The original full-term totals no longer represent the same cash flows.

sections.title: Compare the two offers using the same vehicle and term
paragraphs: Cash back reduces the financed amount, while a promotional interest rate reduces the interest charged on the financed amount. Enter the same price, down payment and repayment term for both options. The comparison is meaningful only when both offers are actually available for the same purchase.

sections.title: Worked rebate-versus-rate comparison
paragraphs: Assume a 35,000 vehicle, 5,000 down and a five-year term. A 2,000 rebate with 6% interest finances 28,000 and costs about 541.32 per month. A 2% rate without the rebate finances 30,000 and costs about 525.83 per month. Including the same down payment, modeled totals are 37,479.11 and 36,549.97 respectively.

table.caption: Illustrative mutually exclusive dealer offers

sections.title: Why early payoff can change the comparison
paragraphs: The base result compares all scheduled installments. If the loan is paid off early, less future interest is paid, while a purchase rebate may already have reduced the amount financed. Examine the actual early-payoff cash flows and any offer restrictions rather than assuming the full-term winner always remains the winner.

sections.title: Bring tax and fee differences into a separate comparison
paragraphs: The simple comparison excludes tax and fees. The expanded state-tax financing method can represent the taxable base, financed costs and separate quoted tax amounts for the two offers. A rebate’s tax treatment should not be inferred from the word rebate alone.

links.label: Compare financing with tax and fees

sections.title: Comparing a rebate with a lower interest rate
paragraphs: A cash rebate reduces the purchase cost or amount financed, while a promotional interest rate changes the cost of borrowing over time. Compare both offers using the same vehicle, down payment, and repayment term. The more attractive monthly payment is not necessarily the lower total-cost offer. Include the applicable fees and tax treatment before drawing a conclusion from the difference.

cash-back-or-low-interest-calculator.seoTitle: Cash Back or Low Interest Calculator: Compare Auto Loans

auto-lease-calculator.description: Estimate a vehicle lease payment from cost, residual value and money factor, or work backward from a monthly payment budget.

faqs.question: What makes up the modeled lease payment?
faqs.answer: It combines depreciation over the lease term with a rent charge based on adjusted cost, residual value and the money factor.

faqs.question: Is residual value the same as the amount I pay each month?
faqs.answer: No. Residual value is the modeled vehicle value at lease end. It helps determine depreciation and may affect an end-of-lease purchase.

faqs.question: What goes in the money-factor field?
faqs.answer: Enter the decimal factor used in the lease quote, for example 0.0025. It is not a field for an annual interest percentage.

faqs.question: What is residual value?
faqs.answer: It is the assumed remaining vehicle value used in this lease calculation. It affects depreciation and the rent charge.

faqs.question: Does the displayed total include buying the car afterward?
faqs.answer: The scheduled lease cost does not automatically include exercising a purchase option or its fees. Add those separate cash flows when comparing ownership.

faqs.question: Can a lower residual increase the payment?
faqs.answer: Yes. A lower residual increases the amount of depreciation allocated across the lease, although it also changes the rent-charge component.

sections.title: Build a lease payment from depreciation and rent charge
paragraphs: Enter the vehicle’s negotiated cost, cost reduction, residual value, lease months and money factor. The modeled pretax payment is the sum of monthly depreciation and the rent charge. The residual is the assumed value remaining at the lease end; it is not an amount you have already paid toward ownership.

sections.title: Worked auto lease with a stated money factor
paragraphs: A 35,000 price with 3,000 down gives a net cost of 32,000. With a 20,000 residual over 36 months, depreciation is (32,000 − 20,000) ÷ 36 = 333.33 per month. A money factor of 0.0025 produces a rent charge of (32,000 + 20,000) × 0.0025 = 130. With 6% tax on the payment, the modeled monthly amount is 491.13.

table.caption: Components of the example lease installment

sections.title: Keep a money factor separate from an annual percentage rate
paragraphs: The field expects the decimal money factor, such as 0.0025. Entering 6 as though it were a 6% rate would describe a completely different charge. This mode uses a common US lease-payment structure and a selected monthly-payment tax assumption; not every lease or jurisdiction follows that structure.

sections.title: Check the contract charges outside this payment model
paragraphs: Acquisition and disposition charges, excess mileage, wear charges, deposits and purchase-option costs can change the full cost of the lease. A residual is not automatically your guaranteed buyout price with all fees included. Use the reverse-price method only with matching assumptions about tax and residual.

links.label: Estimate selling price from a lease payment

sections.title: Understanding a lease payment estimate
paragraphs: A lease payment combines the modeled depreciation and financing charges, with the entered taxes and fees where supported. Residual value describes the vehicle value assumed at the end of the lease, not cash you automatically receive. Compare offers over the same lease term and inspect upfront amounts separately. Mileage charges and end-of-lease conditions require the actual lease agreement.

auto-lease-calculator.seoTitle: Auto Lease Calculator: Monthly Payment & Vehicle Budget

lease-calculator.description: Calculate an asset-financing lease payment or implied rate from asset value, term and residual, with a separate vehicle-lease model.

faqs.question: What does the residual mean in an asset-financing lease?
faqs.answer: The residual is an amount remaining at the end. The model discounts it alongside the monthly payments when valuing the lease.

faqs.question: When are financing-lease payments assumed to occur?
faqs.answer: At month end. Taxes, contract fees and alternative payment timing are excluded from that model.

faqs.question: Does the residual disappear after the final installment?
faqs.answer: No. In the financing method it remains as a separate end-of-term amount, included in the present-value equation.

faqs.question: Are payments modeled at the start or end of the month?
faqs.answer: The financing method assumes end-of-month payments. A contract paid in advance has different timing.

faqs.question: Can the calculator solve an implied interest rate?
faqs.answer: Yes, in the financing method when the other cash-flow inputs are supplied. The rate belongs to that specific payment-and-residual model.

faqs.question: Does the result decide whether a lease is an operating or finance lease?
faqs.answer: No. It performs payment arithmetic and does not apply accounting classification or tax rules.

sections.title: Choose an asset-financing lease or an auto money-factor lease
paragraphs: The financing method treats the asset value as the present value of end-of-month payments plus a final residual. It can solve a payment or implied rate. The separate auto method uses depreciation plus a money-factor rent charge. These are different conventions; select the one represented in the contract.

sections.title: Worked asset-financing lease example
paragraphs: For an asset value of 20,000, a residual of 8,000, 36 end-of-month payments and 6% nominal annual interest, the monthly lease payment is about 405.06. The 8,000 residual remains at the end. Total periodic payments are about 14,582.28, and periodic payments plus the residual exceed the asset value by about 2,582.28.

table.caption: Separate periodic payments from the end residual

sections.title: Do not compare an unpaid residual with a fully repaid loan
paragraphs: A large residual reduces the portion recovered through installments. Comparing its monthly lease payment with a loan that reaches zero at maturity can therefore be misleading. Include the end obligation, any purchase option and the same holding period in both alternatives.

sections.title: Interpret an implied lease rate within the selected cash-flow model
paragraphs: The solved rate fits the entered asset value, payments and residual. It does not classify the lease for accounting or tax purposes, and it excludes fees and taxes absent from the inputs. Check whether payments occur in advance; this financing method assumes month-end timing.

links.label: Compare present values of payment streams

sections.title: Comparing lease structures consistently
paragraphs: Choose the lease mode that matches the agreement you are examining. Asset financing and a residual-value lease answer different questions about repayment and the asset's ending value. Keep the asset price, timing, and any residual assumption visible when comparing payments. A lower installment can reflect a larger amount left at the end rather than a lower overall financing cost.

lease-calculator.seoTitle: Lease Calculator: Payments, Residual Value & Implied Rate

heloc-calculator.description: Estimate HELOC draw-period interest, later repayment payments and home-equity borrowing capacity under a constant-rate scenario.

faqs.question: Why does the payment rise after an interest-only draw period?
faqs.answer: The repayment phase begins paying down principal as well as interest, over the remaining amortization term.

faqs.question: Does the model track changing draws and variable HELOC rates?
faqs.answer: No. It assumes a fully drawn, constant balance during the draw period and an unchanged interest rate.

faqs.question: Should I enter the limit or the amount drawn?
faqs.answer: Enter the outstanding drawn balance for payment arithmetic. A credit limit that has not been used is not automatically interest-bearing debt.

faqs.question: Does interest-only mean the balance is being repaid?
faqs.answer: No. The modeled draw-period payment covers interest while leaving the principal outstanding.

faqs.question: Can the calculator forecast a changing HELOC rate?
faqs.answer: No. It holds the selected rate constant within a scenario. Compare alternative rates to see how sensitive the payment is.

faqs.question: Why can repayment cost more than the draw payment?
faqs.answer: The repayment phase includes principal amortization as well as interest, while the modeled draw phase pays interest only.

sections.title: Separate the draw-period payment from later repayment
paragraphs: This HELOC model assumes a fully drawn balance that stays constant during an interest-only draw period. It then amortizes that balance during the repayment period. Enter the amount drawn, not merely the approved credit limit, unless the whole limit is actually outstanding.

sections.title: Worked payment transition on a 50,000 balance
paragraphs: For a 50,000 balance at an assumed constant 8% rate, the interest-only monthly payment is 333.33. If the same balance is then repaid over 20 years, the monthly installment is approximately 418.22. A ten-year interest-only draw period would create 40,000 of interest without reducing the original principal.

table.caption: Same assumed balance and rate in two phases

sections.title: Use the capacity and fee methods for separate decisions
paragraphs: The capacity method estimates additional borrowing using a selected combined-LTV cap. The fee-schedule method includes an annual account charge on its modeled anniversary schedule. Neither method predicts future withdrawals, rate resets or whether a lender will keep a credit line available.

sections.title: Stress-test the payment when a variable rate changes
paragraphs: Run more than one rate scenario and compare the repayment payment as well as the draw payment. A small current interest-only amount does not show the later principal obligation. Actual HELOC interest may use a daily balance and variable rate, so this constant-balance schedule is a planning reference.

sections.title: Planning for the HELOC repayment period
paragraphs: A HELOC can have different payment behavior during the draw period and the repayment period. Compare both stages instead of using the initial payment as a long-term budget. The account-fee mode lets you include supported recurring charges. The estimate follows the entered balance and rate assumptions; future draws and a changing interest rate can alter the amount ultimately repaid.

heloc-calculator.seoTitle: HELOC Calculator: Draw Payments, Repayment & Credit Limit

fha-loan-calculator.description: Estimate standard FHA fees, mortgage-insurance schedules and extra-payment payoff, or enter rates in a manual premium worksheet.

faqs.question: Are FHA insurance rates selected automatically?
faqs.answer: The verified-policy mode selects the supported standard forward rates from base loan, original LTV, term and policy date. Manual modes use entered rates. Neither determines borrower or property eligibility.

faqs.question: Do extra principal payments lower each future monthly MIP amount?
faqs.answer: The policy mode calculates scheduled MIP from original contractual amortization. Extra payments shorten actual payoff, which ends modeled coverage, but do not rewrite the original premium schedule.

faqs.question: How does financing the upfront premium change the result?
faqs.answer: The premium increases note principal. The HUD worksheet also applies the financed-upfront adjustment when deriving periodic insurance charges.

faqs.question: What is the base loan compared with the note amount?
faqs.answer: The base loan is the purchase borrowing before a financed upfront fee. If that fee is financed, it is added to form the note principal.

faqs.question: Does a financed upfront premium also earn interest?
faqs.answer: It increases the principal being amortized, so the modeled loan payment includes financing that amount over the selected term.

faqs.question: Can I use one MIP cancellation rule for every FHA loan?
faqs.answer: No. Policy vintage, loan term, original LTV and other conditions matter. The historical checker has a stated scope and does not replace servicer confirmation.

faqs.question: Why is the basic insurance estimate different from the HUD ledger?
faqs.answer: The simple mode applies an entered annual percentage to the base loan. The ledger models original amortization balances and specified rounding; it answers a more detailed premium question.

sections.title: Distinguish the base loan, upfront premium and periodic MIP
paragraphs: The basic mode starts from price and down payment, then applies the entered upfront fee and annual-insurance assumption. Financing the upfront fee adds it to note principal. Periodic mortgage insurance is a separate charge; adding an upfront fee does not replace it. The policy and ledger modes address more specific premium calculations.

sections.title: Worked manual FHA fee example
paragraphs: For a 200,000 purchase and 5% down, the base loan is 190,000. If you explicitly enter a 1.75% upfront fee, that fee is 3,325. Financing it produces a 193,325 note. An illustrative annual-insurance input of 0.55% applied to the base loan gives an initial monthly estimate of 87.08. These manual inputs do not determine the applicable policy or eligibility.

table.caption: Manual premium inputs and resulting amounts

sections.title: Choose the policy vintage before interpreting cancellation
paragraphs: The current-policy worksheet, HUD premium ledger and historical cancellation checker answer different questions. Original loan-to-value, term and applicable case dates affect the relevant treatment. A historical threshold result is not an instruction to stop paying MIP, and extra principal does not automatically rewrite the original insurance schedule.

sections.title: Compare ownership costs over a shared horizon
paragraphs: When comparing monthly and accelerated repayment, retain property taxes, insurance and other ownership costs over the same period. A paid-off mortgage does not eliminate those expenses. Use verified program inputs and confirm the applicable mortgage-insurance schedule with the lender or servicer.

links.label: Use the detailed FHA policy worksheet

sections.title: Reading FHA mortgage cost estimates
paragraphs: FHA loan comparisons should include the supported mortgage-insurance and program-fee assumptions alongside principal and interest. Select the schedule or historical branch that matches the loan details, and review its eligibility notes before interpreting the result. The ownership-cost worksheet can help distinguish the mortgage payment from other housing costs. An estimate does not establish loan eligibility or replace a lender's disclosure.

fha-loan-calculator.seoTitle: FHA Loan Calculator: Payments, Fees & Mortgage Insurance

va-mortgage-calculator.description: Estimate VA purchase or refinance funding fees and payments, using the selected fee tier, financing choice and verified exemption assumptions.

faqs.question: Does the calculator choose a funding-fee tier?
faqs.answer: Verified-policy mode uses the selected loan type, first or later use, down-payment tier and entered verified exemption. It does not independently confirm service eligibility or supporting evidence.

faqs.question: Does VA mortgage insurance add a monthly premium?
faqs.answer: The VA policy mode assigns zero monthly mortgage insurance. The funding fee is a separate upfront charge that can be financed in the scenario.

faqs.question: Does ordinary retirement pay prove a funding-fee exemption?
faqs.answer: No. Select an exemption only when the applicable qualifying status has been verified; receiving retirement pay alone does not establish it.

faqs.question: Is the funding fee the interest rate?
faqs.answer: No. It is a separate upfront program cost. The interest rate determines how the note principal accrues interest over repayment.

faqs.question: Can I finance the entered funding fee?
faqs.answer: The basic calculator has that option. Financing adds the fee to note principal; paying it separately leaves the loan smaller but requires more upfront cash.

faqs.question: Does this verify a funding-fee exemption?
faqs.answer: No. It can model an entered verified exemption, but eligibility must be established through the appropriate VA and lender process.

faqs.question: Does no monthly mortgage insurance mean no housing insurance cost?
faqs.answer: No. Property insurance and other ownership costs are separate from monthly mortgage insurance and should still be budgeted.

sections.title: Separate the VA funding fee from mortgage interest
paragraphs: The funding fee is an upfront program cost distinct from the interest rate. In the basic worksheet, you enter the fee percentage and choose whether it is financed. The policy method uses selected loan type, usage and verified exemption information; it does not establish that an applicant is eligible for a VA loan.

sections.title: Worked manual funding-fee example
paragraphs: Suppose the purchase price is 250,000 with no down payment. Enter an illustrative 2.15% funding fee and choose to finance it. The fee is 5,375, bringing the note principal to 255,375. With the fee paid separately, the note stays 250,000 and cash needed at closing increases by 5,375 instead. Confirm the actual fee or exemption before using this as a transaction estimate.

table.caption: Financing versus paying the entered fee separately

sections.title: Use the appropriate funding-fee and exemption inputs
paragraphs: VA publishes fee categories and exemptions. The calculator can model selected assumptions but cannot verify disability documentation, service status or other eligibility facts. The VA policy branch does not add monthly mortgage insurance; property insurance, taxes and other closing costs remain separate expenses.

sections.title: Compare payment schedules without dropping ownership expenses
paragraphs: The ownership comparison keeps program fees, loan payments and recurring housing costs on separate timelines. Evaluate the same holding period for both choices, and include costs that continue after mortgage payoff. A smaller financed principal and a smaller cash requirement are different objectives.

links.label: VA: funding fee and closing costs

sections.title: Separating VA loan fees from monthly costs
paragraphs: The VA mortgage calculator separates the financing estimate from supported program-fee assumptions. Review the entered fee treatment and applicable exemption information before comparing scenarios. Financing a fee changes the borrowed balance, while paying it upfront changes cash needed at closing. Use the ownership-cost mode to consider additional recurring housing expenses rather than treating principal and interest as the entire home budget.

va-mortgage-calculator.seoTitle: VA Mortgage Calculator: Payments & Funding Fees

down-payment-calculator.description: Calculate down-payment cash, a purchase-price budget or a savings timeline while allowing for entered closing costs.

faqs.question: Is the down payment the only cash needed to buy?
faqs.answer: Not in this model. Estimated closing costs are added to the down payment when calculating the cash needed.

faqs.question: Does the savings timeline include investment growth?
faqs.answer: No. It divides the remaining cash target by monthly savings, without interest, investment returns or changing contributions.

faqs.question: Can I find a purchase price from a fixed cash amount?
faqs.answer: Yes. Use the price method with available cash and the chosen down-payment and closing-cost percentages.

faqs.question: What if part of my savings must remain available?
faqs.answer: Subtract the reserve you want to keep from the cash entered for the purchase. The calculator cannot decide an appropriate reserve for you.

sections.title: Include closing costs when setting the cash target
paragraphs: The down payment becomes part of the purchase price paid from your own funds. Closing costs are additional transaction cash and do not automatically increase that down payment. The amount method separates them; the price method works backward from available cash using the entered percentages.

sections.title: Worked cash requirement for a 300,000 purchase
paragraphs: At a 15% down payment and 3% closing-cost assumption, the down payment is 45,000 and closing costs are 9,000. Total modeled initial cash is therefore 54,000. The remaining price to finance is 255,000 before any costs that are actually financed.

table.caption: Separate the two uses of upfront cash

sections.title: Work backward without treating all savings as a deposit
paragraphs: If 54,000 is available and the same 15% down plus 3% closing assumptions apply, maximum price under this cash-only calculation is 54,000 ÷ 0.18 = 300,000. Money reserved for an emergency fund, moving or immediate repairs should be removed from the cash available before solving for price.

sections.title: Translate the cash shortfall into a savings timeline
paragraphs: For a 54,000 target, 24,000 already saved and 1,000 added monthly, the simple timeline is 30 months. It assumes no investment growth and no change in the target. A changing purchase price or closing-cost estimate should be reflected in a new scenario.

links.label: Estimate months to the savings target

sections.title: Planning the cash needed for a purchase
paragraphs: A down payment can be expressed as a cash amount or a percentage of the purchase price. Use the matching mode depending on which figure you know. The savings timeline helps connect a target with regular contributions. Keep closing costs and any cash reserve separate from the down payment unless the selected fields explicitly include them, so the same money is not counted twice.

down-payment-calculator.seoTitle: Down Payment Calculator: Cash Needed & Savings Timeline

house-affordability-calculator.description: Estimate a home-price budget from income and debt limits, or from an entered monthly housing payment allowance.

faqs.question: How do other monthly debts affect the income-based estimate?
faqs.answer: They reduce the amount available under the total debt-to-income limit, which can lower the modeled housing budget.

faqs.question: Does an affordable-price estimate mean a lender will approve it?
faqs.answer: No. Credit history, loan limits, underwriting, local costs and personal spending needs are not fully assessed.

faqs.question: Are 28% and 36% universal approval rules?
faqs.answer: No. They are editable planning inputs. Lenders and loan products may use different limits and count obligations differently.

faqs.question: Should income be gross or take-home?
faqs.answer: The income-ratio method uses gross income. Check affordability separately against actual take-home cash and household expenses.

faqs.question: Why does adding other debt reduce the result?
faqs.answer: Other debt uses part of the chosen total-debt budget, leaving less for housing under that constraint.

faqs.question: Does the estimated price include closing cash?
faqs.answer: The calculation uses the entered down-payment assumption to infer price. Closing costs and cash reserves need their own budget.

sections.title: Choose an income-ratio estimate or a direct housing budget
paragraphs: The income method applies your selected housing-only and total-debt ratios to gross income. The tighter result limits the housing budget. The direct-budget method instead starts with a monthly amount you choose. Neither method performs lender underwriting or decides how much borrowing is comfortable for your household.

sections.title: Worked affordability budget before solving the loan
paragraphs: With annual gross income of 96,000, monthly gross income is 8,000. A 28% housing limit gives 2,240. A 36% total-debt limit less 800 of other monthly debt gives 2,080. Use the smaller 2,080; subtract 400 of nonloan housing costs to leave 1,680 for principal and interest.

table.caption: The tighter constraint determines the modeled loan budget

sections.title: Keep gross-income ratios separate from spendable cash
paragraphs: Gross income is before income tax and many deductions. A ratio-based estimate does not show childcare, irregular expenses, savings goals or the timing of income. Check the resulting payment against a take-home-pay budget rather than assuming the ratio leaves enough cash for every expense.

sections.title: Use the result as a scenario, not a purchase approval
paragraphs: The inferred home price depends on rate, term, down payment and ongoing costs. A higher rate or larger nonloan costs reduces the amount supported by a fixed payment budget. Credit history, appraisal, loan limits and program requirements remain outside this calculation.

links.label: Start from a chosen monthly housing budget

sections.title: Turning a housing budget into a price estimate
paragraphs: Affordability depends on the assumed financing terms and the housing payment available within your budget. Compare the income-based estimate with the mode that starts from a chosen payment. A higher down payment or a different rate can change the estimated purchase price. Treat the result as a planning scenario; it does not confirm that a lender will approve the amount.

house-affordability-calculator.seoTitle: House Affordability Calculator: Home Price & Payment Budget

rent-calculator.description: Estimate a monthly rent budget from gross income, a chosen spending percentage and the utilities you expect to pay.

faqs.question: Why are utilities deducted from the rent allowance?
faqs.answer: The model treats the chosen income share as a housing budget, then reserves the entered utility amount before estimating rent.

faqs.question: Is the suggested percentage suitable for every household?
faqs.answer: No. Debts, savings goals, household needs and local housing costs can make a percentage rule unsuitable.

faqs.question: Is the percentage a mandatory rent limit?
faqs.answer: No. It is an adjustable assumption used to explore a budget. It does not determine a landlord’s requirements.

faqs.question: Do I enter gross or net income?
faqs.answer: This form uses annual gross income. Review the result against take-home cash separately.

faqs.question: How should utilities included in rent be handled?
faqs.answer: Avoid subtracting the same amount twice. Enter only the separate utility allowance relevant to the scenario you are comparing.

faqs.question: Does this include a security deposit?
faqs.answer: No. A deposit is an upfront cash need, not a recurring monthly rent amount in this calculation.

sections.title: Turn an income share into a rent allowance
paragraphs: Enter annual gross income, the share assigned to housing and monthly utilities. The calculator converts income to a monthly amount, applies the share, then subtracts the utilities. The resulting rent allowance is a planning convention; it is not a landlord’s approval rule or a statement that the amount is affordable in every household.

sections.title: Worked rent-budget example
paragraphs: For 72,000 annual gross income, the monthly amount is 6,000. A 30% housing share allocates 1,800 for rent and the included utilities. Subtract 200 of utilities to obtain a rent allowance of 1,600. If utilities are already part of the advertised rent, do not deduct that same cost twice.

table.caption: From annual income to a monthly rent allowance

sections.title: Use the obligations method when debt is part of the same cap
paragraphs: The obligations method applies one chosen income share to housing and debt combined, then subtracts debt payments and utilities. That is a different meaning from assigning 30% to housing alone. Name the policy you are testing before comparing the two results.

sections.title: Check the lease cash requirements beyond monthly rent
paragraphs: Deposits, moving costs, upfront rent, parking and separately billed services can create a cash requirement that is not visible in a monthly ratio. Compare the allowance with a take-home-pay budget and irregular expenses. A percentage of gross income does not automatically reserve money for those items.

links.label: Include debt in a combined allowance

sections.title: Building a rent budget around other obligations
paragraphs: Use the rent budget as a starting point for comparing housing choices. The debt-adjusted mode shows how existing monthly obligations affect the amount available under the entered rule. Check which expenses are included before comparing the result with a rental listing. Utilities, transport, and irregular expenses may need their own allowance even when the advertised rent fits the estimate.

rent-calculator.seoTitle: Rent Calculator: Monthly Rent Budget from Income

debt-ratio-calculator.description: Calculate debt-to-income ratio from gross income and debt payments entered as monthly totals or mixed annual and monthly lines.

faqs.question: Should I use income before or after tax for DTI?
faqs.answer: Use gross income before tax. The mixed-period budget’s spendable-income result is separate from the gross-income denominator used for DTI.

faqs.question: Can I enter annual debt or income amounts?
faqs.answer: Yes. The mixed-period mode normalizes each annual amount to one-twelfth before calculating the ratio.

faqs.question: Does the result establish loan eligibility?
faqs.answer: No. Lenders may count income and obligations differently; use the debts relevant to the comparison.

faqs.question: Should I use loan balances or required payments?
faqs.answer: Use monthly debt payments. The ratio measures the share of gross monthly income needed to service debt.

faqs.question: Does gross income mean before taxes?
faqs.answer: Yes. The simple DTI calculation uses gross monthly income rather than take-home pay.

faqs.question: Do ordinary groceries count as debt payments?
faqs.answer: They are living expenses, not necessarily debt obligations in a DTI calculation. Include them in a cash budget rather than silently treating every expense as debt.

faqs.question: Is a low DTI a guarantee of approval?
faqs.answer: No. Credit, income verification, product rules, collateral and other underwriting factors can matter in addition to the ratio.

sections.title: Use debt payments and gross income from the same period
paragraphs: Debt-to-income compares required monthly debt payments with gross monthly income. Enter the housing obligation separately from other debt payments, without repeating it in both fields. This is a payment ratio, not total outstanding debt divided by annual salary.

sections.title: Worked housing and total DTI example
paragraphs: If gross monthly income is 8,000, housing payments are 2,000 and other monthly debt payments are 600, the housing ratio is 25%. Total DTI is (2,000 + 600) ÷ 8,000 × 100 = 32.5%. A debt balance of 20,000 is not entered as a 20,000 monthly payment.

table.caption: Two ratios from the same household inputs

sections.title: DTI and cash surplus measure different things
paragraphs: An income ratio can look manageable while taxes, food, transport or childcare leave little cash. The period-lines method normalizes monthly and annual entries to show a broader cash budget, including a chosen flat-tax assumption. Keep that estimate separate from a progressive income-tax calculation.

sections.title: A ratio does not establish lending eligibility
paragraphs: Different lenders and products can count debts and income differently. Use the income and obligations relevant to the actual application, and check how variable income, support obligations or other housing costs should be treated. The calculator does not perform those underwriting decisions.

links.label: Compare debts with the full monthly budget
CFPB: DTI definition and lender differences

sections.title: Making income and debt periods comparable
paragraphs: Monthly debt payments of 1,200, 300, and 100 total 1,600. With gross monthly income of 5,000, the modeled debt-to-income ratio is 1,600 ÷ 5,000 × 100 = 32%. Using take-home income of 4,000 would produce 40%, which answers a different question. Enter required debt payments rather than outstanding loan balances. A DTI ratio is not the cash left for living expenses; use the budget worksheet for that, and check the obligations counted by the relevant lender.

refinance-calculator.description: Compare refinancing payments, interest and simple break-even, or evaluate payments and remaining debt over the same holding period.

faqs.question: What does simple refinance break-even measure?
faqs.answer: It divides upfront costs by the monthly payment reduction. That payment-only measure does not account for different balances at a later date.

faqs.question: Why compare remaining balances over the same horizon?
faqs.answer: A lower payment can leave more debt outstanding. The horizon mode compares payment differences, upfront net cash and both ending balances together.

faqs.question: Do I enter the original mortgage term or remaining term?
faqs.answer: Use the remaining term for the existing-loan comparison, unless you deliberately select an inference mode that asks for the original terms.

faqs.question: Why is payment-based break-even incomplete?
faqs.answer: It ignores differences in remaining debt and other timing effects. A lower payment alone does not measure the full benefit over a chosen holding period.

faqs.question: Are financed closing costs free?
faqs.answer: No. They increase the new balance and can earn interest. Include them in principal or the explicit financed-fee inputs, without counting them twice.

faqs.question: Can I compare a cash-out refinance?
faqs.answer: Use the horizon method with the cash-out amount and financing costs. Compare the cash received and the larger remaining obligation together.

sections.title: Compare the old remaining loan with the proposed new loan
paragraphs: Use the current unpaid balance and remaining term for the existing mortgage, not its original principal and full original term. Enter the new rate, term and closing costs separately. The simple comparison divides upfront costs by payment reduction; the horizon method also compares the debt remaining on a chosen future date.

sections.title: Worked payment-based break-even example
paragraphs: For a 200,000 balance with 20 years remaining, lowering the assumed rate from 7% to 5% while keeping 20 years reduces the monthly payment from about 1,550.60 to 1,319.91. The reduction is about 230.69. With 3,000 paid upfront, simple break-even is slightly more than 13 months, so the first whole-month crossover is month 14.

table.caption: Same balance and term, different assumed rates
rows: About 13.005 months; month 14 at whole payments

sections.title: A lower payment can hide a longer repayment horizon
paragraphs: Restarting a long term can reduce the installment while slowing principal repayment. Compare both cash paid and the balance still owed at the same future month. The horizon method keeps those two components visible, which is more informative when a sale or another refinance is expected before maturity.

sections.title: Count financed fees and cash-out proceeds once
paragraphs: Financed closing costs increase the new loan instead of disappearing. Cash-out proceeds increase funds received but also increase debt. The horizon worksheet separates these cash flows so a payment reduction is not mistaken for the entire economic benefit.

links.label: Compare payments and balances at a shared horizon

sections.title: Comparing refinancing over your own time horizon
paragraphs: If upfront refinancing costs are 3,000 and the monthly payment falls by 150, simple payment break-even is 20 months. That comparison only recovers the upfront cost through smaller payments; it does not account for a different remaining loan balance. A longer new term can lower the payment while leaving more debt at your planned sale date. Use the common-horizon mode to compare payments, fees, cash-out proceeds, and both ending balances over the same number of months.

interest-calculator.description: Project compound interest with regular deposits, optional monthly and annual contribution streams, and entered tax and inflation assumptions.

faqs.question: Are monthly and annual contributions alternatives?
faqs.answer: In the dual-stream mode they are additive: the annual contribution is extra to the twelve monthly contributions.

faqs.question: How is tax on interest modeled?
faqs.answer: Tax is applied to positive interest under the stated settlement convention. Account-specific tax treatment and fees are not determined.

faqs.question: Are semimonthly and biweekly compounding the same?
faqs.answer: No. Equivalent nominal rates uses 24 semimonthly periods or 26 biweekly periods per year. It compares equal annual growth, not exact calendar posting dates.

faqs.question: Why is the final balance larger than interest earned?
faqs.answer: The final balance includes your opening money and later deposits. Interest is the part remaining after subtracting those contributions.

faqs.question: Does depositing at the beginning of a period change the result?
faqs.answer: Yes. A beginning-of-period deposit receives one additional deposit period of growth compared with the same end-of-period deposit.

faqs.question: Does the tax rate reproduce my tax return?
faqs.answer: No. It applies a simplified tax assumption to investment growth and does not determine exemptions, allowances or account-specific tax rules.

sections.title: Separate the money deposited from the interest earned
paragraphs: Enter the opening balance, the amount of each additional deposit, its frequency and the annual nominal rate. The projected balance combines your own contributions with growth; it is not all interest. The contribution total includes the opening balance, so subtracting it from the ending balance gives growth after any modeled tax.

sections.title: Worked example: a single deposit earning monthly interest
paragraphs: An opening deposit of 5,000 at an assumed 6% nominal annual rate compounded monthly grows to about 5,983.40 after three years with no further deposits or tax. The monthly rate is 0.06 ÷ 12 = 0.005, and the calculation is 5,000 × 1.005³⁶.

table.caption: Interest and principal are different amounts

sections.title: Match compounding and deposit frequencies to the account
paragraphs: Compounding frequency controls when interest joins the balance. Deposit frequency controls when new money arrives. They need not be identical. For a savings plan funded monthly plus a separate annual bonus, use the two-stream method and enter only the additional bonus in the annual field.

sections.title: Nominal interest, taxes and spending power
paragraphs: A quoted nominal rate and an effective annual yield are different when interest compounds more than once a year. Use the rate-conversion method before comparing unlike quotes. The tax setting is a simplified charge on positive modeled interest, while the inflation setting expresses the result in today’s purchasing power.

sections.title: Interest after tax and inflation
paragraphs: To isolate interest on a deposit, set Regular contribution to 0. Enter your assumed tax rate and inflation rate to compare the ending balance with its purchasing power. For example, 1,000 at 5% compounded annually for 1 year earns 50 before tax. With 20% tax on interest and 0% inflation, the ending balance is 1,040. Actual account tax rules can differ.

sections.title: Keeping rate and contribution timing consistent
paragraphs: Interest growth depends on the starting balance, the rate convention, and when contributions arrive. Use the mode that matches monthly or annual additions instead of combining them into an unexplained total. When comparing rates, check whether they are nominal or effective. The projection follows the entered rate over time; it does not predict future returns or account for omitted charges.

savings-calculator.description: Estimate savings growth from an opening balance and regular deposits, including contribution timing, tax and inflation scenarios.

faqs.question: Does depositing at the start of a period change the result?
faqs.answer: Yes. Beginning-of-period deposits earn interest for that period; end-of-period deposits begin earning afterward.

faqs.question: Is the inflation-adjusted balance a separate account value?
faqs.answer: No. It expresses the projected nominal balance in purchasing-power terms using the inflation assumption you enter.

faqs.question: Does total contributions include my current savings?
faqs.answer: Yes. It includes the opening balance and all modeled deposits.

faqs.question: How do I model no interest?
faqs.answer: Set the annual rate to zero. The ending balance then equals the opening balance plus deposits, provided no other charges are modeled.

faqs.question: Is my annual bonus included in monthly saving?
faqs.answer: Only if you deliberately included it there. In the two-stream method, the annual deposit is added on top of the monthly contributions.

faqs.question: Is the projected interest rate guaranteed?
faqs.answer: No. The rate is an assumption. Actual variable savings rates can change during the period.

sections.title: Build the projection around an actual deposit schedule
paragraphs: Start with money already saved, then enter what you can add each week, month or year. Select whether deposits occur at the beginning or end of the period. Keep the interest assumption separate from the contribution amount so the result shows how much of the goal depends on saving and how much depends on growth.

sections.title: Worked example: 100 saved monthly for two years
paragraphs: With 1,000 already saved, 100 deposited at each month-end and an assumed 6% nominal annual rate compounded monthly, the balance reaches about 3,670.36 after 24 months. You supplied 3,400 in total; the remaining 270.36 is modeled interest, before any tax.

table.caption: A short-term savings plan

sections.title: Use the two-stream method for bonuses and rising deposits
paragraphs: The separate monthly and annual contribution method lets you model regular saving plus an additional yearly deposit. Contribution growth changes future deposit amounts, which can materially increase the result. Check that the assumed increases fit the budget rather than treating them as investment returns.

sections.title: Test the plan when the interest rate changes
paragraphs: Run a low-rate scenario as well as your central assumption, especially when the account rate is variable. For a near-term expense, the required cash amount and withdrawal date matter more than a distant balance projection. Inflation-adjusted value helps compare purchasing power, but the nominal balance is the amount actually projected in the account.

sections.title: Build a regular savings plan
paragraphs: Start with the amount already saved, then enter what you can add each month. Compare a lower deposit or a lower rate to see how your plan changes. At 0% interest, an opening balance of 1,000 plus 100 per month for 12 months gives 2,200. Use the monthly + annual contributions mode when you also plan an extra yearly deposit.

sections.title: Separating deposits from savings growth
paragraphs: A savings balance contains both money you contributed and modeled interest. Compare those parts to see how much of the ending value comes from your own deposits. Regular contributions and an initial lump sum have different amounts of time to grow. Keep contribution timing consistent across scenarios, and test a lower rate if you want to understand how dependent a target is on growth.

future-value-calculator.description: Estimate the future value of savings and recurring deposits, including separate monthly and annual contributions and assumed purchasing power.

faqs.question: What is the difference between future value and purchasing power?
faqs.answer: Future value is the projected nominal balance. The inflation-adjusted figure discounts that balance using the assumed change in prices.

faqs.question: Can contributions increase over time?
faqs.answer: The dual-stream mode supports separate increases for monthly and annual contributions. Returns and inflation remain modeled assumptions.

faqs.question: How do I calculate future value without extra deposits?
faqs.answer: Set the recurring contribution to zero and enter only the initial amount, rate, duration and compounding convention.

faqs.question: Is projected growth the same as the ending balance?
faqs.answer: No. Growth is the balance above the total contributions, after any modeled tax.

faqs.question: Why does contribution timing affect future value?
