The simple method keeps the total starting budget available as balances are cleared. Avalanche sends extra money toward the highest rate; snowball prioritizes the smallest remaining balance.

sections.title: Worked example: compare priorities with the same budget
paragraphs: Consider 1,000 at 12% with a 100 payment and 500 at 0% with a 50 payment. Adding 50 extra gives a fixed 200 monthly budget. Under the calculator’s monthly-interest convention and no new charges, avalanche clears the debts in eight months with about 40.11 interest; snowball also takes eight months but costs about 51.28 interest.

table.caption: Same debts and cash budget, different priority

sections.title: Keep freed payments working after a debt is cleared
paragraphs: When one debt is paid off, retaining its old payment in the budget accelerates the others. The detailed budget-ledger method makes budget policy, payment dates, annual extras and one-time additions explicit. A plan that reduces spending on debt as accounts close will produce a different payoff path.

sections.title: Use the schedule as a plan, then update it
paragraphs: Minimum-payment formulas, variable rates and lender posting dates can change real balances. The entered minimums are modeled amounts, not a live copy of your contracts. Update balances after statements arrive and include only extra payments that the household budget can sustain.

links.label: Check the monthly budget supporting repayment

sections.title: Comparing payoff priorities with the same budget
paragraphs: Keep the total payment budget constant when comparing debt-payoff strategies. Otherwise, a faster result may come from paying more rather than changing which debt receives extra money first. Check how minimum payments, rollover amounts, and dated extras are entered. The schedule assumes the modeled debts and rates, so new borrowing or a rate change requires an updated scenario.

debt-payoff-calculator.seoTitle: Debt Payoff Calculator: Avalanche & Snowball Schedules

credit-card-payoff-calculator.description: Plan payoff across multiple credit cards using avalanche or snowball ordering, entered minimum payments and a monthly extra-payment budget.

faqs.question: Does the schedule recalculate card minimums as balances fall?
faqs.answer: No. Entered minimum payments remain fixed until payoff, unlike issuer formulas that may change the minimum each statement.

faqs.question: Does dividing the annual APR by 12 match every card statement?
faqs.answer: No. This schedule uses that monthly approximation; daily interest methods, fees, rate changes and new purchases can produce different statement amounts.

faqs.question: Does this follow my card issuer’s changing minimum-payment formula?
faqs.answer: No. It uses the payment amounts supplied. Update those inputs when your repayment plan or contractual minimum changes.

faqs.question: Can a balance-transfer promotion be modeled indefinitely?
faqs.answer: Only if that is the assumption you enter. For a promotion that ends, recalculate at the new rate and remaining balance rather than extending 0% forever.

faqs.question: Why might statement interest differ from the estimate?
faqs.answer: Statements may use daily balances, actual cycle lengths, fees and payment posting dates rather than a uniform monthly calculation.

faqs.question: Should extra payments go to every card equally?
faqs.answer: The selected strategy allocates the extra after minimums. Avalanche prioritizes the highest rate; snowball prioritizes the smallest remaining balance.

sections.title: Coordinate payments across several card balances
paragraphs: Use one row per card balance with its APR and planned minimum payment, then enter the extra amount available across the cards. The calculator allocates minimums first and directs extra money according to the selected priority. For a card with several promotional and purchase-rate balances, a single blended rate may hide important differences.

sections.title: Worked example: a fixed 250 monthly card budget
paragraphs: Card A has 2,000 at 24% with a 75 minimum, and Card B has 1,000 at 12% with a 50 minimum. An extra 125 makes the total budget 250. Under the monthly model, no new charges and avalanche priority, the balances clear in 14 months with about 351.24 interest.

table.caption: Inputs for the payoff illustration

sections.title: Minimum payments and promotional rates need attention
paragraphs: The model uses the entered minimums; it does not automatically reproduce each issuer’s percentage-of-balance formula. If a promotional rate expires, rerun the plan with the changed rate and remaining balance. The detailed ledger is useful for adding a one-time payment or choosing how the budget behaves after a card is cleared.

sections.title: Monthly estimates can differ from statement interest
paragraphs: Many card issuers calculate interest using daily balances and daily periodic rates, so exact charges depend on transaction and payment dates. This monthly projection is most useful for comparing repayment choices. Avoid adding new spending to the modeled balances if you want the displayed payoff path to remain meaningful.

links.label: CFPB: how card interest is calculated
Calculate one balance with a fixed payment

sections.title: Planning payments across multiple cards
paragraphs: Enter each card balance and rate separately so that the payoff schedule can allocate payments to the correct debt. Compare strategies using the same overall budget and review what happens when a cleared card's payment rolls over. A statement's changing minimum-payment rules may differ from the model. Adding purchases during repayment also changes the balance path shown by the estimate.

credit-card-payoff-calculator.seoTitle: Credit Card Payoff Calculator: Multiple Card Repayment

debt-consolidation-calculator.description: Compare current debt obligations with a consolidation loan, including financed fees, the new payment and repayment-term effects.

faqs.question: Are consolidation fees added to the new loan?
faqs.answer: The modeled financed fees are added to the combined debt balance before calculating the new loan payment.

faqs.question: Is a lower monthly payment necessarily a cheaper consolidation?
faqs.answer: No. A longer repayment term can reduce payments while increasing total interest. Compare fees, interest and time in debt together.

faqs.question: Are fees included in the new loan balance?
faqs.answer: The basic method finances the entered fee. Use the fee-comparison method when the fee is paid upfront or withheld from proceeds.

faqs.question: Does a lower monthly payment prove consolidation saves money?
faqs.answer: No. The term and fees can offset a lower payment. Compare total cost and payoff timing.

faqs.question: Does the calculator check whether I qualify for the proposed rate?
faqs.answer: No. The rate and term are assumptions or figures from an offer you provide.

faqs.question: Why compare the original debts with the same monthly budget?
faqs.answer: It shows whether the advantage comes from a lower rate or simply from changing how much you pay and how long repayment lasts.

sections.title: Combine balances and show where the fee goes
paragraphs: The basic method sums the entered debts and adds the consolidation fee to the new principal. It then calculates a fixed-payment loan using the proposed rate and term. The fee-comparison method distinguishes financed fees, fees paid separately and fees withheld from proceeds, because those arrangements do not deliver the same cash or repayment balance.

sections.title: Worked example: refinance 8,000 of debts with a fee
paragraphs: Combining balances of 5,000 and 3,000 with a 200 financed fee creates an 8,200 loan. At an assumed 8% nominal rate over three years, the monthly payment is about 256.96, with 1,050.50 interest over the schedule. The fee remains an additional cost even though it is not paid upfront.

table.caption: From balances to the new loan

sections.title: A lower installment does not necessarily mean lower total cost
paragraphs: Extending the repayment term can lower monthly payments while increasing the time interest accrues. Compare the new schedule with a realistic payoff plan for the existing debts, including fees, remaining balances and the same available monthly budget. The sum of current minimums is a cash-flow reference, not a full interest-cost comparison.

sections.title: Keep consolidation distinct from debt settlement
paragraphs: A consolidation loan replaces multiple obligations with another borrowing arrangement; it does not automatically reduce the amount owed. Collateral, promotional rates and contract terms may also differ. Confirm the offered rate and costs before interpreting a hypothetical lower-rate scenario as an available offer.

links.label: Model the existing debts without consolidation

sections.title: Checking whether consolidation reduces total cost
paragraphs: Consolidation replaces several payment streams with a new borrowing arrangement. Compare the new term, fees, and total repayment with the existing debts, not just the first monthly payment. A longer term may make the payment smaller while keeping debt outstanding for longer. Use the fee-adjusted comparison to see how supported upfront charges affect the apparent savings.

debt-consolidation-calculator.seoTitle: Debt Consolidation Calculator: Payments, Fees & Savings

student-loan-calculator.description: Model standard student-loan repayment or annual borrowing during school, with explicit delay-interest and capitalization choices.

faqs.question: Is unpaid school interest always added to principal?
faqs.answer: In the school-borrowing mode, it stays separate unless hypothetical capitalization is selected. The standard deferment mode uses its stated one-time capitalization assumption.

faqs.question: Does this determine federal income-driven payments or forgiveness?
faqs.answer: No. Interest treatment is a scenario choice, not an inference about program eligibility. Income-driven plans and forgiveness require current program-specific guidance.

faqs.question: When is new school borrowing assumed to occur?
faqs.answer: The model adds the annual borrowing at the start of each school year, then tracks each amount over its time outstanding.

faqs.question: Is interest accrual the same as capitalization?
faqs.answer: No. Accrual means interest accumulates; capitalization means qualifying unpaid interest is added to principal.

faqs.question: Does the deferred-interest example apply to every student loan?
faqs.answer: No. It illustrates the selected model. Actual subsidy and capitalization rules depend on the loan and circumstances.

faqs.question: Can I estimate how much principal fits a monthly budget?
faqs.answer: Yes. Select the principal-from-payment method and enter the affordable payment, rate and term.

sections.title: Choose a repayment or school-borrowing scenario
paragraphs: Use the standard loan method for a balance entering repayment, the school-borrowing method for new borrowing during study, or the payment-budget method to estimate a supportable principal. The school method separates interest accrual, paying interest during study and capitalization rather than assuming all loans handle these identically.

sections.title: Worked example: six months of modeled deferred interest
paragraphs: A hypothetical 10,000 balance at 6% accrues 300 of simple interest over six months. In the basic method’s scenario where that interest is added before repayment, the starting repayment balance becomes 10,300. Repaying that amount over ten years at 6% requires about 114.35 per month.

table.caption: Illustrative capitalization scenario

sections.title: Accrued interest and capitalized principal are different
paragraphs: Interest can accumulate without immediately becoming principal. Capitalization adds eligible unpaid interest to principal, which can then increase future interest. Actual treatment depends on loan type and the relevant event; choose the school-method settings that match the loan instead of assuming the example applies to all federal or private loans.

sections.title: A fixed-payment schedule does not calculate every repayment program
paragraphs: This worksheet does not determine income-driven plan eligibility, forgiveness or a current government repayment offer. It compares the supplied borrowing and payment assumptions. If making extra payments, check how the servicer applies them and use updated principal and accrued-interest figures from the account.

links.label: Estimate the education funding gap first
Federal Student Aid: interest and capitalization terminology

sections.title: Separating school borrowing from repayment
paragraphs: Borrowing during school and repaying an existing student loan are different stages. Choose the mode that matches the balance and timing you know. The repayment-budget mode works backward from a payment, while fixed-payment payoff estimates how long a balance takes to clear. These scenarios follow the stated loan model and do not automatically reproduce income-based repayment or forgiveness programs.

student-loan-calculator.seoTitle: Student Loan Calculator: Payments & Borrowing During School

bond-calculator.description: Calculate regular-coupon bond price or yield, including dated settlement, accrued interest and selectable day-count conventions.

faqs.question: Is accrued interest included in the bond price?
faqs.answer: The dated mode reports clean price, accrued interest and dirty price separately. Its cash settlement amount includes accrued interest. The basic years-to-maturity mode assumes coupon-date valuation.

faqs.question: Why does the day-count convention change the answer?
faqs.answer: The convention determines the accrued portion of a coupon and the time to the next payment. US-NASD and European 30/360 can differ at month ends.

faqs.question: Does the yield account for default or early redemption?
faqs.answer: No. These modes assume the scheduled regular coupons and redemption amount are paid.

faqs.question: Why can a bond trade below face value?
faqs.answer: If the required yield exceeds its fixed coupon rate, discounting the scheduled cash flows can produce a price below face value.

faqs.question: Is coupon rate the same as yield to maturity?
faqs.answer: No. Coupon rate determines scheduled interest on face value; yield relates the price paid to the future cash-flow schedule.

faqs.question: What is the difference between clean and dirty price?
faqs.answer: Dirty price includes accrued interest; clean price excludes it.

faqs.question: Does the calculated price guarantee that I can sell at that amount?
faqs.answer: No. It is a value under the entered yield and cash-flow assumptions, not a live market quote or liquidity guarantee.

sections.title: Distinguish coupon rate from yield to maturity
paragraphs: The coupon rate determines the stated cash coupon on face value. Yield is the rate used to discount those coupons and the maturity payment into a price. Choose whether to solve for price or yield, and match payment frequency to the bond’s coupon schedule. The simple term method assumes regular coupon periods.

sections.title: Worked example: a coupon below the required yield
paragraphs: For a 1,000 face-value bond with a 5% annual coupon paid semiannually, each coupon is 25. With five years remaining and a 6% nominal yield compounded semiannually, the ten coupons and final principal have a combined present value of about 957.35. The price is below face value because the coupon rate is lower than the assumed yield.

table.caption: Regular-coupon bond illustration

sections.title: Use settlement dates for accrued-interest questions
paragraphs: The dated method distinguishes a quoted clean price from a dirty price that includes accrued coupon interest. Day-count conventions affect the fraction of the coupon period elapsed, particularly around month ends. Select the convention in the actual instrument rather than assuming every bond uses the same calendar rule.

sections.title: The discounting model does not assess the issuer
paragraphs: The price calculation assumes the entered contractual cash flows are paid. It does not estimate default probability, a call option, market liquidity or transaction charges. A callable or irregular-coupon instrument can require a different valuation even when the simple coupon and maturity inputs look similar.

links.label: SEC Investor.gov: bond characteristics and risks

sections.title: Reading bond price and yield together
paragraphs: A bond's coupon rate, market price, and yield describe different things. When working with settlement dates, check the payment schedule and day-count convention because accrued interest and remaining cash flows depend on them. Compare clean and settlement-related values using the labels shown. A calculated yield assumes the modeled payments and does not remove the possibility of default or changing market prices.

bond-calculator.seoTitle: Bond Calculator: Price, Yield & Accrued Interest

average-return-calculator.description: Compare arithmetic and geometric period returns, or estimate annual money-weighted return from dated deposits and receipts.

faqs.question: Which average reflects compound growth across equal periods?
faqs.answer: The geometric average links the period growth factors. The arithmetic average adds percentage returns and divides by their count.

faqs.question: What if my deposits and withdrawals occur on irregular dates?
faqs.answer: Use the dated money-weighted mode with negative investor payments and positive receipts. It accounts for unequal intervals using elapsed days.

faqs.question: Why can the average be zero while money is lost?
faqs.answer: Percentages apply to different balances. A 20% loss after a 20% gain reduces 1,200 to 960, not back to 1,000.

faqs.question: Which average describes compound growth?
faqs.answer: The geometric average gives the constant per-period growth rate matching the full sequence.

faqs.question: Should monthly and annual returns be entered together?
faqs.answer: No. Use equal-length periods or an appropriate dated cash-flow method.

faqs.question: Can I calculate performance from opening and closing balances if I added money?
faqs.answer: Not reliably without separating deposits and withdrawals from gains. Use the dated money-weighted method for those cash flows.

sections.title: Use arithmetic and geometric averages for different questions
paragraphs: The arithmetic average adds the period returns and divides by their count. The geometric average finds the constant compounded rate producing the same cumulative growth. Enter percentage returns for equal-length periods, such as one value per year, without mixing annual and monthly observations.

sections.title: Worked example: a gain followed by an equal percentage loss
paragraphs: Returns of +20% and −20% have an arithmetic average of zero. But an opening 1,000 becomes 1,200 after the gain and 960 after the loss. The cumulative return is −4%, and the geometric average is about −2.0204% per period.

table.caption: Equal percentages do not cancel on changing balances

sections.title: Do not use balance changes as returns when cash moved
paragraphs: A deposit can increase an account balance without being an investment gain, and a withdrawal can lower it without being a loss. For cash flows on specific dates, use the dated money-weighted method with negative amounts invested and positive amounts received, including the final account value as a terminal inflow.

sections.title: Period labels determine how the result is read
paragraphs: A geometric average of monthly observations is a monthly rate; it is not automatically an annual return. Cumulative return describes the entire entered span. The unlevered return-list model does not accept losses below −100%, and one −100% period reduces its compounded wealth product to zero.

links.label: Measure gain relative to total cost

sections.title: Choosing an average that matches the question
paragraphs: A gain of 50% followed by a loss of 50% has an arithmetic average of 0%, but 100 invested becomes 150 and then 75. The total loss is 25%; the geometric average is about −13.40% per period. Use equal-length periods for this comparison. If you added or withdrew money between dates, use the dated money-weighted mode instead: the timing and size of those cash flows affect your personal return.

average-return-calculator.seoTitle: Average Return Calculator: Arithmetic & Geometric Returns

roi-calculator.description: Calculate ROI and annualized return from a holding period or exact dates, or use dated cash flows for money-weighted return.

faqs.question: How does exact-date annualized ROI handle time?
faqs.answer: It uses the actual elapsed calendar days and a 365-day annualization convention between the initial cost and final proceeds.

faqs.question: Which mode fits several deposits and withdrawals?
faqs.answer: Use dated money-weighted return with signed cash flows. Simple ROI annualization assumes one initial investment and one final receipt.

faqs.question: Should I enter profit or total proceeds?
faqs.answer: Enter total money received as proceeds. The calculator subtracts the total cost to find profit.

faqs.question: Where do fees go?
faqs.answer: Enter eligible investment costs once in the fee field or in your cost basis, without counting them in both.

faqs.question: Why is annualized ROI not total ROI divided by years?
faqs.answer: The annualized method uses compound growth, so it takes a root of the ending-to-starting ratio.

faqs.question: Can one ROI figure accurately describe repeated deposits?
faqs.answer: It omits timing. Use the dated cash-flow method when money moves in or out during the investment.

sections.title: Compare the net gain with the full investment cost
paragraphs: The basic calculation uses total cost = purchase cost + entered fees, net profit = proceeds − total cost, and ROI = net profit ÷ total cost. Proceeds should include the amount received at the end, not only the gain. Include fees once and keep all amounts in the same currency.

sections.title: Worked example: a two-year investment with fees
paragraphs: Paying 1,000 plus 100 in fees and later receiving 1,300 creates a 200 net profit. Total ROI is 200/1,100 = 18.1818%. Over two years, the compound annualized return is about 8.7115%, because (1,300/1,100)^(1/2) − 1 differs from simply halving total ROI.

table.caption: Cost, gain and annualization

sections.title: Choose the dated method when the calendar matters
paragraphs: The date-based method derives the holding period from the entered dates. For extra investments, distributions or withdrawals during the holding period, use dated cash flows instead of compressing everything into one beginning amount and one ending amount. Timing changes a money-weighted return.

sections.title: A return percentage does not describe every investment tradeoff
paragraphs: The same ROI can come from different holding periods, risk levels and cash requirements. This calculator does not adjust for inflation or establish tax treatment. Compare annualized rates on the same timing basis and examine the underlying cash flows before using the percentage to rank alternatives.

links.label: Convert a nominal amount for inflation

sections.title: Putting return on investment in context
paragraphs: ROI compares the gain or loss with the amount invested, but a percentage alone does not describe how long the investment lasted. Use the exact-date annualized mode when duration matters. If money enters or leaves at several dates, the dated cash-flow mode is more informative than treating everything as one initial purchase. Keep costs consistent across investments being compared.

roi-calculator.seoTitle: ROI Calculator: Total & Annualized Investment Return

irr-calculator.description: Estimate periodic or dated internal rates of return, including recurring cash-flow scenarios and detected multiple solutions.

faqs.question: Is every IRR result automatically an annual rate?
faqs.answer: No. Periodic IRR uses the cash-flow interval. Dated IRR uses elapsed days with a 365-day annualization convention; recurring mode also shows annual conversion.

faqs.question: Can the same cash flows have more than one IRR?
faqs.answer: Yes. Multiple sign changes can create multiple roots. The calculator reports detected solutions within its supported search range.

faqs.question: Why must at least one cash flow be negative and another positive?
faqs.answer: IRR balances money paid out against money received. A sequence of only one sign cannot offset to zero in the usual model.

faqs.question: Is the periodic IRR always annual?
faqs.answer: No. It is per entered interval. Annual cash flows produce an annual rate; monthly cash flows produce a monthly rate.

faqs.question: Why should a zero-cash-flow period remain in the list?
faqs.answer: Removing it moves later money earlier on the timeline and changes the return.

faqs.question: Why are several IRRs possible?
faqs.answer: Multiple changes between positive and negative cash flows can make the NPV equation cross zero more than once.

sections.title: Put each cash flow on the correct timeline
paragraphs: For equal intervals, enter the initial investment as a negative first cash flow and later receipts as positive values. Include zeros for periods with no cash flow rather than deleting those periods. The dated method uses actual dates; the regular-payment method describes repeated equal cash flows and a terminal amount.

sections.title: Worked example: a two-period investment
paragraphs: Cash flows of −1,000 now, 0 after one period and +1,210 after two periods have an IRR of 10% per period. At that rate, −1,000 + 1,210/1.10² = 0. At a 5% discount rate, their NPV is about 97.51 instead.

table.caption: Cash-flow timing matters

sections.title: IRR is the rate where net present value becomes zero
paragraphs: The periodic result is a rate per entered interval. If intervals are monthly, annualize consistently before comparing it with an annual rate. The discount-rate input calculates NPV; it does not tell the solver what IRR to return. NPV measures value at your chosen rate, while IRR solves for a zero-value rate.

sections.title: Check unusual cash flows before trusting one percentage
paragraphs: A sequence that changes sign more than once can have multiple IRRs, and some cash flows have no usable solution. The periodic search reports detected sign-changing roots within its supported range and may miss a tangent root. Read the cash-flow pattern and NPV alongside the detected rates.

sections.title: Reading an internal rate of return carefully
paragraphs: IRR is the rate that makes the modeled cash flows balance in present-value terms. Enter outgoing and incoming amounts with the required signs, and select periodic or dated cash flows according to their timing. Irregular sign changes can make interpretation more difficult. Compare the cash-flow schedule and investment size alongside the rate rather than ranking projects from IRR alone.

irr-calculator.seoTitle: IRR Calculator: Periodic & Dated Cash Flow Returns

payback-period-calculator.description: Estimate simple or discounted payback from entered periodic cash flows or an annual return stream with assumed growth.

faqs.question: How is a fractional payback period calculated?
faqs.answer: The model interpolates cash within the recovery period. Actual receipts arriving only at period end can produce a different practical recovery date.

faqs.question: Does the shortest payback always identify the best investment?
faqs.answer: No. Payback alone does not value all later cash flows or fully describe risk. Discounted payback also depends on the chosen discount rate.

faqs.question: Why is discounted payback usually longer?
faqs.answer: At a positive discount rate, future receipts are worth less at the starting date, so more receipts are needed to recover the outlay.

faqs.question: What does “not recovered” mean?
faqs.answer: The entered cash flows do not recover the initial investment within the supplied periods under that method.

faqs.question: Does a 2.5-year result mean cash is actually received halfway through year 3?
faqs.answer: It is an interpolation. If the third receipt arrives only at year-end, actual cash recovery occurs on that payment date.

faqs.question: Can payback alone identify the most profitable project?
faqs.answer: No. It does not account for all cash flows after recovery and should be considered alongside return and present-value measures.

sections.title: Measure how long cash receipts take to recover the initial outlay
paragraphs: Enter a negative initial investment followed by net cash receipts for equal periods. Simple payback adds those receipts without discounting. Discounted payback first reduces each future receipt to its value at the entered discount rate. Use cash flow rather than accounting profit if the question is recovery of cash invested.

sections.title: Worked example: 10,000 recovered from annual receipts
paragraphs: An initial outlay of 10,000 followed by 4,000 at the end of each of three years has simple payback of 2.5 years under within-period interpolation. Discounting each receipt at 5% gives a discounted payback of about 2.7416 years.

table.caption: Simple cumulative cash recovery

sections.title: A fractional payback is an interpolation assumption
paragraphs: If all cash actually arrives in one lump at year-end, recovery occurs at that payment date rather than continuously during the year. The fraction indicates how much of the next modeled cash flow is needed. The growing-cash-flow method generates a schedule from the first annual receipt and its growth assumption.

sections.title: Payback omits part of the investment decision
paragraphs: Simple payback ignores the time value of money, and both payback measures ignore returns arriving after the recovery point. Two projects with the same payback can have different total value. Compare NPV or IRR when later cash flows or scale differences matter.

links.label: Compare NPV and internal rate of return

sections.title: What a payback period does and does not show
paragraphs: The payback period identifies when accumulated modeled inflows recover the initial outlay. Check whether the selected result uses discounted cash flows before comparing it with another payback estimate. Cash received after the recovery point still matters to total project value. A short payback therefore describes recovery speed, rather than proving that a project has the highest overall return.

payback-period-calculator.seoTitle: Payback Period Calculator: Simple & Discounted Recovery

depreciation-calculator.description: Compare book-depreciation schedules, including fiscal dates, partial-year conventions and an optional switch to straight-line expense.

faqs.question: Is this a complete tax-depreciation calculation?
faqs.answer: No. These are book-depreciation scenarios. MACRS, bonus depreciation and section 179 eligibility are not determined.

faqs.question: What does the fiscal-year mode add?
faqs.answer: It accepts a service date, fiscal-year start, declining factor and partial-year convention. It can switch permanently to straight-line when that gives the higher annual rate.

faqs.question: Will every declining-balance schedule reach salvage value?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. With the straight-line switch disabled, the model leaves unused basis rather than forcing a final writeoff.

faqs.question: Is salvage value subtracted before straight-line depreciation?
faqs.answer: Yes. The amount allocated over useful life is cost minus salvage value.

faqs.question: Can book value fall below the entered salvage value?
faqs.answer: The schedule limits depreciation to the depreciable amount and retains the entered salvage floor.

faqs.question: Does depreciation measure cash paid each year?
faqs.answer: No. It allocates the cost of the asset. Cash payments and financing follow their own schedules.

faqs.question: Can I copy the result directly into a tax return?
faqs.answer: Only if the method and assumptions match the applicable tax rules. The calculator does not determine asset eligibility or all tax-specific depreciation elections.

sections.title: Separate depreciable cost from residual value
paragraphs: Enter asset cost, estimated salvage value and useful life. Depreciable amount is cost minus salvage. Straight-line depreciation spreads that amount evenly; accelerated methods allocate more to earlier years. The fiscal method adds a service date, fiscal-year boundary and timing convention for a partial-year schedule.

sections.title: Worked example: straight-line depreciation over five years
paragraphs: An asset costing 12,000 with an estimated salvage value of 2,000 has a depreciable amount of 10,000. Over five years, straight-line depreciation is 2,000 per year. Book value falls from 12,000 to 10,000 after year one and reaches the 2,000 salvage value after year five.

table.caption: Straight-line book value

sections.title: An accelerated method changes timing, not the salvage floor
paragraphs: Double-declining balance applies its rate to declining book value, subject to the model’s salvage limit and final-year adjustment. Sum-of-the-years’ digits uses declining fractions of the depreciable amount. The detailed fiscal method makes the optional switch to straight line explicit, which can change later-year allocations.

sections.title: Book depreciation is not a market appraisal or tax election
paragraphs: The schedule allocates cost under the selected method; it does not predict resale value. Tax systems may require their own asset classes, recovery periods, conventions or special deductions. This worksheet is not a complete US MACRS, Section 179 or bonus-depreciation calculation.

links.label: IRS: tax depreciation methods and requirements
Include operating costs in business cash planning

sections.title: Allocating asset cost across accounting periods
paragraphs: Book depreciation spreads the depreciable amount across periods according to the selected method. Enter the asset cost, residual value, and useful life consistently, and use the fiscal-year mode when the acquisition date affects the schedule. The remaining book value is an accounting result rather than a prediction of resale price. Tax depreciation can follow separate rules from the displayed book schedule.

depreciation-calculator.seoTitle: Depreciation Calculator: Asset Value & Book Schedules

margin-calculator.description: Calculate profit margin and markup, solve a target selling price, or explore simplified stock and currency margin requirements.

faqs.question: Why are margin and markup different percentages?
faqs.answer: Margin divides profit by revenue; markup divides profit by cost. The profit-and-margin inverse requires positive profit and positive margin in this model.

faqs.question: Do the stock and FX modes apply my broker’s exact requirements?
faqs.answer: No. They use entered ratios, leverage and exchange rates. Broker rules, financing charges and instrument requirements can differ.

faqs.question: How do I price for a target margin?
faqs.answer: For cost C and target margin m as a decimal, price = C/(1 − m). A target below 100% is required for a finite positive price.

faqs.question: Does the profit result include overhead and taxes?
faqs.answer: Only if the costs you enter include the relevant amounts. The basic calculation does not add them automatically.

faqs.question: Is stock margin the same as sales profit margin?
faqs.answer: No. Stock margin concerns borrowed funds and account equity; sales margin measures profit relative to selling price.

sections.title: Profit margin and markup use different denominators
paragraphs: Profit is selling price minus cost. Margin divides that profit by selling price; markup divides it by cost. Use the basic or known-pair method to recover missing amounts, or use target margin to find the price needed for a chosen margin. Include the same cost categories consistently when comparing products.

sections.title: Worked example: a 60 cost and a 100 selling price
paragraphs: A product costing 60 and selling for 100 produces 40 of profit before any costs you have omitted. Margin is 40/100 = 40%, while markup is 40/60 = 66.67%. A 40% markup on 60 would instead produce a price of 84 and a margin of only 28.57%.

table.caption: Margin and markup are not interchangeable

sections.title: Use a complete cost figure for the decision
paragraphs: Product cost alone may describe gross product margin but omit payment fees, shipping, returns or overhead. The calculator reports the relationship between the entered cost and revenue; it does not decide which accounting costs belong in your analysis. For marketplace sales, the seller-profit calculator separates several of those charges.

sections.title: Trading margin is a separate calculation
paragraphs: The stock and foreign-exchange methods estimate financing or collateral requirements from the entered purchase, leverage and maintenance assumptions. They do not calculate a product’s profit margin or determine a broker’s actual requirements. Choose the method by the meaning of margin in your question.

links.label: Include selling fees and fulfillment costs
Find the volume needed to cover fixed costs

sections.title: Distinguishing profit margin from markup
paragraphs: An item that costs 80 and sells for 100 earns 20 before other costs. Its margin is 20 ÷ 100 = 20%, while its markup is 20 ÷ 80 = 25%. To achieve a 30% margin on a cost of 80, divide 80 by 0.70 to get approximately 114.29; adding 30% to cost would give only 104. Include the costs you intend the margin to cover. Stock and foreign-exchange margin modes calculate collateral requirements, a different use of the word margin.

margin-calculator.seoTitle: Margin Calculator: Profit Margin, Markup & Selling Price

commission-calculator.description: Calculate flat or tiered sales commission, total compensation, or the sales and rate needed for a target commission.

faqs.question: Do tiered rates apply to all sales once a threshold is reached?
faqs.answer: No. This is a marginal schedule: each rate applies only to sales within its tier, rather than retroactively to all sales.

faqs.question: What happens above the highest entered tier?
faqs.answer: The final tier's rate continues above its upper limit. Confirm that this matches the actual commission agreement.

faqs.question: Should I enter invoiced sales or collected cash?
faqs.answer: Use the commissionable basis defined by the agreement. The calculator cannot determine that contract term.

faqs.question: Does total compensation include tax deductions?
faqs.answer: No. It adds modeled commission and entered base pay before withholding or other deductions.

sections.title: Choose flat commission, reverse calculation or marginal tiers
paragraphs: The flat method multiplies eligible sales by the commission percentage and adds any base pay. The inverse method finds a missing sales amount or rate. For a tiered plan, enter increasing thresholds and the rate applying to each sales band. Confirm that the contract defines eligible sales the same way you do.

sections.title: Worked example: a two-tier commission plan
paragraphs: Suppose the first 10,000 of sales earns 5%, and sales above that threshold earn 10%. At 15,000 of sales, commission is 500 on the first band plus 500 on the remaining 5,000, giving 1,000. With 2,000 of base pay for the same period, total compensation is 3,000.

table.caption: Marginal tiers apply only to their band

sections.title: Marginal and retroactive commission plans differ
paragraphs: This tier method applies each rate to the sales within its band. It does not apply the highest achieved rate to every sale. The final tier continues above its lower threshold in the calculator, so check the result table and do not interpret the final entered upper number as a hard sales cap.

sections.title: Keep sales basis and payment period consistent
paragraphs: A contract may calculate commission on collected revenue, invoiced sales, gross profit or an amount after returns. Enter the basis required by that agreement. Base pay must cover the same time period as the sales figure. Draws, chargebacks and tax withholding are not automatically included.

links.label: Check gross profit before a profit-based commission

sections.title: Understanding flat and tiered commission
paragraphs: A flat commission applies one rate to the selected sales amount. A marginal tier schedule applies different rates to portions of that amount, rather than automatically applying the highest rate to all sales. Enter the tiers in the order requested and compare the total commission with the underlying sales figure. The result follows the entered schedule, not an employer's unentered bonus or clawback rules.

commission-calculator.seoTitle: Commission Calculator: Flat Rates, Tiers & Sales Targets

discount-calculator.description: Calculate sale price and savings, combine a percentage and fixed reduction, or recover the original price from a known pair.

faqs.question: In what order are a percentage and fixed discount applied?
faqs.answer: The main calculation applies the percentage reduction first, then subtracts the fixed amount. The known-pair mode solves one discount relationship from the selected inputs.

faqs.question: Can a zero final price determine the original price?
faqs.answer: At 100% off, every original price produces zero. That inverse case is indeterminate; a positive final price with 100% off is inconsistent.

faqs.question: Is sales tax included in the discounted price?
faqs.answer: The optional tax field applies your entered rate to the price after the percentage and fixed discounts. It does not determine the applicable rate or the legal tax treatment of a coupon; delivery charges are not included.

faqs.question: Is a fixed voucher deducted before the percentage discount?
faqs.answer: In the sale-price method, the percentage discount is applied first and the fixed discount is deducted afterward.

faqs.question: Why do I divide by the remaining percentage to find original price?
faqs.answer: The sale price is only the remaining fraction of the original. Dividing by that fraction reverses the discount.

faqs.question: Does savings include the tax amount?
faqs.answer: The displayed savings figure is before tax; the final total separately includes the entered post-discount tax.

faqs.question: Can the calculator tell whether a coupon applies to my item?
faqs.answer: No. Eligibility, stacking restrictions and taxable treatment come from the retailer and applicable rules.

sections.title: Follow the order of percentage discount, fixed discount and tax
paragraphs: The sale-price method reduces the original price by the percentage discount, subtracts the additional fixed discount, then applies the entered tax to that reduced amount. Use the known-pair method when you know two values and need to recover the original price, final price, amount saved or discount rate.

sections.title: Worked example: a percentage sale plus a voucher
paragraphs: An original price of 120 with 20% off becomes 96. Applying an additional fixed discount of 10 makes the pre-tax price 86. At an illustrative 5% tax applied after discounts, the final total is 90.30 and the pre-tax saving is 34.

table.caption: Order of operations for the example

sections.title: Recover the original price by dividing, not adding
paragraphs: If an item sells for 80 after a single 20% discount, its original price was 80/(1 − 0.20) = 100. Adding 20% to 80 gives 96, because the second percentage uses a different base. A full 100% discount cannot reveal a unique original price from a zero final price alone.

sections.title: Check coupon eligibility and taxable amount
paragraphs: The calculator follows the stated discount order; a retailer may restrict coupon stacking or apply tax under different local rules. Shipping, minimum-spend thresholds and excluded products are not inferred. For two successive percentage discounts, use the percent-off calculator’s sequential method.

links.label: Add or remove a separately known tax

sections.title: Checking the price before and after a discount
paragraphs: For an original price of 120, a 25% discount removes 30 and leaves 90. If you also enter a fixed discount of 10, this calculator applies it afterward, giving a final price of 80. Reversing the order would give 82.50, so check the promotion's terms before comparing the result with a checkout total. Use the known-pair mode when you know the sale price and need the original price or discount. The optional tax rate applies after the discounts; delivery charges are not included.

percent-off-calculator.description: Calculate percent-off savings and final prices, or combine two successive percentage discounts without simply adding them.

faqs.question: Do discounts of 20% and then 10% equal 30% off?
faqs.answer: No. Each percentage acts on the current price, so a $100 item falls to $80 and then $72, for a 28% combined reduction.

faqs.question: Can I recover an original price from the sale price?
faqs.answer: Use the known-pair mode with final price and percent off. A zero final price at 100% off cannot identify one original price.

faqs.question: Why is 20% off plus 10% off only 28% off?
faqs.answer: You pay 80% of the original and then 90% of that reduced amount: 0.8 × 0.9 = 0.72, leaving a 28% reduction.

faqs.question: Does the order of two percentage discounts matter?
faqs.answer: For pure percentage reductions without rounding or other conditions, no. Multiplying the retained fractions gives the same result.

faqs.question: How do I find the discount from original and sale prices?
faqs.answer: Divide original minus sale price by original, then multiply by 100.

faqs.question: Can I compare promotions with different starting prices?
faqs.answer: Yes. Calculate each final amount and compare the totals, including any relevant shipping and tax.

sections.title: Turn a discount into the fraction of the price you still pay
paragraphs: For one discount, sale price = original price × (1 − discount percentage/100). The amount saved is the difference between the original and sale prices. The reverse method can recover the original amount or percentage when the relevant known values are supplied.

sections.title: Worked example: 20% off followed by another 10%
paragraphs: A 200 item becomes 160 after 20% off, then 144 after a further 10% off the reduced price. Total savings are 56, equivalent to 28% of the original price. The combined discount is not 30%, because the second discount applies to 160 rather than 200.

table.caption: Successive percentage reductions

sections.title: Use the retained fractions to combine discounts
paragraphs: Two discounts d₁ and d₂ combine as 1 − (1 − d₁)(1 − d₂), with rates expressed as decimals. For pure percentage reductions, swapping their order produces the same price. A fixed-value voucher can make order matter, so use the method matching the promotion’s terms.

sections.title: Compare the amount paid, not just the largest percentage
paragraphs: A larger advertised percentage on a higher starting price can still leave a higher final price. Compare shipping, taxes and any excluded items separately. The single-discount method applies its entered tax after reductions; it does not establish the retailer’s legal tax base.

links.label: Combine a percentage discount with a fixed voucher

sections.title: Why successive discounts do not simply add
paragraphs: A second percentage discount normally applies to the price remaining after the first reduction. Use the consecutive-discount mode to see that effect rather than adding the two percentages. The known-pair mode can work backward from a final price or saving. Keep the original price visible when comparing promotions so that a larger advertised percentage is not mistaken for a lower final cost.

percent-off-calculator.seoTitle: Percent Off Calculator: Sale Price & Combined Discounts

sales-tax-calculator.description: Calculate net price, sales tax, gross price or an implied tax rate from a selected pair of known values.

faqs.question: How do I remove tax already included in a total?
faqs.answer: Divide the total by one plus the tax rate. The known-pair mode also solves from net and gross prices or from tax amount and a positive rate.

faqs.question: Does the calculator find the sales-tax rate for my address?
faqs.answer: No. You supply the rate and determine whether the transaction is taxable or exempt.

faqs.question: How do I remove tax from an inclusive price?
faqs.answer: Divide the total by 1 plus the tax rate as a decimal. Tax is the difference between the gross and net amounts.

faqs.question: Does the calculator find my local rate?
faqs.answer: No. You supply the rate applicable to the transaction.

faqs.question: Can I use one rate for a basket with exempt items?
faqs.answer: Apply the rate only to the taxable portion, or calculate items with different treatments separately.

faqs.question: Why can a receipt differ by a cent?
faqs.answer: Line-by-line and total-level rounding can produce slightly different totals.

sections.title: Choose whether the entered amount already includes tax
paragraphs: For a tax-exclusive price, the calculator adds tax. For a tax-inclusive total, it separates the net price and tax using division. The known-pair method can recover a rate or missing amount from supported combinations of net price, gross total and tax.

sections.title: Worked example: remove an 8% tax from a 108 total
paragraphs: When a total of 108 already includes 8% tax, the net price is 108/1.08 = 100 and tax is 8. Subtracting 8% of 108 would give 99.36, which is not the original taxable price because the tax percentage is defined relative to the net amount.

table.caption: Exclusive and inclusive calculations agree

sections.title: Use the applicable rate and taxable portion
paragraphs: The tool does not look up a jurisdiction from an address or decide which goods, services, delivery charges or discounts are taxable. Enter the combined applicable rate only when it applies to the same taxable base. For a mixed basket with exemptions or different rates, calculate the groups separately.

sections.title: Understand why receipt rounding can differ
paragraphs: A retailer can round tax on individual lines while a simple estimate rounds the aggregate result. Small differences can occur even with the same rate. Use the net, tax and gross outputs to check arithmetic while keeping actual invoice rules and the transaction date in view.

links.label: Apply discounts before a modeled tax

sections.title: Working with tax-inclusive and pre-tax prices
paragraphs: At an entered rate of 8%, a pre-tax price of 100 becomes 108. If 108 already includes tax, divide by 1.08 to recover the pre-tax price of 100; the tax is 8. Multiplying 108 by 8% would incorrectly calculate tax on the tax-inclusive total. Choose the inclusive or exclusive mode to match your receipt. You supply the rate: the calculator does not look up an address, determine taxability, or apply exemptions.

sales-tax-calculator.seoTitle: Sales Tax Calculator: Add Tax or Find the Pre-Tax Price

vat-calculator.description: Calculate VAT, net or gross amounts, or an implied VAT rate from the values you already know.

faqs.question: How is VAT extracted from a tax-inclusive price?
faqs.answer: Net equals gross divided by one plus the entered rate. VAT is the difference. The known-pair mode can also start from tax amount and a positive rate.

faqs.question: Does this decide which VAT rate or exemption applies?
faqs.answer: No. Rate selection, place of supply, exemptions and recoverability are outside this arithmetic model.

faqs.question: How do I extract 20% VAT from a gross total?
faqs.answer: Divide gross by 1.20 to find net, then subtract net from gross. The VAT fraction of gross is 20/120.

faqs.question: Is 20% the VAT rate in every country?
faqs.answer: No. It is an example rate. Enter the rate applicable to your country and supply.

faqs.question: Are zero-rated and exempt transactions the same?
faqs.answer: No. Their legal treatment can differ even when simple price arithmetic adds no VAT.

faqs.question: Does this calculate how much VAT my business can reclaim?
faqs.answer: No. It splits or adds a supplied rate and does not determine input-tax recovery or return liability.

sections.title: Add VAT to a net amount or extract it from a gross amount
paragraphs: With a net price N and rate r, VAT = N × r and gross price = N × (1 + r). If the price already includes VAT, net = gross/(1 + r). Select the matching direction before entering the amount so VAT is not added twice.

sections.title: Worked example: split a VAT-inclusive invoice amount
paragraphs: At an illustrative 20% VAT rate, a gross amount of 240 consists of 200 net and 40 VAT. The tax is one-sixth of this gross amount, since 0.20/1.20 = 1/6. It is not 20% of 240.

table.caption: A single-rate VAT illustration

sections.title: An entered rate does not determine VAT liability
paragraphs: VAT rates and exemptions depend on the country, supply and circumstances. A numerical zero rate is not the same legal category as exemption, even though both may produce no tax added in simple arithmetic. The calculator does not determine registration requirements, place of supply or reverse-charge obligations.

sections.title: A price split is not a VAT return
paragraphs: For a mixed-rate invoice, separate the amounts by applicable rate. Input-tax recovery, allowable deductions, credits and accounting periods require their own records and rules. Use the output to check the net/tax/gross relationship, then apply the relevant local requirements to the transaction.

links.label: GOV.UK: an example of rate and exemption distinctions

sections.title: Extracting VAT from an inclusive price
paragraphs: A price of 120 including VAT at an illustrative rate of 20% contains 100 net and 20 VAT: 120 ÷ 1.20 = 100. Taking 20% of 120 would give 24 because it uses the wrong base. To add VAT instead, multiply the net price by 1.20. Use one currency consistently and select whether your known amount includes VAT. The entered rate is an assumption; the tool does not determine the applicable rate or whether VAT can be recovered.

vat-calculator.seoTitle: VAT Calculator: Add or Remove VAT from a Price

salary-calculator.description: Convert hourly wages to annual salary or yearly pay to hourly, weekly, biweekly and monthly amounts. Compare gross pay and unpaid leave.

faqs.question: Why do biweekly and semimonthly pay differ?
faqs.answer: Annualization uses 26 biweekly periods and 24 semimonthly periods. Quarterly pay uses four periods.

faqs.question: Do holidays and vacation automatically reduce annual salary?
faqs.answer: Only the separate unpaid-day scenario reduces earnings. Paid leave does not automatically reduce a fixed annual salary.

faqs.question: Is the converted salary my take-home pay?
faqs.answer: No. These are gross-pay conversions before taxes, benefits and payroll deductions.

faqs.question: How much is $25 an hour per year?
faqs.answer: At 40 paid hours per week for 52 weeks, $25 an hour is $52,000 a year before taxes and deductions. Unpaid time and a different work schedule change that amount.

faqs.question: Does an hourly conversion include overtime premiums?
faqs.answer: No. The basic conversion multiplies the entered rate by the schedule. Overtime or other premiums require a separate earnings assumption.

sections.title: Convert gross pay using the working schedule
paragraphs: Select the period for the entered pay amount and provide working hours and days per week. The calculator annualizes the amount using its displayed convention, then converts that annual figure into other periods. These are gross equivalents before taxes, benefits and other payroll deductions.

sections.title: How do I convert hourly pay to yearly salary?
paragraphs: Multiply your hourly rate by paid hours per week and 52 weeks. For example, $25 per hour × 40 hours × 52 weeks = $52,000 per year before taxes and deductions. To convert annual salary back to hourly pay, divide it by the same scheduled hours: $52,000 ÷ 2,080 = $25 per hour. Change the hours and days to match your own schedule.

sections.title: Compare salary across pay periods
paragraphs: The same annual salary produces different paycheck amounts depending on the number of pay periods. Biweekly means every two weeks, usually 26 payments per year in this conversion; semimonthly means twice per month, or 24 payments. The table below uses a $52,000 gross salary, 40 hours per week and five working days. Amounts are rounded to cents.

table.caption: Example gross-pay conversion: $52,000 per year

links.label: Compare pay periods and unpaid days

sections.title: Gross pay, take-home pay and unpaid leave
paragraphs: The salary conversion is gross pay, before tax withholding, benefits and other payroll deductions. Overtime, bonuses and variable shifts are not automatically included. A real payroll calendar can have a different number of pay dates from the fixed annualization used here.

Paid vacation does not automatically reduce a fixed annual salary. Enter only unpaid days in the separate adjustment: at $25 per hour and eight hours per day, ten unpaid days reduce annual earnings by $2,000, from $52,000 to $50,000. The conversion table continues to show the gross schedule before this adjustment.

links.label: Convert a freelance income goal into a billing rate

salary-calculator.seoTitle: Salary Calculator: Hourly to Annual Pay Converter

budget-calculator.description: Build a monthly budget from take-home totals or mixed-period gross-income lines, with pretax savings, assumed tax and debt payments.

faqs.question: Should I enter gross salary or take-home income?
faqs.answer: Use take-home income in the simple budget. In Mixed-period budget & debt ratio, use gross income; that mode separately subtracts pretax saving and the entered flat tax.

faqs.question: Can I combine annual and monthly amounts?
faqs.answer: Yes. Each mixed-period line has its own annual or monthly selector; annual amounts are divided by twelve.

faqs.question: How can I avoid counting a debt payment twice?
faqs.answer: Enter a payment in either living expenses or debt payments, not both. The mixed-period model deducts the two groups separately.

faqs.question: Should simple-budget income be gross or take-home?
faqs.answer: Take-home income usually makes the cash budget easier to interpret because taxes and payroll deductions have already been removed.

faqs.question: Why does saving reduce the remaining balance?
faqs.answer: Saving is a planned allocation of cash. The remaining balance shows money not assigned to any entered category.

faqs.question: How should I include an annual bill?
faqs.answer: Convert it to a monthly equivalent by dividing by 12, or use the period-line method.

faqs.question: Does a positive remaining amount mean every future cost is covered?
faqs.answer: Only the entered categories are covered. Include irregular bills, maintenance and other relevant obligations before treating the remainder as available.

sections.title: Put income and spending on the same monthly basis
paragraphs: Use take-home monthly income in the simple budget and enter housing, utilities, food, transport, insurance, debt payments, savings and other allocations. Savings is treated as an assigned use of money, so it reduces the remaining balance even though it is not consumption. The period-line method can normalize mixed income and expense frequencies.

sections.title: Worked example: a 4,000 monthly income
paragraphs: Allocating 1,200 to housing, 250 to utilities, 450 to food, 300 to transport, 200 to insurance, 300 to debt, 500 to saving and 300 to other costs uses 3,500. The remaining monthly balance is 500, and the savings allocation is 12.5% of income.

table.caption: A budget separates assignments from the remaining buffer

sections.title: Normalize irregular costs instead of forgetting them
paragraphs: An annual insurance bill or membership belongs in a monthly plan at one-twelfth of its annual amount. Weekly and biweekly cash flows use their own yearly frequencies. The detailed period-line method provides this conversion and separates pre-tax retirement entries from its simplified flat income-tax assumption.

sections.title: Avoid counting the same expense twice
paragraphs: If card purchases are already classified as food or transport, paying the resulting current card bill is a transfer rather than another copy of those purchases. Existing debt repayment can still be a separate obligation. Likewise, if income is already take-home after a payroll deduction, do not deduct that same amount again without intentionally reconstructing gross income.

links.label: Build a target for emergency savings

sections.title: Making a monthly budget from mixed expenses
paragraphs: Convert income and expenses to a common period before comparing the totals. A yearly bill can be easy to miss in a monthly budget unless an allowance is made for it. Review the remaining balance after recurring obligations, then consider irregular spending separately. The mixed-period mode helps align timing; it does not know about transactions that have not been entered.

budget-calculator.seoTitle: Budget Calculator: Monthly Income, Expenses & Debt

tax-calculator.description: Estimate 2025 or 2026 US federal tax with combined income, deduction and credit scenarios, plus focused tax worksheets.

faqs.question: Does this produce one complete federal tax result?
faqs.answer: No. The composed federal mode combines its supported income and additional-tax calculations, while the individual worksheets answer narrower questions. Unsupported deductions, credits, state taxes, and special cases can still change an actual return. Do not add a composed total to its component figures or to overlapping worksheet totals.

faqs.question: Which years and income rules are covered?
faqs.answer: The detailed ordinary-income mode offers 2025 and 2026. Other modes state their own scope; qualified-gain, dependent-credit and AMT branches exclude the special cases listed with their results.

faqs.question: Does the dependent-credit worksheet establish eligibility?
faqs.answer: No. Eligibility is supplied as an assumption. The basic refundable branch is limited to at most two qualifying children and excludes the special Schedule 8812 branches.

faqs.question: Does moving into a higher bracket apply that rate to all my income?
faqs.answer: No. Progressive bracket rates apply to successive slices of taxable income. The $60,000 single-filer example uses both 10% and 12% rates after its standard deduction.

faqs.question: Is a deduction the same as a tax credit?
faqs.answer: No. A deduction reduces the income subject to tax, while an allowed credit reduces tax itself. Refundable and nonrefundable credits also have different limits.

faqs.question: Why can my refund change when the tax estimate stays the same?
faqs.answer: A refund compares payments and refundable credits with tax. Changing withholding can change the refund or amount due without changing the underlying tax liability.

faqs.question: Does the calculator automatically know my state tax rate?
faqs.answer: No. State and local entries are manual amounts or explicit planning assumptions, depending on the mode. They do not implement a complete state tax return.

sections.title: Selecting the correct US tax worksheet
paragraphs: Start with the tax year and the specific income, deduction, or credit question you need to model. The calculator contains separate supported branches, so a result from one worksheet should not be assumed to represent an entire return. Review eligibility and limitation notes beside the selected mode. Changing the website language or currency does not convert these US federal rules into another country's tax system.

sections.title: Choose a worksheet by the question it answers
paragraphs: Use the 2025/2026 ordinary-income worksheet to see income, deductions and progressive bracket arithmetic. Use the composed federal mode to combine its supported income sources, deductions, credits and additional taxes. A focused worksheet, such as self-employment tax or qualified dividends and gains, explains one component rather than automatically replacing the combined calculation.

The 2026 federal wage estimate is a narrower wage-only starting point. Some worksheets have a year selector and others are explicitly limited to 2026. Check the selected mode before transferring a value between worksheets. Ordinary income after deductions, gross wages, business profit and modified adjusted gross income are different inputs.

sections.title: Worked example: tax on $60,000 of ordinary income in 2026
paragraphs: Choose the ordinary-income worksheet, tax year 2026, Single, one income total of $60,000, zero adjustments and the basic standard deduction. The deduction is $16,100, leaving $43,900 of taxable income. The first $12,400 is taxed at 10% and the remaining $31,500 at 12%, for bracket-formula income tax of $5,020.

The marginal rate on the last dollar in this example is 12%; it is not applied to the entire $60,000. Dividing $5,020 by $60,000 gives an effective ordinary income-tax rate of about 8.37% before other taxes or credits. These are bracket calculations; IRS Tax Table rounding can produce a different filed amount.

table.caption: 2026 single-filer example with the basic standard deduction

sections.title: Enter deductions and credits once, in their correct category
paragraphs: An income adjustment can reduce adjusted gross income; a standard or itemized deduction reduces taxable income. A tax credit instead reduces tax, subject to its own limits. The composed mode separates these stages so a number should not be copied into multiple categories merely because each reduces a result.

Optional worksheets cover supported senior, tip, overtime, vehicle-interest, education, IRA, student-interest and business-income calculations. Eligibility still has to be established. Qualified tips or overtime must already be included in income before an applicable deduction is computed, and a separately verified total must exclude deductions or credits the tool has already calculated.

links.label: IRS: deductions for workers and seniors

sections.title: Separate final tax, payroll tax and payments toward the return
paragraphs: Federal income tax withheld and estimated payments are prepayments, not deductions from taxable income. In the composed mode they affect the estimated refund or amount due after modeled tax and refundable credits are determined. Ordinary employee Social Security and Medicare withholding are separate from federal income-tax withholding; do not enter all payroll taxes as a federal payment.

For example, if the modeled final burden after refundable credits is $5,020 and federal payments total $6,000, the arithmetic refund is $980. Reducing payments to $4,000 changes that to $1,020 due without changing the underlying $5,020 tax burden. State and local planning amounts are reported separately and do not automatically populate federal itemized deductions.

sections.title: Reconcile the result before using it in a tax plan
paragraphs: Compare the selected tax year, filing status, income categories, deduction and credit assumptions with the records you are modeling. W-2 federal wages, Social Security wages and Medicare wages can differ; the composed mode provides separate wage bases for each person. Capital-gain classifications and prior losses also need the correct treatment before a preferential-income amount is entered.

A zero estimate in one narrow worksheet does not establish that no return is required or that no other tax is due. The page is useful for checking assumptions and individual calculations, but it does not determine filing eligibility, implement every state return or replace unsupported Form 1040 schedules. For a decision that depends on those exceptions, use the applicable IRS instructions or a qualified tax professional.

tax-calculator.seoTitle: US Federal Tax Calculator: Income & Tax Worksheets

take-home-pay-calculator.description: Estimate annual take-home cash for 2025 or 2026, or calculate 2026 paycheck withholding with separate tax wage bases.

faqs.question: Can I estimate withholding for one paycheck?
faqs.answer: Yes. The W-4 mode uses taxable wages for that pay, pay frequency and the entered W-4 Step 2, 3 and 4 amounts. It is separate from the annual wage-tax estimate.

faqs.question: Are gross wages and payroll-tax wages always identical?
faqs.answer: No. Federal withholding, Social Security and Medicare can use different taxable wage amounts. Enter the wage base requested by each mode.

faqs.question: Does Additional Medicare withholding use my filing status?
faqs.answer: The paycheck FICA branch uses the employer’s $200,000 withholding trigger. Final Additional Medicare liability uses a separate filing-status calculation.

faqs.question: Is biweekly the same as twice monthly?
faqs.answer: No. Biweekly usually produces 26 paychecks per year, while twice monthly produces 24. Use your actual payroll frequency.

faqs.question: Is W-4 Step 4(c) an annual amount?
faqs.answer: No. Step 4(c) is extra withholding per paycheck. Step 3 and Steps 4(a) and 4(b) use annual amounts in this worksheet.

faqs.question: Should the year-to-date wage input include this paycheck?
faqs.answer: No. Enter the same-employer wages accumulated before the current pay. The calculator adds the current wage base when applying the threshold.

faqs.question: Why does a $300 pretax deduction not always reduce my check by $300?
faqs.answer: An eligible deduction can reduce withholding as well as cash pay. Its net effect depends on which tax wage bases it reduces; each deduction line must use the correct treatment.

sections.title: Separating tax liability from paycheck withholding
paragraphs: An annual tax estimate and withholding from a particular paycheck are related but different calculations. Choose the mode that matches the pay period, wage base, and deduction treatment you want to examine. Compare gross pay, deductions, and the resulting net amount using consistent timing. The supported federal calculations do not automatically include every state, local, employer, or benefit-plan adjustment.

sections.title: Choose annual take-home or an individual paycheck
paragraphs: Annual take-home with multiple income sources estimates annual cash after supported taxes and deductions, then shows period equivalents. It accepts 2025 or 2026 and distinguishes employee income from business receipts and expenses. A period average from that mode is not a prediction of the exact withholding on every pay date.

For a particular 2026 paycheck, use Paycheck with deduction wage bases. It combines cash gross pay, employee deduction lines, federal withholding and employee payroll taxes. The separate W-4 and FICA worksheets let you inspect those components individually. State/local withholding is supplied by you.

links.label: Calculate a paycheck with deduction lines

sections.title: Worked example: a $5,000 monthly paycheck
paragraphs: Use the composed paycheck mode with $5,000 cash gross pay, 12 periods per year, Single filing status, no deductions or noncash benefits, no Step 2 check, zero W-4 adjustments, zero wages before this paycheck and zero state/local withholding. Modeled federal withholding is about $418.33, employee Social Security is $310 and regular Medicare is $72.50, leaving about $4,199.17.

This example stays below the payroll thresholds and assumes regular pay. It is not a claim that every employee earning $60,000 annually receives that amount: benefits, state withholding, multiple jobs, W-4 entries and the timing of payroll deductions can change the check.

table.caption: One regular monthly paycheck under the stated 2026 assumptions

sections.title: Give each deduction its actual effect on each wage base
paragraphs: In the deduction-lines mode, an employee deduction reduces cash pay once. Separate flags indicate whether it also reduces federal, Social Security or Medicare wages. Apply the treatment documented for that particular benefit; the word pretax alone does not establish all three effects.

For example, add a $300 deduction to the monthly example and mark it as reducing federal wages only. Federal taxable wages become $4,700, while Social Security and Medicare wages stay $5,000. Modeled net cash pay becomes about $3,935.17: a $264 cash decrease because federal withholding fell by $36. A noncash taxable benefit works differently: it can increase a tax base without increasing the cash received.

sections.title: Use W-4 amounts and pay frequency in their stated units
paragraphs: Step 3 is an annual credit amount. Steps 4(a) and 4(b) also use annual amounts, while Step 4(c) is additional withholding per paycheck. Entering an annual extra-withholding target in Step 4(c) would apply it on every check. The Step 2 selection changes the withholding schedule used for the multiple-job assumption.

Biweekly commonly means 26 pays a year; twice monthly means 24. Select the actual payroll frequency. If work covers only part of the year, income changes or several jobs are involved, an annualized regular-pay worksheet can differ from the amount needed for the full-year return.

sections.title: Check year-to-date payroll thresholds separately from filing status
paragraphs: For 2026, employee Social Security is 6.2% up to the $184,500 wage base, while regular Medicare is 1.45% without that cap. Enter wages before the current paycheck in the year-to-date fields so the current check is not counted twice.

Employers begin withholding the additional 0.9% Medicare tax after that employer’s Medicare wages exceed $200,000, regardless of the W-4 filing status. Final Additional Medicare liability instead uses filing-status thresholds and can differ from withholding. Separate-employer histories and final return adjustments need reconciliation rather than treating one paycheck as the entire annual calculation.

links.label: SSA: 2026 payroll rates and wage base

take-home-pay-calculator.seoTitle: US Take-Home Pay Calculator: Tax & Paycheck Withholding

marriage-calculator.description: Compare supported 2025 or 2026 federal filing scenarios and separate state/local assumptions, including income, deductions and credits.

faqs.question: How do the marriage-tax comparison modes differ?
faqs.answer: The ordinary-income comparison uses the selected brackets and deductions. The composed federal comparison also recalculates its supported income types, additional taxes, and credits for the two individual scenarios and the joint scenario. Separately verified adjustments remain your inputs. Neither comparison implements every rule of a complete return.

faqs.question: Does it decide whether a married couple should file separately?
faqs.answer: No. It compares eligible individual before-marriage scenarios with a joint scenario; the ordinary-income mode uses two single scenarios. It does not compare joint filing with married filing separately, which has different rules for credits and other taxes.

faqs.question: What does a negative joint tax reduction mean?
faqs.answer: It means the modeled joint tax exceeds the sum of the two individual scenarios. The sign follows individual totals minus joint total.

faqs.question: Why can the same household income give a different comparison?
faqs.answer: The split between earners determines how two individual deductions and progressive brackets are used. Equal and unequal income splits can produce different results even when their sum is unchanged.

faqs.question: Should I include each child in both individual scenarios?
faqs.answer: No. Enter a dependent once and identify the eligible individual claimant in the composed comparison. Eligibility and any joint credit must be established for the relevant scenario.

faqs.question: Does changing withholding change the marriage tax difference?
faqs.answer: No. Withholding affects payments and settlement of a return. The comparison concerns modeled tax burden, so increasing withholding does not itself create a tax saving.

sections.title: Comparing filing scenarios consistently
paragraphs: A marriage-tax comparison needs the same underlying incomes and supported deductions in both scenarios. Review the year and filing assumptions before interpreting the difference. A change in total modeled tax is not a complete measure of the financial effects of marriage. Credits, eligibility rules, and income types outside the selected branch may require a more complete return calculation.

sections.title: Compare three hypothetical scenarios with the same household income
paragraphs: The ordinary-income comparison calculates Person A as single, Person B as single and the combined income as a joint return. Select 2025 or 2026 and use either basic standard deductions or separately verified deductions for each scenario. This isolates the bracket-and-deduction effect.

The composed comparison adds supported income types, dependent allocations, additional taxes and credits. Each before-marriage filing status must be eligible on its own facts. A hypothetical two-single-versus-joint comparison does not give a married couple permission to file two single returns.

sections.title: Worked example: one income of $120,000 and a second income of zero
paragraphs: Choose 2026 ordinary-income comparison, Person A income $120,000, Person B income $0 and basic standard deductions. The single scenario has taxable income of $103,900 and bracket tax of $17,570. The joint scenario has taxable income of $87,800 and bracket tax of $10,040. The difference is $7,530 less ordinary income tax in this limited joint scenario.

Now divide the same $120,000 equally: $60,000 for each person. Each single scenario has bracket tax of $5,020, totaling $10,040, the same as the joint scenario. Equal household income can therefore produce a different marriage comparison depending on how that income is distributed.

table.caption: Same $120,000 household income, different earning split; 2026 basic deductions

sections.title: Read positive and negative differences as modeled tax changes
paragraphs: Joint tax reduction means the combined individual-scenario tax minus the joint-scenario tax. A positive number indicates a reduction under the entered assumptions; a negative number indicates an increase. Withholding does not create or remove that difference because withholding is a prepayment rather than the underlying tax liability.

The composed output also separates federal tax from optional state/local assumptions. Entered state rates and bases are independent planning assumptions for each scenario, not automatic state-law calculations. Compare the federal difference first, then examine whether those state inputs are justified.

sections.title: Recalculate eligibility and credits instead of adding two tax returns
paragraphs: A joint return combines household income, but it does not simply add every deduction limit or credit from two single returns. Income bands and phaseouts can change. In the composed mode, enter each dependent once with a unique identifier and the eligible claimant for the individual scenario.
