sections.title: Understand differences before using a result elsewhere
paragraphs: Record the equation name with the result. A value labeled only “lean mass” hides whether it came from a tape-based body-fat estimate, a scale estimate or a height-and-weight regression. Use consistent measurement conditions and methods for comparisons.

The Katch–McArdle energy equation also depends on estimated lean mass, so uncertainty in a body-fat input carries into an energy estimate. Neither this calculator nor a linked energy calculator determines a clinical dose, diagnosis or individual nutrition requirement.

links.label: Body-fat estimation and its input limits

lean-body-mass-calculator.seoTitle: Lean Body Mass Calculator: Body Fat & Equation Estimates

body-surface-area-calculator.description: Estimate body surface area with eight named equations, age-specific branches and metric or US area units.

faqs.question: What is the Mosteller formula?
faqs.answer: BSA in m² equals the square root of height in centimeters multiplied by weight in kilograms and divided by 3600.

faqs.question: What does 1.84 m² mean?
faqs.answer: It is an estimated area of the body’s external surface under the selected equation, not a body-fat percentage or a direct measurement.

faqs.question: Why do BSA equations give different answers?
faqs.answer: They use different coefficients, mathematical forms and source populations. Keep the named method with the result.

faqs.question: Can I enter feet and inches as 5.9?
faqs.answer: No. In the US input mode, use total inches. Five feet nine inches is 69 inches.

faqs.question: Are square feet and square meters interchangeable?
faqs.answer: They describe the same type of quantity but have different scales. Convert area with a squared-unit factor; the extended mode does this for you.

faqs.question: Does the calculator provide a medicine dose?
faqs.answer: No. A BSA estimate alone does not establish which dosing method or treatment is appropriate.

sections.title: Estimate surface area from height and weight
paragraphs: Body surface area (BSA) estimates external body area, usually in square meters. Choose a named equation, enter height and weight in the selected measurement system, then keep the equation name alongside the result. The basic mode offers Mosteller, Du Bois and Haycock.

The extended mode offers eight published equation choices and output in square meters, square feet or square inches. It includes age-specific and sex-specific methods, so changing the equation can change which personal inputs matter.

links.label: Open the extended equation and unit options

sections.title: Worked Mosteller calculation
paragraphs: Mosteller BSA = √[height(cm) × weight(kg) / 3600]. At 175 cm and 70 kg, multiply to obtain 12,250, divide by 3,600 to obtain 3.402777…, then take the square root. The result is approximately 1.8447 m².

table.caption: One calculated surface area in three units

sections.title: Equations differ in their mathematical form
paragraphs: The Du Bois equation uses 0.007184 × weight(kg)^0.425 × height(cm)^0.725. Haycock uses 0.024265 × weight(kg)^0.5378 × height(cm)^0.3964. These are different fitted relationships, not alternative unit conversions of Mosteller.

The extended choices also include Gehan & George, Boyd in its gram-based form, age-specific Fujimoto, the stated 0.007241 Takahira variant and adult sex-specific Schlich. Their source populations, coefficients and units differ. The calculator converts inputs for each selected formula; do not manually convert only one field to a formula’s native unit.

sections.title: Avoid the common height and area-unit mistakes
paragraphs: In US input mode, height is total inches. For example, 5 feet 9 inches is 69 inches, not 5.9 inches. A square-foot result must be converted with an area conversion factor: 1 ft² = 0.09290304 m². A length conversion factor alone gives the wrong answer.

The square root in Mosteller also means weight and area do not change proportionally. At fixed height, multiplying weight by 1.10 multiplies BSA by √1.10, about 1.0488. This is a property of the formula, not a description of someone’s health.

sections.title: What a BSA result can and cannot establish
paragraphs: A useful comparison preserves the measurement date, units and equation name. If two calculators disagree, check those details before assuming an arithmetic error. Averaging several equations does not validate the average for an individual.

BSA appears in medical contexts, but this page does not calculate a medication dose or choose an equation for a clinical protocol. Clinical use requires the specified method and professional interpretation. BSA is also distinct from BMI and body-fat percentage; neither of those can be read from a surface-area result.

body-surface-area-calculator.seoTitle: Body Surface Area Calculator: Compare BSA Equations

ideal-weight-calculator.description: Compare historical adult reference-weight equations or use CDC child BMI-for-age references without setting a personal target weight.

faqs.question: Which ideal-weight formula is the correct one?
faqs.answer: There is no universally correct personal ideal from these height-only equations. The comparison shows how the named historical methods differ.

faqs.question: Does current weight affect these four estimates?
faqs.answer: No. This mode uses height and the selected sex category; current body weight is not an input.

faqs.question: Why do the equations disagree?
faqs.answer: Their starting constants and added weight per inch differ. The disagreement is model variation, not a recommended range.

faqs.question: Can I use the adult formulas for a child?
faqs.answer: Use the separate Child & teen BMI-for-age mode. It reports a growth-reference percentile instead of an adult reference weight.

faqs.question: Should I average the four results?
faqs.answer: An arithmetic average would not create a validated personal target. Interpret the particular reference relevant to your situation.

faqs.question: Does this account for pregnancy or muscle mass?
faqs.answer: The four historical formulas do not. Those circumstances require additional assessment.

sections.title: Read the four outputs as historical reference equations
paragraphs: Choose Reference weight equations, select the equation’s sex category and enter height. Finflo compares Devine, Robinson, Miller and Hamwi values. These are historical height-based formulas, not measurements of your body or personalized weight goals.

The formulas do not use your current weight, training history or clinical circumstances. Agreement between two formulas is therefore not independent confirmation of an ideal weight; they may share similar input assumptions.

sections.title: Compare the same height rather than changing several inputs
paragraphs: For a male equation input at 175 cm, the displayed values are approximately 70.46 kg for Devine, 68.91 kg for Robinson, 68.75 kg for Miller and 72.30 kg for Hamwi. The range reflects formula choice, not a medically approved interval.
Devine starts with 50 kg at 60 inches and adds 2.3 kg per inch above that height. At 175 cm, height is about 68.8976 inches; 50 + 2.3 × 8.8976 ≈ 70.46 kg.

table.caption: Historical estimates for the same illustrative 175 cm male input

links.label: Published comparison of historical reference-weight equations

sections.title: Keep feet-and-inches notation out of a decimal height field
paragraphs: In US mode, enter a single height in total inches. Five feet nine inches is 69 inches; it is not 5.9 feet. Metric mode expects centimeters. Consistent conversion should reproduce the same physical height and corresponding estimates.

This mode accepts heights of at least 5 feet (152.4 cm); it rejects shorter heights rather than extending the historical formulas below that point. Acceptance of a height still does not validate the equation for every person with that height.

sections.title: Use the child mode for a different question
paragraphs: Child & teen BMI-for-age is a separate calculation for ages 2 to under 20. It uses height, weight, completed age and the sex-specific CDC reference to report a percentile. It does not adapt the four adult equations to children.

For example, the initial male-reference input of 30 kg, 135 cm and age 9 years 6 months gives BMI about 16.46 and percentile about 51.35. These compare growth measurements with a reference; they are not suggested weight changes.

links.label: CDC child and teen BMI interpretation

sections.title: Choose a reference without turning it into a prescription
paragraphs: If the question is simply which adult weights correspond to specified BMI boundaries, the Healthy Weight Calculator provides that transparent arithmetic. If the question concerns body composition or a change in health, these height-only equations cannot settle it.

Pregnancy, growth, body composition and medical nutrition needs require context beyond a height-based estimate. Use the named methods to understand a reference you encountered, not to choose whichever output gives the smallest number.

links.label: Understand the adult BMI-based reference interval

ideal-weight-calculator.seoTitle: Ideal Weight Calculator: Historical Reference Equations

healthy-weight-calculator.description: Explore the adult BMI-based reference weight interval for a height, including the exclusive upper boundary and screening limitations.

faqs.question: Is the upper boundary included?
faqs.answer: No. The displayed upper boundary corresponds to BMI 25 and is exclusive for the stated 18.5-to-below-25 interval.

faqs.question: Why does changing age not change the result?
faqs.answer: Within this adult mode, the formula uses height and fixed BMI boundaries. Age keeps the input within the adult scope.

faqs.question: Is the lower boundary a target I should aim for?
faqs.answer: No. Neither end of this screening interval is a personal recommendation.

faqs.question: Can I enter height in feet?
faqs.answer: Choose US units and enter total inches: feet × 12 plus remaining inches.

faqs.question: Can this be used for children?
faqs.answer: No. Use child BMI-for-age references, which account for age and sex, rather than fixed adult boundaries.

faqs.question: Why is this different from an ideal-weight formula?
faqs.answer: This tool reverses BMI boundaries. Historical reference-weight equations use different assumptions and can return different values without identifying a personal ideal.

sections.title: Understand the height-based interval this calculator returns
paragraphs: This calculator rearranges BMI = weight ÷ height² into weight = BMI × height². Enter an adult height and age to see the weight boundaries corresponding to BMI 18.5 and 25. It accepts ages 20 and over.

The output is a population screening interval for that height. It is not an individualized ideal weight, a minimum to maintain or a deadline-based weight-change plan. Body composition and medical circumstances are outside the equation.

sections.title: Reproduce the reference boundaries for 175 cm
paragraphs: A height of 175 cm is 1.75 m, and 1.75² = 3.0625. Multiplying by 18.5 gives 56.65625 kg. Multiplying by 25 gives 76.5625 kg. The first boundary is included; the second is excluded from the stated BMI reference interval.

Therefore the mathematical interval is 56.65625 kg up to, but not including, 76.5625 kg. Displayed values are rounded for readability, which should not turn the exclusive upper boundary into an inclusive one.

table.caption: Boundary arithmetic for an illustrative 175 cm adult

sections.title: Why taller heights change both ends of the range
paragraphs: The boundaries scale with the square of height, not in a straight line. Raising the entered height by 10% raises both calculated weight boundaries by 21%, because 1.10² = 1.21.
This is a property of the BMI formula. It does not mean two people of different heights should have matching builds or pursue weights at the same point within their respective intervals.

sections.title: Use the selected units consistently
paragraphs: Choose Metric for centimeters, or US for total inches. The reference-boundary results are reported in kilograms, including when height is entered in inches. A height of 5 feet 9 inches should be entered as 69 inches.

Measure height rather than estimating it from shoe size or a previous record when precision matters. Small differences in entered height shift both reference boundaries because the denominator is squared.

sections.title: Separate reference arithmetic from a personal assessment
paragraphs: The same adult boundaries apply across the adult ages accepted here, so changing age alone will not alter this interval. Age is used to keep the calculation in the adult pathway. Children require a growth reference rather than these fixed bands.

Pregnancy, unusual muscle mass and clinical nutrition needs are reasons not to interpret these numbers as personal goals. Discuss the context with a qualified health professional if you are using measurements to understand a health concern.

links.label: Calculate adult BMI or child percentiles

healthy-weight-calculator.seoTitle: Healthy Weight Calculator: Adult BMI Reference Range

body-type-calculator.description: Explore body proportions and the 2020 revised FFIT fashion descriptors with their measurement limitations.

faqs.question: Does this calculate ectomorph, mesomorph or endomorph?
faqs.answer: No. It provides two circumference ratios and a separate revised FFIT apparel-rule calculation.

faqs.question: What is the difference between hips and high hips?
faqs.answer: They are separate circumference locations in the apparel method. Do not substitute one for the other; measurement placement affects the rule results.

faqs.question: Can my measurements match two descriptions?
faqs.answer: Yes. This calculator shows every matching revised FFIT rule instead of choosing the first one.

faqs.question: What does no classification mean?
faqs.answer: The supplied measurements do not satisfy any rule in this particular set. It is a limit of the classification, not a judgment about your body.

faqs.question: Can I mix centimeters and inches?
faqs.answer: Use the individual-unit option and choose the correct unit for each field. In shared-unit mode, all four values must use the selected common unit.

faqs.question: Does a descriptor determine health or fitness?
faqs.answer: No. These apparel terms do not diagnose health, set body-composition goals or predict fitness.

sections.title: Choose between body proportions and apparel descriptors
paragraphs: Body proportions mode calculates waist-to-hip and waist-to-height ratios. It answers how one measurement compares with another. The revised FFIT mode applies an adult apparel-research rule set to bust, waist, hip and high-hip circumferences.

These modes do not identify a metabolic type, judge appearance or prescribe exercise. Apparel labels describe relationships among measurements, while ratios describe divisions. Neither tells you a clothing size without the particular garment’s measurements and fit information.

sections.title: Worked example for the two ratios
paragraphs: For waist 80 cm, hips 100 cm and height 175 cm, waist-to-hip = 80 ÷ 100 = 0.80. Waist-to-height = 80 ÷ 175 ≈ 0.4571. The results have no length unit because matching units cancel.

table.caption: Different denominators answer different questions

sections.title: An apparel-rule example you can reproduce
paragraphs: Select shared inches in the revised FFIT mode and enter bust 36, waist 26, hips 36 and high hips 30. The displayed differences are 10 inches for bust minus waist and 10 inches for hip minus waist; high-hip divided by waist is approximately 1.1538. These inputs match the Hourglass descriptor under the implemented rules.

The mode evaluates all nine rules rather than stopping after the first match. Some measurements can match more than one descriptor, while others match none. That outcome describes the coverage of the rule set, not a problem with the person’s body.

sections.title: Measurement placement can change a descriptor
paragraphs: Hip and high-hip measurements are separate inputs; copying one into the other can change the rules that match. The source was developed in apparel research using body scans, and a home tape measurement is not automatically equivalent to that protocol. Keep your measurement locations consistent and record how you measured.

The shared-unit option applies one unit to all four circumferences. The individual-unit option allows each field to specify inches or centimeters. Differences are converted to inches for the rule evaluation. Mixing centimeters with inches while leaving the wrong unit selected can completely change the result.

sections.title: Use descriptors as context for fit, not a universal label
paragraphs: A fitted garment depends on more than four circumferences: dimensions, construction and ease also matter. Use actual product measurements when comparing clothing. A descriptor cannot guarantee that a particular size or style will fit.

The revised FFIT method was developed to improve the handling of body proportions that older formulas classified poorly. Online calculators can disagree because they use different revisions, omit high-hip measurements or stop at the first match. Compare the named rules and measurements before comparing labels.

links.label: Measurement guidance and classification reliability study

body-type-calculator.seoTitle: Body Type Calculator: Proportions & Clothing Descriptors

calories-burned-calculator.description: Estimate activity calories using METs, selected Compendium activities or a distance-and-speed approximation, with gross and net energy shown.

faqs.question: What does MET mean?
faqs.answer: A metabolic equivalent describes activity intensity relative to a specified resting reference. The calculator shows the selected activity’s reference value and source where available.

faqs.question: Should I compare gross or active calories?
faqs.answer: Gross includes the modeled resting baseline; above-rest removes it. Compare outputs with the same definition because watches and other tools may label them differently.

faqs.question: Why does the distance mode ask for speed?
faqs.answer: Distance and speed determine duration, and speed helps select the implemented activity reference. Distance alone is not enough for this calculation.

faqs.question: Does doubling duration double the result?
faqs.answer: With body weight and the same MET value held fixed, yes. That is a mathematical assumption of the model, not a guarantee about measured personal expenditure.

faqs.question: Can I apply the adult formula to MET_WC?
faqs.answer: No. The wheelchair reference uses its own baseline. The activity-library mode applies the matching calculation.

faqs.question: Can this tell me exactly how much to eat after exercise?
faqs.answer: No. It estimates activity energy under population assumptions and does not establish individual nutrition needs.

sections.title: Choose an activity estimate that matches your session
paragraphs: Use the MET mode when you already have an appropriate metabolic-equivalent value. The activity modes supply named reference activities with their source codes. The distance mode estimates duration from distance and speed, then selects the implemented reference intensity for walking, running or cycling.

Enter the body weight, duration and activity description that belong to the same session. A reference for level walking is not a model of a steep hike, and an active exercise interval is not the same as total time including long rests. The 2024 Adult Compendium is a population reference for ages 19–59, with separate references for other populations.

sections.title: Gross calories and above-rest calories are different
paragraphs: For standard adult MET entries, gross kcal = MET × 3.5 × weight(kg) × minutes / 200. Gross energy includes the baseline energy represented by one MET. The above-rest estimate subtracts that baseline by using MET − 1 and never reports a negative amount.

At 70 kg, 3.5 MET and 60 minutes, the shared factor is 3.5 × 70 × 60 / 200 = 73.5. Gross energy is 3.5 × 73.5 = 257.25 kcal; above-rest energy is 2.5 × 73.5 = 183.75 kcal. The difference of 73.5 kcal is the model’s resting baseline for that hour.

table.caption: Same 70 kg, 3.5 MET activity with different durations

sections.title: Distance becomes duration before energy is estimated
paragraphs: For a 5 km walk at 5 km/h, duration is 5 ÷ 5 = 1 hour. The implemented walking reference at this speed is 3.8 MET, giving about 279.3 gross kcal and 205.8 above-rest kcal for 70 kg. The result identifies the selected reference, which makes the assumption visible.

Changing pace may change both the time spent moving and the selected intensity category. Consequently, the distance mode should not be interpreted as a precise continuous model of energy at every speed. Terrain, load carried, technique and individual physiology are not fully represented.

sections.title: Check the reference population and MET definition
paragraphs: The activity library includes a wheelchair reference labeled MET_WC. It uses its own source baseline and calculation factor. Do not apply the standard adult 3.5 mL/kg/min factor manually to that label or compare the numeric MET values as though they had identical baselines.

The activity description and source code are more informative than an activity name alone. “Cycling” can refer to different speeds or measured power levels; “walking” can refer to different surfaces and gradients. Choose the closest supported description and retain that assumption with the estimate.

sections.title: Use energy estimates without counting the same activity twice
paragraphs: A daily energy estimate based on an activity multiplier already represents some movement across the day. Adding a full gross exercise estimate to it can count resting energy and activity more than once. Review what each starting estimate includes before combining numbers.

A watch and a MET calculator may disagree because they use different inputs and models. These outputs cannot measure an individual session’s expenditure or determine food intake needed to compensate for exercise. Their useful role is explaining the arithmetic and making broad comparisons under stated assumptions.

links.label: What a daily energy estimate includes

calories-burned-calculator.seoTitle: Calories Burned Calculator: Activity & MET Estimates

one-rep-max-calculator.description: Estimate a one-repetition maximum from a submaximal lift using Epley, Brzycki and supported Lombardi comparisons.

faqs.question: What is an estimated one-rep max?
faqs.answer: It is a formula-based estimate of a single-repetition maximum inferred from the load and repetition count you enter.

faqs.question: Why are the three answers different?
faqs.answer: Epley, Brzycki and Lombardi model the relationship differently. Their disagreement is expected and does not identify a uniquely correct estimate.

faqs.question: Why is Lombardi missing at 12 repetitions?
faqs.answer: This implementation shows Lombardi only for inputs up to 10 repetitions and marks higher-repetition estimates as more uncertain.

faqs.question: What happens if I enter one repetition?
faqs.answer: The displayed estimates equal the entered load. The calculator cannot determine whether that repetition was actually maximal.

faqs.question: Can I add repetitions from several sets?
faqs.answer: No. The equations require one set’s load and repetitions; adding several sets changes the meaning of the input.

faqs.question: Should I attempt the predicted weight?
faqs.answer: A calculated estimate does not establish that attempting the load is appropriate or safe. It is not a lifting prescription.

sections.title: Estimate maximum strength from a completed set
paragraphs: Enter the load used in a set, its repetition count and the load unit. The calculator compares Epley, Brzycki and, within its supported repetition range, Lombardi estimates. Use repetitions from one completed set of the same exercise, with a consistent range of motion and equipment.

These equations model a relationship between a repetition maximum and a single-repetition maximum. An easy set stopped well before the person’s capacity does not provide the same information as the sets studied for prediction. Do not add repetitions you did not complete or treat the output as an instruction to attempt that load.

links.label: Reynolds and colleagues: repetition-based prediction study

sections.title: Worked example: 100 kg for five repetitions
paragraphs: With weight 100 kg and repetitions 5, Epley gives 100 × (1 + 5/30) = 116.67 kg. Brzycki gives 36 × 100 / (37 − 5) = 112.50 kg. Lombardi gives 100 × 5^0.1 ≈ 117.46 kg.
The spread between 112.50 and 117.46 kg shows disagreement among equations. It is not a confidence interval or evidence that a true maximum must fall inside that range.

table.caption: Three estimates from the same set

sections.title: Repetition count changes what is reported
paragraphs: The tool accepts whole repetition counts from 1 to 15. Lombardi is shown only through 10 repetitions; higher-repetition inputs display the other estimates with greater-uncertainty context. For a single repetition, the calculation returns the entered load rather than adding an Epley multiplier.
A one-repetition result is still only the load supplied. The calculator cannot know whether that repetition was a true maximum, a warm-up, assisted or performed with a different technique.

sections.title: Keep exercise and load definitions consistent
paragraphs: For a barbell lift, record the total loaded weight, including the bar if that is how the lift is logged. For dumbbells, be explicit in your own record about whether the load is per hand or combined. The equation does not infer that distinction.

A machine stack, free-weight lift and different exercise variation are not interchangeable simply because their labels use kilograms. Comparisons are most interpretable when exercise, equipment, technique and units remain consistent. Selecting pounds labels the entered load as pounds; verify the displayed load whenever you change units.

sections.title: Use estimates to understand a training record
paragraphs: An estimated 1RM can summarize how load and repetitions relate across otherwise comparable sets. Fatigue, rest, technique and exercise choice affect that relationship, so a small change between estimates does not necessarily show a true change in maximum strength.

This page does not provide a maximal testing protocol, prescribe training loads or assess readiness to lift. Use a qualified coach or clinician when personal circumstances require an individualized approach. Keep the original set alongside the estimate so the calculation remains understandable.

one-rep-max-calculator.seoTitle: One Rep Max Calculator: Compare Estimated 1RM Equations

target-heart-rate-calculator.description: Compare estimated maximum heart rates and target ranges, or use the talk test to check exercise intensity.

faqs.question: What is heart-rate reserve?
faqs.answer: It is maximum heart rate minus resting heart rate. A reserve-based target adds the chosen fraction of that difference back to resting heart rate.

faqs.question: Why do the two 50–70% ranges differ?
faqs.answer: One applies percentages to the full maximum; the other applies them to the reserve and then adds resting rate. The percentages are not interchangeable.

faqs.question: Which maximum equations are available?
faqs.answer: The basic mode uses 220 − age. The additional mode offers a supplied measured maximum, Tanaka’s 208 − 0.7 × age and Nes’s 211 − 0.64 × age.

faqs.question: Does the calculator measure my maximum heart rate?
faqs.answer: No. It either estimates it from age or uses a measured value you supply.

faqs.question: Can the talk test give a precise pulse target?
faqs.answer: No. It describes relative effort from speech and breathing rather than calculating a beats-per-minute range.

faqs.question: Can I use the result if medicine affects my heart rate?
faqs.answer: Generic equations may be unsuitable in that situation. Follow personalized guidance from the health professional managing your care.

sections.title: Choose how the heart-rate range is calculated
paragraphs: The basic mode uses age-estimated maximum heart rate, 220 − age. You can apply percentages directly to that maximum or use heart-rate reserve, which also includes resting heart rate. Enter lower and upper percentages as whole percentages, such as 50 and 70.

The additional methods mode allows a supplied measured maximum or the Tanaka and Nes age equations. A separate talk-test mode describes perceived relative intensity without calculating a pulse range. These methods provide different information; one result should not be silently substituted for another.

links.label: AHA explanation of estimated heart-rate ranges

sections.title: Worked example: maximum percentage versus reserve
paragraphs: For age 30, the basic maximum estimate is 220 − 30 = 190 beats/min. A 50–70% range based directly on maximum is 95–133 beats/min. With resting heart rate 60, reserve is 190 − 60 = 130, so the same numerical percentages give 60 + 0.50 × 130 = 125 and 60 + 0.70 × 130 = 151 beats/min.

The difference is not a calculator error. Fifty percent of maximum and fifty percent of reserve are different quantities. This example explains the math rather than assigning an individual training zone.

table.caption: Same age and percentages, different definitions

sections.title: Age equations estimate an average relationship
paragraphs: The alternatives are Tanaka: maximum = 208 − 0.7 × age, and Nes: maximum = 211 − 0.64 × age. At age 30, those give 187 and 191.8 beats/min, respectively. A measured maximum supplied to the tool is used directly; the calculator does not verify how it was obtained.

Do not average several predicted maxima and treat the result as a validated personal measurement. A population equation cannot account for every individual’s response, and the highest pulse seen casually on a watch is not automatically a measured maximum.

sections.title: The talk test adds a different kind of context
paragraphs: The talk-test option distinguishes comfortable conversation with difficulty singing from being able to say only a few words before pausing for breath. CDC describes these as clues to moderate and vigorous relative intensity, respectively. The unsure option avoids assigning either category.
This is a description of effort, not a conversion to exact beats per minute or a medical assessment. It can explain why an activity with a fixed speed feels different to different people.

sections.title: Interpret the range with the right personal context
paragraphs: Resting heart rate should represent rest, not a reading immediately after exercise. For reserve calculations it must be below the selected maximum, and the lower percentage must not exceed the upper percentage. Recheck these inputs if the calculation is rejected.

Some medicines and medical conditions change heart-rate response. A generic calculated zone cannot override individualized advice or assess symptoms. For those circumstances, use the exercise guidance provided by the relevant health professional rather than adjusting effort to satisfy this number.

target-heart-rate-calculator.seoTitle: Target Heart Rate Calculator: Ranges & Exercise Intensity

pace-calculator.description: Calculate pace, speed, time and distance, review cumulative splits, or project a finish from the average pace so far.

faqs.question: Is a smaller pace number faster?
faqs.answer: Yes, within the same unit. Taking 5 minutes per kilometer is faster than taking 6 minutes per kilometer.

faqs.question: How do I enter 5 minutes 30 seconds?
faqs.answer: Use 5.5 in a decimal-minute field, or 00:05:30 where the HH:MM:SS input is offered.

faqs.question: How do I convert pace to km/h?
faqs.answer: For pace in minutes per kilometer, divide 60 by the pace. Six minutes per kilometer equals 10 km/h.

faqs.question: Are split inputs cumulative or individual laps?
faqs.answer: They are cumulative distance and cumulative elapsed time. The calculator subtracts adjacent checkpoints to derive each segment.

faqs.question: Why not average my segment paces?
faqs.answer: Segments may cover different distances. Overall pace is total elapsed time divided by total distance.

faqs.question: Does a finish projection predict my race performance?
faqs.answer: No. It extends the current average pace across the full distance without modeling changes in effort, terrain or conditions.

sections.title: Solve for the quantity you do not know
paragraphs: Pace is time per unit distance; speed is distance per unit time. Choose pace from a known distance and elapsed time, time from distance and pace, or distance from time and pace. Additional modes analyze cumulative splits, project a finish time at the current average pace and convert common pace or speed units.

The extended measurement-units mode supports kilometers, miles, meters and yards, with decimal minutes or HH:MM:SS elapsed time. Choose the units before interpreting a number: 6 minutes per kilometer and 6 minutes per mile describe different speeds.

links.label: Open the extended distance and time options

sections.title: Worked example: 5 kilometers in 30 minutes
paragraphs: Pace = time ÷ distance, so 30 ÷ 5 = 6 minutes/km. Speed = 60 ÷ pace in minutes/km, giving 10 km/h. One international mile equals 1.609344 km, so the mile pace is 6 × 1.609344 = 9.656064 decimal minutes, approximately 9 minutes 39 seconds.

table.caption: Consistent results from the same average pace

sections.title: Decimal minutes are not minutes and seconds
paragraphs: A decimal-minute value of 5.5 means 5 minutes 30 seconds because 0.5 × 60 = 30. For 5 minutes 45 seconds, enter 5.75 in a decimal field. Entering 5.45 would mean 5 minutes 27 seconds.

Where HH:MM:SS is offered, enter 00:05:45 for five minutes forty-five seconds. Elapsed durations may exceed 23 hours; they are durations, not clock times. Minutes and seconds within that notation must each be below 60.

sections.title: Analyze cumulative splits without averaging paces incorrectly
paragraphs: The split mode expects cumulative distance and cumulative elapsed time at each checkpoint. For checkpoints 1 km at 00:06:00, 3 km at 00:17:00 and 5 km at 00:29:00, the segment distances are 1, 2 and 2 km. Their segment paces are 6:00, 5:30 and 6:00 per km.

Overall pace is total time divided by total distance: 29 ÷ 5 = 5.8 decimal minutes, or 5:48/km. Simply averaging the three segment paces would incorrectly give equal importance to unequal distances. Checkpoints must progress in both distance and elapsed time.

sections.title: A projected finish assumes the average pace continues
paragraphs: If 5 km takes 30 minutes, maintaining that average over 21.0975 km gives 126.585 minutes, displayed as 02:06:35. The remaining time is approximately 01:36:35. The projection uses total distance divided by completed distance multiplied by elapsed time.

This arithmetic does not predict fatigue, stops, elevation or changing conditions. Use elapsed time consistently when comparing race results, and distinguish it from moving time when reviewing an activity record.

links.label: Project a finish from current progress

pace-calculator.seoTitle: Pace Calculator: Running Time, Distance, Speed & Splits

pregnancy-calculator.description: Estimate pregnancy dates from menstrual history, conception, ultrasound, IVF transfer or a known due date, with dating assumptions explained.

faqs.question: How many weeks pregnant am I on a particular date?
faqs.answer: Select a dating method, enter its reference information and set the as-of date. The result shows completed gestational weeks plus remaining days.

faqs.question: Why is gestational age about two weeks ahead of conception age?
faqs.answer: The usual dating convention counts a 280-day pregnancy reference while conception-based arithmetic uses 266 days. The difference is conventional and does not prove an exact ovulation date.

faqs.question: Does changing the as-of date change the due date?
faqs.answer: No. It changes the date on which gestational age is evaluated; the due date remains anchored to the supplied reference.

faqs.question: Can I use an IVF transfer date?
faqs.answer: Yes. Choose IVF mode and supply the transfer date together with embryo age in days.

faqs.question: Does 14 weeks and 2 days mean 14.2 weeks?
faqs.answer: No. Two days are 2/7 of a week. The display uses completed weeks and remaining days, not decimal weeks.

faqs.question: Which date should I use if the scan and period estimates differ?
faqs.answer: Use the established clinical dating record for care. A clinician can assess the references and whether redating is appropriate; the calculator cannot make that decision.

sections.title: Build a pregnancy timeline from the reference you know
paragraphs: Choose the source of your dates: the first day of the last menstrual period, an estimated conception date, an IVF transfer, ultrasound-reported gestational age or an established due date. The calculator turns that reference into an estimated due date and gestational age on your chosen as-of date.

Use the date associated with the selected method. An ultrasound mode needs the scan date and the gestational age reported on that scan, while IVF mode needs the transfer date and embryo age. Substituting the appointment date for a last menstrual period changes the meaning of the calculation.

links.label: ACOG guidance on assigning a due date

sections.title: Gestational age and time since conception are different
paragraphs: Conventional gestational dating uses a 40-week, 280-day reference to the estimated due date. Conception-based arithmetic uses 266 days to that date. The two-week difference is a dating convention; it is not evidence that conception occurred exactly two weeks after every period.

The calculator finds gestational days on the as-of date as 280 plus the number of days from the estimated due date to the as-of date. It then divides by seven to show completed weeks and remaining days. “14 weeks, 2 days” therefore represents 100 elapsed gestational days, not 14.2 decimal weeks.

sections.title: Worked timeline with a 28-day cycle
paragraphs: Enter July 1, 2026 as the first day of the last period, a 28-day cycle and October 9, 2026 as the as-of date. The estimated due date is April 7, 2027, the modeled conception date is July 15, 2026 and gestational age on the selected date is 14 weeks, 2 days.

table.caption: Dates from one consistent example

sections.title: Understand how each method anchors the estimate
paragraphs: Last-period mode adds 280 days plus the difference between the entered cycle length and 28 days. Conception mode adds 266 days. IVF mode adds 266 minus embryo age in days to the transfer date. Ultrasound mode adds the days remaining until 280 gestational days, using the age reported on the scan.
Known-due-date mode works backward from the established due date. It does not require a guessed last period. Changing the as-of date updates gestational age without changing the due-date reference.

sections.title: Use the clinical dating record for care decisions
paragraphs: A due date is an estimate, not an appointment for delivery. Period uncertainty and variation in ovulation limit calendar dating. Ultrasound-based clinical dating can improve the estimate; deciding whether a pregnancy should be redated requires the relevant clinical context.

This tool does not interpret ultrasound images, assess fetal growth or determine a delivery plan. If several references disagree, take the original dates and reports to your maternity care team instead of averaging calculator outputs. For reverse conception arithmetic, the separate page explains why a date cannot identify a particular encounter.

pregnancy-calculator.seoTitle: Pregnancy Calculator: Due Date & Gestational Age

due-date-calculator.description: Estimate a due date from the last period, conception date, IVF transfer or ultrasound dating, using the selected method's inputs.

faqs.question: Is the due date 280 days after conception?
faqs.answer: No. The conventional last-period reference uses 280 days for a 28-day cycle; conception-based arithmetic uses 266 days.

faqs.question: Which day of my period should I enter?
faqs.answer: Enter the first day of the last menstrual period in last-period mode.

faqs.question: How does a longer cycle affect this estimate?
faqs.answer: The model adds the number of days by which the cycle exceeds 28. A 30-day cycle shifts the estimate two days later than a 28-day cycle with the same period date.

faqs.question: How is a five-day IVF transfer calculated?
faqs.answer: The tool adds 261 days to the transfer date: 266 minus the embryo age of five days.

faqs.question: Can the calculator interpret a scan image?
faqs.answer: No. It uses the gestational weeks and days already reported for the scan date.

faqs.question: Does the result predict the exact birth date?
faqs.answer: No. It is an estimated reference date, and care decisions should use the established clinical dating record.

sections.title: Select the date source before calculating an estimated due date
paragraphs: This calculator offers four routes to an estimated due date: last menstrual period, conception, IVF transfer and ultrasound-reported gestational age. Choose the reference you actually have rather than entering the same date into every mode.

For the last-period method, use the first day of the period rather than its last day. For ultrasound, use the scan date and the gestational weeks and days reported at that time. For IVF, use the transfer date and the embryo’s age as documented by the clinic.

sections.title: Four date formulas with one consistent result
paragraphs: Each method counts a different number of days because its starting point is different. The examples below all correspond to an estimated due date of April 7, 2027. Their agreement is deliberate for explaining the formulas; independent real-world estimates need not agree exactly.

table.caption: Matching date references for an example due date

sections.title: How the cycle-length adjustment works
paragraphs: Last-period due date = first day of the last period + 280 days + (cycle length − 28 days). A 30-day cycle therefore shifts the model two days later than a 28-day cycle using the same starting date. With July 1, 2026 entered, those estimates are April 9 and April 7, 2027, respectively.

This adjustment assumes a predictable relationship between cycle length and ovulation. It does not observe ovulation or make irregular cycles predictable. The accepted input range is a software boundary, not a declaration that every cycle within it is clinically equivalent.

sections.title: IVF and ultrasound require their own time references
paragraphs: For IVF, the date arithmetic is transfer date + 266 days − embryo age. A five-day transfer adds 261 days; a three-day transfer adds 263. Use the documented embryo age, not the number of days since the appointment.

For ultrasound, the remaining interval is 280 − (7 × reported weeks + reported days). At 8 weeks 6 days, 62 gestational days have elapsed and 218 remain in the conventional estimate. The calculator uses the reported age; it does not derive that age from a scan measurement.

links.label: ACOG: methods for estimating the due date

sections.title: An estimated due date is a reference for a timeline
paragraphs: The as-of date controls the gestational-age display, not the estimated due date itself. Keep the source of the due date with your result, especially when comparing a period estimate with an established clinical date.

Actual delivery can occur before or after an estimated date. This calculator cannot decide clinical redating or timing of care. If you already have an established due date and want gestational age on another day, use the known-due-date mode in the pregnancy calculator.

links.label: Calculate gestational age from a known due date

due-date-calculator.seoTitle: Due Date Calculator: Period, Conception, IVF & Ultrasound

pregnancy-conception-calculator.description: Estimate conception timing from a known due date or other pregnancy-dating information, while keeping the uncertainty of dates explicit.

faqs.question: Can I find conception from a due date?
faqs.answer: You can calculate the conventional estimate by subtracting 266 days. It remains an estimate rather than a confirmed fertilization date.

faqs.question: Why is the gestational start two weeks earlier?
faqs.answer: The conventional pregnancy timeline uses 280 days to the due date, whereas conception-based arithmetic uses 266 days.

faqs.question: Can this determine which intercourse date caused a pregnancy?
faqs.answer: No. Biological timing and uncertainty in pregnancy dating prevent this calendar calculation from identifying a particular encounter.

faqs.question: Can the dates establish paternity?
faqs.answer: No. A conception-date estimate is not evidence that can establish or rule out paternity.

faqs.question: Does changing the as-of date move conception?
faqs.answer: No. With the same underlying pregnancy reference, only the gestational age on the selected date changes.

faqs.question: Should I use this to revise a clinical due date?
faqs.answer: No. Any decision to change an established pregnancy date belongs with the maternity care team and the original clinical records.

sections.title: Estimate a conception date from an existing pregnancy timeline
paragraphs: Use this page to understand the conventional conception date implied by a pregnancy reference. Available methods include a known due date, last period, ultrasound-reported gestational age, IVF transfer and a conception date you already know or are exploring.

The result is a modeled date, not a test of when fertilization occurred. It cannot identify the exact day of intercourse or determine paternity. Those questions cannot be resolved by comparing rounded pregnancy dates.

sections.title: Worked reverse calculation from a due date
paragraphs: Select known due date and enter April 7, 2027. Subtracting 266 days gives the modeled conception date of July 15, 2026. Subtracting 280 days gives July 1, 2026 as the conventional gestational start. On October 9, 2026, the resulting gestational age is 14 weeks, 2 days.

table.caption: Three dates with different meanings

sections.title: An ultrasound reference is not an observed conception date
paragraphs: If a September 1, 2026 scan reports 8 weeks 6 days, the calculator uses 62 gestational days at that date. It projects the same April 7, 2027 due date and July 15, 2026 conception estimate. The scan’s reported age is an estimate of gestational age, not a timestamp of fertilization.

Changing the as-of date changes the current age display but does not move the modeled conception date. A different underlying dating reference can move it; do not average differing estimates to create a false impression of precision.

links.label: Calculate from a reported ultrasound age

sections.title: What an IVF transfer date means in the arithmetic
paragraphs: For a transfer on July 20, 2026 with a five-day embryo, subtracting the embryo age gives July 15 as the modeled fertilization reference. The due-date calculation then adds 266 days to that reference, giving April 7, 2027.

Use the clinic’s documented transfer information and dating record. This tool does not interpret embryo development, laboratory records or clinical changes to the due date. A guessed embryo age creates a corresponding shift in the answer.

sections.title: Keep calendar estimates separate from fertility planning
paragraphs: The interval between intercourse and fertilization can vary, and calendar dating has uncertainty. A single estimated conception date therefore should not be used to include or exclude a particular encounter. The display reports date arithmetic, not a certainty interval.

If the question is about a future cycle rather than an existing pregnancy, use the conception or ovulation calendar. Those tools model a possible fertile window from cycle assumptions and do not confirm ovulation or pregnancy.

links.label: Estimate a possible future fertile window
NHS explanation of the menstrual cycle

pregnancy-conception-calculator.seoTitle: Pregnancy Conception Calculator: Estimated Conception Date

conception-calculator.description: Estimate a possible fertile window from cycle history and explore menstrual, conception, ultrasound or IVF pregnancy-dating methods.

faqs.question: How is the possible fertile window calculated?
faqs.answer: The tool displays the five days before modeled ovulation plus the modeled ovulation day. It does not verify the actual fertile interval.

faqs.question: Is a 14-day luteal phase always correct?
faqs.answer: No. It is the default assumption. The input can be adjusted, and real timing may vary between people and cycles.

faqs.question: Does cycle length mean the number of bleeding days?
faqs.answer: No. It is the interval between the first days of consecutive periods. Bleeding duration is a different measure.

faqs.question: Can I use the predicted dates to prevent pregnancy?
faqs.answer: No. Dates outside a calendar estimate are not established safe days, and this tool does not monitor fertility signs.

faqs.question: Does a conception-date input confirm pregnancy?
faqs.answer: No. That mode assumes the date you supply and performs pregnancy-date arithmetic; it does not detect pregnancy.

faqs.question: Why can later predicted cycles be inaccurate?
faqs.answer: Each row repeats the same cycle assumptions. Any difference between modeled and actual cycle length can shift later dates.

sections.title: Plan around a possible fertile window, not a guaranteed day
paragraphs: The default fertile-window mode uses the first day of your last period, usual cycle length and an assumed luteal phase to estimate future period and ovulation dates. It shows a possible window consisting of the five days before modeled ovulation plus that day.

This is a repeating calendar model. It cannot detect whether ovulation occurred or whether pregnancy has begun, and dates outside the displayed window are not established safe days for preventing pregnancy.

sections.title: Worked example using a 28-day cycle
paragraphs: Enter July 1, 2026 as the period start, cycle length 28 and luteal phase 14. The next period estimate is July 29. Subtracting 14 days gives July 15 as modeled ovulation; the displayed possible fertile window is July 10–15, inclusive.

table.caption: Two repeated cycles with unchanged assumptions

sections.title: Separate cycle length from luteal phase
paragraphs: Cycle length is the interval from the first day of one period to the first day of the next. The luteal input represents the assumed interval from ovulation to the next period. They are different quantities: next period = period start + cycle length, then modeled ovulation = next period − luteal length.

The default of 14 luteal days is an assumption, not a measurement. With the same 28-day cycle and July 1 start, changing that input to 12 days moves the ovulation estimate from July 15 to July 17 while leaving July 29 as the next-period estimate. Real cycle timing can vary in ways a fixed calendar does not capture.

sections.title: Choose a pregnancy-dating mode for a different question
paragraphs: This page also includes last-period, conception-date, IVF and ultrasound modes for estimating a pregnancy timeline. They calculate a due date and gestational age from the selected reference, rather than predicting multiple future fertile windows.

For example, entering July 15, 2026 in conception mode gives April 7, 2027 as the estimated due date. That forward arithmetic should not be mistaken for confirmation that conception occurred on July 15. To work backward from an established due date, use the pregnancy conception calculator.

links.label: Estimate a timeline from a conception date
Work backward from an established due date

sections.title: Update assumptions when actual cycle dates become available
paragraphs: Further-ahead rows repeat the entered cycle length. They do not become more certain because the calculator displays more months. Replace a prediction with the actual period start when you have it and retain uncertainty if cycle lengths vary.

Calendar estimates alone are unsuitable for contraception and do not assess fertility problems. If you need personalized fertility advice or are concerned about a change in your cycle, the recorded dates and relevant clinical history are more useful than treating one predicted date as confirmed.

conception-calculator.seoTitle: Conception Calculator: Fertile Window & Pregnancy Dates

ovulation-calculator.description: Estimate ovulation timing and a possible fertile window from cycle length and luteal-phase assumptions, without confirming ovulation.

faqs.question: Does ovulation always occur on the same cycle day?
faqs.answer: No. The calculator derives a date from cycle length and an assumed luteal phase; it cannot confirm actual ovulation timing.

faqs.question: What does the luteal-phase input represent?
faqs.answer: It is the assumed number of days from ovulation to the next period. The default 14 is an assumption, not a measured result.

faqs.question: Why did my ovulation estimate move when I changed the luteal input?
faqs.answer: The tool subtracts luteal days from the next-period estimate. More days move modeled ovulation earlier; fewer days move it later.

faqs.question: How many days are in the displayed window?
faqs.answer: Six calendar dates: the five days before estimated ovulation and the estimated ovulation day, inclusive.

faqs.question: Can I use dates outside the window as safe days?
faqs.answer: No. Calendar uncertainty means the displayed window cannot establish days without pregnancy risk.

faqs.question: Does this calculator read an ovulation test?
faqs.answer: No. It uses entered dates and cycle assumptions only; it does not interpret hormone tests or confirm ovulation.

sections.title: Estimate ovulation from a cycle-length assumption
paragraphs: Enter the first day of the last period, usual cycle length, assumed luteal-phase length and number of cycles to display. The calculator first estimates the next period, then counts backward by the luteal-phase input to place ovulation.

The output is a calendar estimate, not evidence that an egg was released. A default luteal phase of 14 days is convenient for arithmetic but is not a measurement of your cycle. The possible fertile window shown includes five days before modeled ovulation and the modeled day itself.

links.label: NHS explanation of ovulation and cycle timing

sections.title: Follow the dates in a worked example
paragraphs: With a July 1, 2026 period start, a 28-day cycle and 14 luteal days, the next period is estimated for July 29. Counting back 14 days gives July 15 for ovulation. Counting back another five days sets the displayed window to July 10–15.

table.caption: Changing only cycle length, keeping a July 1 start and 14 luteal days

sections.title: Why cycle length and luteal length affect different dates
paragraphs: Next period = last period start + cycle length. Estimated ovulation = next period − assumed luteal days. Increasing cycle length moves both dates later. Increasing luteal length while holding cycle length fixed moves the ovulation estimate earlier without changing the predicted next period.

For the 28-day example, a 12-day luteal input gives July 17, while a 16-day input gives July 13. These are sensitivity examples showing what the assumption does. They do not tell you which value applies to a particular cycle.

sections.title: Understand the repeated-cycle table
paragraphs: Each later row repeats the same cycle length from the original start. With 28-day cycles, the next period dates after July 1 are July 29, August 26 and September 23. The calendar advances by days, so those dates do not stay on the same day of each month.

When an actual period begins, use that observed date for a new estimate. If cycles vary, projecting more rows extends the assumptions farther into the future; it does not add information about ovulation. The tool does not import temperature charts, ovulation tests or ultrasound findings.

sections.title: Use the estimate for calendar context
paragraphs: A displayed window cannot rule out fertility on other dates, and this calculator is not a contraceptive method. It also cannot diagnose a cause of irregular periods or determine whether fertility treatment is needed.

Use the period calculator when the main question concerns bleeding dates, and the pregnancy calculator when working from an established pregnancy reference. If cycle timing or symptoms are a concern, clinical interpretation should use the actual history rather than a predicted calendar alone.

period-calculator.description: Project a next-period date from menstrual history and assumed cycle length, with associated cycle estimates and their limitations.

faqs.question: What is cycle length?
faqs.answer: It is the interval between the first day of one period and the first day of the next, not the number of days spent bleeding.

faqs.question: Why does a five-day period end four days after it starts?
faqs.answer: The start date is day one. Five inclusive bleeding dates end at start plus four days.

faqs.question: Does changing bleeding duration move the next period?
faqs.answer: No. It changes the estimated bleeding end. Cycle length determines predicted period starts.

faqs.question: Why are the predicted dates not the same day each month?
faqs.answer: The tool adds a fixed number of days, while calendar months have different lengths.

faqs.question: Can the calculator tell why my period is late?
faqs.answer: No. It forecasts dates from assumptions and cannot determine pregnancy or diagnose a cause of a cycle change.

faqs.question: Should I update the start date after a real period?
faqs.answer: Yes. An observed new start is more useful for a new projection than continuing to rely on an earlier predicted start.

sections.title: Estimate the next period and a possible bleeding end date
paragraphs: Start with the first day of the last period and the usual interval between period starts. Enter the usual bleeding duration separately. The calculator projects future starts, estimates the end of each bleeding interval and also shows ovulation and possible fertile-window dates using the assumed luteal phase.
Cycle length and bleeding duration are not interchangeable. If a period starts July 1 and the next starts July 29, that is a 28-day cycle even if bleeding lasted only five days.

links.label: NHS: how menstrual-cycle days are counted

sections.title: Worked example: 28-day cycles with five bleeding days
paragraphs: Use July 1, 2026 as the last-period start, cycle length 28, luteal phase 14 and bleeding duration 5. The first predicted period starts July 29 and ends August 2. The end date counts the start as bleeding day one: start + duration − 1 day.

table.caption: Three projected periods using unchanged assumptions

sections.title: Days repeat; calendar months do not have equal lengths
paragraphs: The tool adds cycle-length days rather than advancing to the same date in the next month. For cycle number n, predicted start = original period start + n × cycle length. This explains why a 28-day pattern moves earlier through successive calendar months.

The prediction assumes each cycle has the same length. Selecting more future cycles repeats that assumption; it does not account for real variation. Recalculate from an observed new start instead of carrying an old prediction forward indefinitely.

sections.title: Ovulation dates are a separate estimate within the table
paragraphs: The ovulation estimate is predicted next period minus assumed luteal days. The displayed possible fertile interval extends from five days before that estimate through the estimated ovulation day. Changing the luteal input changes these dates but does not change the period-start or bleeding-end arithmetic.

Changing bleeding duration has the opposite scope: it changes the predicted bleeding end, not the next start or ovulation estimate. Keeping the inputs separate makes it easier to see why a particular column changes.

sections.title: A period forecast does not explain a late or changed cycle
paragraphs: A predicted start is not a deadline that establishes a medical problem if it passes. This calculator cannot determine pregnancy, explain changes in bleeding or evaluate pain. Use actual records and appropriate clinical advice when a change is concerning.

The calendar is also unsuitable as a stand-alone way to prevent pregnancy. Its useful role is organizing dates under clearly stated assumptions, while recognizing that future bleeding and ovulation may differ from the projection.

period-calculator.seoTitle: Period Calculator: Next Period & Cycle Date Estimates

pregnancy-weight-gain-calculator.description: Compare pregnancy weight gain with BMI-specific singleton or twin reference guidance, without prescribing an exact week-by-week target.

faqs.question: Should I enter current weight to calculate the BMI group?
faqs.answer: No. The reference group uses pre-pregnancy weight and height; current weight is used separately to calculate cumulative change.

faqs.question: Is the total range the amount expected by my selected week?
faqs.answer: No. It is a total-pregnancy reference, not an exact requirement at that week.

faqs.question: Does the calculator support twins?
faqs.answer: Yes. Select twins to use the separate total-gain reference. It does not apply a universal weekly twin range.

faqs.question: Why are there no exact weekly targets?
faqs.answer: Published totals and weekly ranges do not define an exact required trajectory for an individual pregnancy.

faqs.question: Can I double the singleton range for twins?
faqs.answer: No. Twin references are separately derived and are not calculated by doubling the singleton values.

faqs.question: Can this decide whether my current gain is healthy?
faqs.answer: No. A clinician must interpret the pattern alongside fetal growth and other relevant circumstances; one calculated comparison cannot make that assessment.

sections.title: Compare recorded gain with the relevant reference context
paragraphs: Enter pre-pregnancy weight, current weight, height, pregnancy week and whether the pregnancy involves one baby or twins. The calculator uses pre-pregnancy BMI to select the reference group and subtracts pre-pregnancy weight from current weight to show cumulative change.

Use weight before pregnancy for the BMI classification. Substituting current pregnancy weight would change the reference group for the wrong reason. A result should be discussed alongside the pattern over time, fetal growth and the clinical situation.

sections.title: Worked singleton example at 24 weeks
paragraphs: For pre-pregnancy weight 65 kg, current weight 70 kg, height 175 cm, week 24 and one baby, pre-pregnancy BMI = 65 ÷ 1.75² ≈ 21.22. Cumulative gain = 70 − 65 = 5 kg. The displayed total reference is 11.5–16 kg, with a second/third-trimester reference rate of 0.35–0.50 kg/week.

Those figures have different time meanings. Five kilograms is the recorded change to date; 11.5–16 kg is a total-pregnancy reference; the weekly range is a source reference for the later trimesters. Comparing the current change directly with the total range does not determine whether gain at week 24 is appropriate.

table.caption: Outputs in the example answer different questions

sections.title: Singleton reference groups use pre-pregnancy BMI
paragraphs: The implemented kilogram ranges are summarized below. Boundary comparisons use the calculated BMI before display rounding. The source’s total and weekly values are separately rounded, so they should not be forced into one exact trajectory.
These are the cited US reference ranges, not a universal clinical standard for every country or population. Follow the maternity guidance appropriate to your care setting.

table.caption: Published singleton reference ranges used by the calculator

links.label: National Academies: Table 7-3 and reference context

sections.title: Twins require a different reference
paragraphs: Selecting twins changes the total-gain reference and removes a universal weekly range. Twin guidance should not be generated by doubling the singleton rates. The published twin total ranges are provisional and require individual clinical interpretation.

For the underweight twin group, this tool follows the additional CDC range rather than attributing it to the 2009 Institute of Medicine guideline. That distinction appears in the result notes. The tool does not supply a reference for triplets or higher-order pregnancies.

sections.title: Why the page does not give an exact required weight by week
paragraphs: In weeks up to 13, the singleton result provides first-trimester context rather than applying later-trimester weekly rates. Later weeks show the source rate for the relevant group. Neither output defines an exact required weight on a particular date.

Weight measurements and clinical circumstances can vary, so an individual point cannot establish whether a pregnancy is progressing appropriately. Review a concerning pattern with the maternity care team. This calculator does not prescribe calorie changes or weight-loss goals during pregnancy.

pregnancy-weight-gain-calculator.seoTitle: Pregnancy Weight Gain Calculator: Reference Ranges

gfr-calculator.description: Estimate eGFR with adult race-free CKD-EPI 2021 or pediatric bedside Schwartz equations, using creatinine and model-specific inputs.

faqs.question: Does this eGFR calculation include race?
faqs.answer: No. Adult mode uses the race-free 2021 CKD-EPI creatinine equation.

faqs.question: How do I convert creatinine from µmol/L to mg/dL?
faqs.answer: Divide by 88.4. The calculator performs that conversion when µmol/L is selected.

faqs.question: Is eGFR a percentage of kidney function?
faqs.answer: No. It is a filtration-rate estimate reported in mL/min per 1.73 m² of standardized body surface area.

faqs.question: Why does my laboratory report show a different result?
faqs.answer: Check the equation version, units, entered details and rounding. Laboratories may use a different equation or reporting convention.

faqs.question: Does pediatric mode use CKiD U25?
faqs.answer: No. It uses the 2009 bedside Schwartz expression 0.413 × height(cm) ÷ creatinine(mg/dL). The source link explains other pediatric options.

faqs.question: Can one eGFR result diagnose kidney disease?
faqs.answer: No. It needs clinical interpretation with trends and other findings. The calculator does not diagnose disease or determine medication dosing.

sections.title: Use the named equation and the laboratory units
paragraphs: Adult mode calculates estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) with the race-free 2021 CKD-EPI creatinine equation for adults aged 18 and older. Enter age, the equation’s sex category and serum creatinine with the unit printed on the laboratory report.

The pediatric mode implements the 2009 bedside Schwartz calculation using height and creatinine. It is a distinct equation, not the adult equation with a younger age. This page does not implement cystatin C, combined-marker equations or the newer CKiD U25 equations.

sections.title: Worked adult example and unit conversion
paragraphs: For the male equation at age 50 and creatinine 1.00 mg/dL, the estimated GFR is approximately 91.69 mL/min/1.73 m². Entering the equivalent 88.4 µmol/L produces the same result because the tool divides µmol/L by 88.4 before applying the formula.
Entering 88.4 while leaving mg/dL selected is not a small rounding difference; it changes the quantity by a factor of 88.4. Check the unit before interpreting any discrepancy.

table.caption: Equivalent creatinine inputs for the same adult example

sections.title: What the adult equation calculates
paragraphs: The implemented equation is 142 × min(Scr/κ, 1)^α × max(Scr/κ, 1)^−1.200 × 0.9938^age, with a multiplier of 1.012 for the female coefficient. Scr is creatinine in mg/dL. For the male coefficient, κ = 0.9 and α = −0.302; for the female coefficient, κ = 0.7 and α = −0.241.

The min and max terms apply different exponents below and above the equation’s creatinine reference. There is no race input or race multiplier. Calculators using older equations may therefore produce different results even when the entered laboratory value matches.

sections.title: Reproduce the bedside Schwartz example
paragraphs: The pediatric formula is 0.413 × height(cm) ÷ creatinine(mg/dL). With height 140 cm and creatinine 0.60 mg/dL, the result is 0.413 × 140 ÷ 0.60 ≈ 96.37 mL/min/1.73 m². The mode can convert height in inches and creatinine in µmol/L before calculating.

This historical bedside estimate is not a universal choice for every child or young adult. NIDDK describes additional equations, including CKiD U25, whose applicability depends on the clinical population. The calculator’s available method does not determine which equation should guide care.

sections.title: Interpret an estimate alongside clinical information
paragraphs: The unit mL/min/1.73 m² indicates a filtration estimate indexed to a standard body surface area. It is not a percentage, and 91.69 does not mean 91.69% kidney function. This page does not convert the indexed result into an individualized absolute filtration rate.

A single estimate cannot diagnose kidney disease or establish a treatment plan. Trends, urine findings, the laboratory method and factors affecting creatinine all matter. Review unexpected results with the clinician who requested the test; do not use the displayed number alone to change medication doses or dietary treatment.

gfr-calculator.seoTitle: GFR Calculator: Adult & Pediatric eGFR Estimates

bac-calculator.description: Explore a rough Widmark blood-alcohol estimate from one drink input or multiple beverages, with major safety limitations made explicit.

faqs.question: Does the calculator measure my BAC?
faqs.answer: No. It produces a simplified estimate from entered amounts and assumptions. Actual blood alcohol can differ substantially.

faqs.question: Should 5% ABV be entered as 5 or 0.05?
faqs.answer: Enter 5. The formula divides the percentage by 100 internally.

faqs.question: How are mixed drinks handled?
faqs.answer: Enter the volume and strength of each alcoholic component or an accurately known combined amount and ABV. The calculator cannot infer a recipe or alcohol content from a drink name.

faqs.question: Are US and Imperial pints the same?
faqs.answer: No. They represent different volumes. Use the explicit-unit mode and choose the matching measurement.

faqs.question: Does a zero result mean I can drive?
faqs.answer: No. The model’s zero floor cannot establish sobriety, legal compliance or safe driving.

faqs.question: Can I use the elapsed-time field to find when it is safe to drive?
faqs.answer: No. The assumed elimination rate is not a personal measurement, and the tool must not be used as a driving countdown.

sections.title: Understand what the BAC model can estimate
paragraphs: This calculator converts beverage amounts into grams of alcohol and applies a simplified Widmark-style model using body weight, a distribution coefficient and elapsed time. It does not measure blood alcohol, assess impairment or establish whether driving is safe or legal.

Use single-beverage mode for one amount and strength, or a multiple-beverage mode for different drinks. The extended unit modes let you specify body-weight and volume units explicitly. Enter alcohol by volume as a percentage: a label showing 5% ABV is entered as 5, not 0.05.

links.label: Research on uncertainty in alcohol calculations

sections.title: Worked example: calculate grams of alcohol first
paragraphs: For 355 mL at 5% ABV, pure ethanol volume is 355 × 0.05 = 17.75 mL. Using the model’s density factor of 0.789 g/mL gives 17.75 × 0.789 = 14.00475 g of alcohol. This quantity depends on beverage volume and strength, not the person’s body weight.

table.caption: The alcohol calculation for three beverage examples

sections.title: Multiple beverages are added by alcohol mass
paragraphs: Two 330 mL beverages at 5% and one 150 mL beverage at 12% contain 2 × 330 × 0.05 × 0.789 + 150 × 0.12 × 0.789 = 40.239 g under the model. Averaging their ABV values without accounting for their volumes would be incorrect.

In the basic multiple-beverage text mode, each line uses count, volume in mL, ABV percent. This example is entered as “2,330,5” on one line and “1,150,12” on another. The extended mode provides the separate volume-unit choice. Check count and serving volume so a shared bottle is not accidentally counted once per serving at its full bottle volume.

sections.title: The time and distribution assumptions are not personal measurements
paragraphs: The simplified BAC calculation divides alcohol grams by body weight in grams and an assumed distribution factor, multiplies by 100, then subtracts 0.015 percentage points per entered hour. The implemented factors are 0.68 for the male coefficient and 0.55 for the female coefficient. Negative modeled values are displayed as zero.

Absorption and elimination do not follow this simple line identically for everyone. Timing, food, physiology and other factors can change the relationship between drinks and actual BAC. A zero estimate means only that the formula reached its display floor; it does not establish sobriety or a safe departure time.

sections.title: Check volume units and avoid safety decisions from the output
paragraphs: US and Imperial fluid ounces and pints have different volumes. Select the unit that belongs to the beverage measurement; an unspecified “pint” is not enough to reproduce the calculation reliably. The explicit-unit mode also distinguishes metric cups from US cups.

Do not use the model as a countdown for driving or as a way to dismiss symptoms. If someone is difficult to wake, has trouble breathing or may have alcohol poisoning, seek emergency medical help immediately rather than waiting for a calculated value to change.

bac-calculator.seoTitle: BAC Calculator: Blood Alcohol Estimate & Limitations

average-calculator.description: Calculate the mean of a number list and compare it with the median, range and other measures of the dataset's spread.

faqs.question: Can one unusually large value change the average?
faqs.answer: Yes. The mean uses every value, so an extreme value can shift it substantially. Comparing the median helps reveal that effect.

faqs.question: Is this a weighted average?
faqs.answer: No. Each entered value contributes equally. A weighted mean requires explicit weights and a different calculation.

faqs.question: Should zero values be included in an average?
faqs.answer: Include an observed zero. Leave out a missing observation only when that matches the data collection rule; replacing missing values with zero changes the result.

faqs.question: Why is the average different from the median?
faqs.answer: The mean uses every magnitude, while the median depends on the sorted middle position. For 6, 8, 8, 10, 18, they are 10 and 8 respectively.

faqs.question: Can I average averages from groups of different sizes?
faqs.answer: Weight each group mean by its observation count. Ten observations averaging 70 and thirty averaging 90 combine to 85, not 80.

faqs.question: Can I paste numbers with thousands separators?
faqs.answer: Remove commas used inside individual numbers first. Commas separate observations in this input, so 1,200 would be interpreted as 1 and 200.

sections.title: Choosing what an average should describe
paragraphs: For the values 10, 12, 14, and 100, the sum is 136 and the arithmetic mean is 34. The median is 13, halfway between the two middle values after sorting. The large value of 100 pulls the mean upward, which is why reporting only the average can hide the shape of the data. Include each observation once and use consistent units. For course grades or other weighted observations, use a tool that accepts weights rather than treating every value equally.

sections.title: Calculate the mean by keeping the total and count together
paragraphs: Enter one observation per number, separated by spaces, commas or new lines. The arithmetic mean is the total divided by the number of observations. Include a genuine zero as 0; omitting it changes both the count and the average. Do not insert commas inside a number: enter 1200 rather than 1,200, which would be read as two observations.

sections.title: Worked example: compare a mean with its underlying observations
paragraphs: For the five values 6, 8, 8, 10 and 18, the sum is 50 and the count is 5, so the mean is 10. Sorting gives a median of 8, and 8 is also the mode. The mean is higher because the value 18 pulls the total upward.

If 18 was a valid observation, keeping it and reporting the median alongside the mean is different from deleting it. Investigate a possible data-entry error before deciding that a value should be excluded.

table.caption: One dataset, several different summaries

sections.title: Combine group averages using group sizes
paragraphs: Suppose one group has 10 observations with mean 70 and another has 30 observations with mean 90. The combined mean is (10 × 70 + 30 × 90) ÷ 40 = 85. Averaging 70 and 90 to get 80 would give the groups equal weight despite their different sizes.

This page accepts raw observations rather than a separate frequency or weight column. Use the original observations when available; otherwise calculate the weighted total and total count explicitly. Do not enter a group mean several times unless that repetition correctly represents its weight.

sections.title: Keep averages compatible with the question
paragraphs: An arithmetic mean describes additive quantities measured on the same scale. A geometric mean describes multiplicative factors when its domain is appropriate; it is not a replacement for the arithmetic mean of ordinary counts. The calculator also shows median and spread so that one number does not hide an uneven distribution.

A mean cannot repair a biased sample, mixed units or unequal time exposure. Convert measurements to one unit before entering them, and retain the count when reporting an average so readers know how much data it summarizes.

mean-median-mode-range-calculator.description: Find mean, median, mode and range from a dataset and compare what each measure reveals about its center and spread.

faqs.question: Why can the mean and median be different?
faqs.answer: The mean uses the sum of all values; the median uses their sorted middle. Skewed or extreme values can separate them.

faqs.question: Can a dataset have more than one mode?
faqs.answer: Yes. Several values can tie for the highest frequency. A mode describes frequency, not necessarily the center of the data.

faqs.question: How is the median calculated for an even count?
faqs.answer: Sort the values, then average the two central positions. For 2, 3, 3, 7, 7, 20, the middle values are 3 and 7, giving 5.

faqs.question: What does No repeated values mean?
