faqs.answer: Every input appears once, so there is no repeated value to identify as the most frequent. This is distinct from a numeric mode of zero.

faqs.question: Does a small range prove that most values are close to the mean?
faqs.answer: Range uses only the minimum and maximum. Inspect standard deviation and the underlying observations to understand how values are distributed inside those endpoints.

sections.title: Reading the center and spread of a dataset
paragraphs: The mean, median, mode, and range answer different questions about the same data. The mode identifies repeated values, while the range depends only on the smallest and largest entries. Two datasets can share a mean and still have very different distributions. Review the original values as well as these summaries, especially when the list contains outliers or repeated measurements.

sections.title: Find four summaries that answer different questions
paragraphs: The mean divides the sum by the count. The median locates the middle after sorting. The mode identifies the most frequent value, and the range subtracts the smallest value from the largest. Enter raw observations, including repeated values; sorting them yourself is optional.
These measures need not agree. A useful report explains whether its goal is a typical observation, the most common response or the distance between the extremes.

sections.title: Worked example with two middle values and two modes
paragraphs: Enter 2, 3, 3, 7, 7, 20. Their sum is 42, so the mean is 7. Six observations leave two middle positions, occupied by 3 and 7; the median is their average, 5. Both 3 and 7 occur twice, making the dataset bimodal. The range is 20 − 2 = 18.

table.caption: Interpreting 2, 3, 3, 7, 7, 20
rows: Two values share the highest frequency

sections.title: See how an extreme observation changes the summaries
paragraphs: Replace 20 with 200 in the example. The mean becomes 37 and the range becomes 198, while the median stays 5 and the modes stay 3 and 7. This comparison shows why a center and a spread measure should often be reported together.
Neither unchanged median nor a familiar mode proves that the records are correct. Check the unusually large observation against its source rather than deleting it merely because it affects the mean.

sections.title: Interpret ties, no repeated values and measurement units
paragraphs: Finflo reports the values tied for the greatest repeated frequency. If every number occurs once, it reports No repeated values. Mode conventions can differ when all values have the same frequency, so describe the frequency pattern when that distinction matters.

The range has the same unit as the inputs but uses only two observations. Standard deviation incorporates every observation and gives a different view of spread. Use consistent units throughout the list.

statistics-calculator.description: Summarize a numeric dataset with measures of center, spread and distribution, including sample and population variance.

faqs.question: Should I use the sample or population variance?
faqs.answer: Use population variance when the list is the full population of interest; use sample variance when estimating spread from a sample.

faqs.question: Do these summary statistics establish that data are normally distributed?
faqs.answer: No. Mean, median and standard deviation describe features of a dataset; they do not by themselves demonstrate a normal distribution.

faqs.question: What should I check after pasting a dataset?
faqs.answer: Start with Count, Sum, Minimum and Maximum. Unexpected values there often reveal a missing row, an accidental thousands separator or a mixed unit.

faqs.question: What is the difference between sum of squares and variance?
faqs.answer: Sum of squares adds x² directly. Variance instead uses squared distances from the mean and divides their total by n or n − 1.

faqs.question: Does the calculator accept a frequency table?
faqs.answer: It accepts a list of observations, not value-frequency columns. Expand frequencies into repeated observations where practical, or use a method designed for frequency weights.

faqs.question: Can these results show whether one factor causes another?
faqs.answer: No. Descriptive summaries of a single numeric list do not test causal relationships, control confounding or establish the quality of a study design.

sections.title: Preparing data for a statistical summary
paragraphs: Before calculating, make sure the dataset contains comparable observations and that missing entries have not been replaced with zeros unless zero is an actual measurement. The summary describes the list you enter. Compare measures of center with measures of spread to avoid presenting a typical value without context. Descriptive statistics alone do not establish a cause or support a population-wide conclusion.

sections.title: Prepare one clean list of numeric observations
paragraphs: Paste observations separated by commas, spaces or line breaks. Remove column headings and unit suffixes first. If records contain missing values, decide how to handle them before entering the list; a blank record and an observed zero are different. Do not include commas used as thousands separators.

Repeated values represent repeated observations. This summary tool does not accept a second column of frequencies, pair x and y values, fit a regression model or decide whether your observations form a representative sample.

sections.title: Use count and sum to audit the input before interpreting it
paragraphs: For 2, 4, 4 and 10, the count is 4 and the sum is 20. These are useful first checks when pasting data. The mean is 5, the median and mode are 4, and the range is 8. The sum of squares is 136, which is different from the squared-deviation total of 36.

table.caption: Descriptive summary of 2, 4, 4, 10

sections.title: Choose the mean that matches additive or multiplicative data
paragraphs: The arithmetic mean of positive factors 2 and 8 is 5, whereas their geometric mean is √(2 × 8) = 4. Geometric means summarize products or compound factors; an arithmetic average describes additive observations. The calculator reports zero geometric mean if a zero is present and no real geometric-mean result when negative inputs occur.
For growth-rate analysis, rates must first become factors, such as 1.10 for +10%. Do not take the geometric mean of raw signed percentages and call it compound growth.

sections.title: Keep descriptive summaries separate from statistical inference
paragraphs: Count, center and spread describe the records entered. They do not by themselves supply a p-value, establish causation or quantify sampling bias. Two datasets can have matching means and variances while arranging their observations very differently.

If your next question concerns a population mean, use a suitable confidence interval with a stated sample size and sampling model. For a test statistic, choose a distribution and tail in the P-value Calculator.

statistics-calculator.seoTitle: Statistics Calculator: Mean, Variance & Standard Deviation

standard-deviation-calculator.description: Calculate sample and population standard deviation and variance from a number list, with the different denominators explained.

faqs.question: Why is sample standard deviation usually larger?
faqs.answer: Sample variance divides squared deviations by n − 1 instead of n. Taking the square root preserves that difference.

faqs.question: Does standard deviation use the same units as my data?
faqs.answer: Yes. Variance uses squared units, while standard deviation takes the square root and returns to the original unit.

faqs.question: Does adding the same constant to every value change standard deviation?
faqs.answer: No. Adding a constant shifts the mean by that constant but leaves each deviation from the mean unchanged, so variance and standard deviation stay the same.

faqs.question: Can I calculate sample standard deviation from one number?
faqs.answer: No. Its denominator n − 1 would be zero. Finflo can describe the population spread of that one value but omits the sample estimate.

faqs.question: Is standard deviation the same as standard error?
faqs.answer: No. Standard deviation describes variability among observations. The standard error of an independent-sample mean is commonly estimated as s ÷ √n.

sections.title: Population and sample standard deviation
paragraphs: For 2, 4, and 6, the mean is 4. Squared deviations are 4, 0, and 4, totaling 8. Treating the list as the whole population gives variance 8 ÷ 3 and standard deviation about 1.63. Treating it as a sample gives variance 8 ÷ 2 = 4 and standard deviation 2. Choose the interpretation that matches your data, not the smaller answer. Standard deviation uses the original unit; variance uses its square.

sections.title: Choose the population or sample result deliberately
paragraphs: Use population standard deviation when the entered values constitute the complete population you intend to describe. Use sample standard deviation when estimating variation in a broader population from a sample. Finflo returns both when at least two values are available; these are different denominators applied to the same deviations.

Population variance divides the squared-deviation total by n. Sample variance divides by n − 1 because the sample mean was estimated from the same observations. Taking the square root gives standard deviation in the original measurement unit.

sections.title: Work through the squared deviations before taking the root
paragraphs: For 4, 6, 8 and 10, the mean is 7. The deviations are −3, −1, 1 and 3; their squares total 20. Population variance is 20 ÷ 4 = 5, giving standard deviation √5 ≈ 2.2361. Sample variance is 20 ÷ 3, giving sample standard deviation ≈ 2.5820.

table.caption: Calculating spread for 4, 6, 8, 10

sections.title: Separate standard deviation, variance and standard error
paragraphs: If the inputs are millimeters, standard deviation is in millimeters and variance is in square millimeters. Standard error of a sample mean is s ÷ √n under the relevant sampling assumptions; it describes uncertainty in the estimated mean rather than the spread of individual measurements.

For the four-value example, s ÷ √4 ≈ 1.2910. A confidence interval additionally needs a critical value and appropriate assumptions. Do not label the sample standard deviation itself a margin of error.

links.label: Build a confidence interval for a mean

sections.title: Check extreme values and the meaning of a zero spread
paragraphs: All identical observations produce zero standard deviation. A single observation also has zero population spread, but sample standard deviation is unavailable because n − 1 is zero. The page omits that sample result rather than inventing an estimate.

Large deviations receive extra weight because they are squared. Validate unexpected values and measurement units before interpreting the spread. The familiar approximately 68% within one standard deviation rule needs a normal-distribution model; it does not apply to every dataset.

links.label: NIST: definitions and behavior of scale measures

percent-calculator.description: Find a percentage, percentage change or difference, adjust a value, and reverse a change to recover the original amount.

faqs.question: How is percentage difference different from percentage change?
faqs.answer: Change uses an original value as its base. Difference compares two nonnegative values using their average as the base.

faqs.question: Can I reverse a 100% decrease to find the original value?
faqs.answer: No. Every original value becomes zero after a 100% decrease, so the final value does not identify a unique original.

faqs.question: Should I enter 15 or 0.15 for fifteen percent?
faqs.answer: Enter 15 in a field labeled Percentage or %. The calculator divides by 100 when converting that percentage to a multiplier.

faqs.question: How do I find a price before a percentage increase?
faqs.answer: Divide the final value by 1 + p/100. A final value of 276 after a 15% increase corresponds to 240.

faqs.question: Why do a 20% increase and a 20% decrease not cancel?
faqs.answer: They act on different bases. Multiplying by 1.20 and then 0.80 gives 0.96, leaving 96% of the starting amount.

faqs.question: How is a percentage point different from a percent change?
faqs.answer: A change from 20% to 25% is 5 percentage points, or a 25% relative increase from the original 20% rate.

sections.title: Choosing the correct percentage question
paragraphs: A percentage of a number, a percentage change, and a percentage difference use different comparison bases. Select the mode that matches the wording of the problem before entering values. When reversing a percentage change, work from the relationship to the original amount rather than subtracting the same percentage from the final amount. The displayed formula shows which value serves as the base.

A rate rising from 5% to 6% increases by 1 percentage point and by 20% relative to the original rate. Percentage points subtract the two rates; percentage change divides that difference by the original rate.
If an item costs 80 after a 20% discount, the original price was 100: divide 80 by 0.8. Adding 20% to 80 gives 96, because that percentage uses a different base.

sections.title: Match the percentage formula to the unknown quantity
paragraphs: Percentage of a number multiplies the base by p ÷ 100. What percentage? divides a part by its whole and multiplies by 100. Find the original whole reverses that relationship. Enter 15 for 15%, not 0.15, in fields explicitly labeled as percentages.

The base determines the meaning. A share of a total, an increase from an old value and a symmetric comparison between two values require different denominators; they cannot be substituted without changing the question.

sections.title: Follow one example through the forward and reverse calculations
paragraphs: A 15% share of 240 is 36. Conversely, 36 out of 240 is 15%, and a known part of 36 representing 15% implies a whole of 240. Increasing 240 by 15% produces 276, while reversing that increase divides 276 by 1.15 to return to 240.

table.caption: Percentage questions built around 240

links.label: Find a percentage of a number

sections.title: Distinguish percentage change from percentage-point change
paragraphs: A rate moving from 20% to 25% increases by 5 percentage points, but its relative increase is (25 − 20) ÷ 20 = 25%. State which quantity is being reported. For ordinary values, moving from 80 to 100 is a 25% increase, while moving back from 100 to 80 is a 20% decrease.

Finflo uses the magnitude of the original value in Percentage change, which defines a particular convention when the starting value is negative. Change from zero remains undefined because there is no nonzero comparison base.

sections.title: Check successive changes instead of adding their percentages
paragraphs: A 20% reduction followed by another 10% reduction multiplies the original by 0.80 × 0.90 = 0.72, for a combined 28% reduction. It is not a 30% reduction. Likewise, an increase and decrease of the same percentage do not generally cancel.
Percentage difference uses the average of two nonnegative values as its denominator. For 80 and 100, it is 20 ÷ 90 × 100 ≈ 22.22%, a different result from change relative to either endpoint.

percent-error-calculator.description: Compare an observed value with a nonzero accepted value to calculate absolute percentage error and signed error.

faqs.question: Why must the accepted value be nonzero?
faqs.answer: Percentage error divides by the magnitude of the accepted value. A zero reference makes that relative comparison undefined.

faqs.question: What does signed error add to absolute percentage error?
faqs.answer: Absolute percentage error describes the size of the discrepancy. Signed error also preserves whether the observation lies above or below the reference.

faqs.question: Can percentage error be negative?
faqs.answer: The magnitude returned here is nonnegative. The separate Signed error result can be negative when the experimental value is below the accepted value.

faqs.question: Which value belongs in the denominator?
faqs.answer: Use the accepted reference, not the experimental value and not their average. Those alternative denominators answer different comparison questions.

faqs.question: Does 0% error mean a measurement has no uncertainty?
faqs.answer: No. It means the entered measurement equals the entered reference. Their measurement uncertainty and rounding may still be substantial.

sections.title: Choosing the reference value for percent error
paragraphs: Percent error compares a measured or estimated value with a reference value. The reference belongs in the denominator, so swapping the two values changes the meaning of the answer. Check the selected formula's treatment of the sign and absolute difference. If the reference is zero, a relative percentage cannot be interpreted in the same way as an ordinary nonzero comparison.

sections.title: Use an accepted reference rather than an arbitrary comparison base
paragraphs: Percentage error is 100 × |experimental − accepted| ÷ |accepted|. Enter the observed measurement and the reference in the same unit. The accepted reference must be nonzero; it supplies the scale against which the discrepancy is measured.
This page also shows signed error, experimental minus accepted. Its sign tells you the direction of the difference, whereas the percentage-error result is a nonnegative magnitude.

sections.title: Worked example: a measurement below its accepted value
paragraphs: Suppose a measurement is 48.5 and its accepted reference is 50. The signed error is −1.5, and the absolute error is 1.5. Dividing by 50 gives 0.03, or 3%. A measurement of 51.5 has the same 3% magnitude but a positive signed error.

table.caption: Equal error sizes with opposite directions

sections.title: Do not substitute percentage difference or a confidence interval
paragraphs: When neither value is an accepted reference, Percentage difference may better describe the comparison. It divides the absolute gap by the average of two nonnegative values. Percentage change instead identifies one value as the starting point.

A small percentage error for one measurement does not establish measurement precision, calibration quality or a confidence interval. Repeated measurements, instrument resolution and uncertainty in the reference require their own analysis.

links.label: Compare values without selecting a reference

sections.title: Handle zero, signs and unit changes explicitly
paragraphs: An accepted value of zero makes the percentage formula undefined, even if the observed value is also zero. Report an absolute discrepancy in the measurement unit or choose an appropriate domain-specific measure.

For a negative accepted value, Finflo divides by its magnitude. Multiplying both measurements by the same nonzero unit-conversion factor preserves percentage error, but adding an offset to both measurements generally does not. This matters for scales whose zero points differ.

percent-error-calculator.seoTitle: Percent Error Calculator: Absolute & Signed Error

scientific-calculator.description: Evaluate mathematical expressions with powers, logarithms and trigonometric functions, using an explicit degree or radian setting.

faqs.question: What is the difference between log and ln?
faqs.answer: In this expression calculator, log means base 10 and ln means the natural logarithm with base e.

faqs.question: How should I write multiplication next to parentheses?
faqs.answer: Use an explicit multiplication sign, such as 2 * (3 + 4). Select the angle unit before evaluating trigonometric functions.

faqs.question: Why is sin(30) not 0.5?
faqs.answer: Check the angle setting. It equals 0.5 when 30 means degrees; in radian mode use pi/6 for that angle.

faqs.question: Does sqrt(9) return both square roots?
faqs.answer: No. It returns the principal square root, 3. Solving the equation x² = 9 gives two solutions, +3 and −3.

faqs.question: Can I enter an equation with an unknown variable?
faqs.answer: This tool evaluates numerical expressions rather than solving general equations. Use a dedicated equation solver such as the Quadratic Formula Calculator when appropriate.

sections.title: Checking expression structure before evaluating
paragraphs: Use parentheses to make the intended order of operations explicit, particularly around fractions, powers, and negative values. Check the supported function names and angle convention before entering a trigonometric expression. A mathematically valid expression can still answer the wrong question if the grouping is different. Compare the entered expression with the original problem before relying on the numerical result.

sections.title: Choose degrees or radians before evaluating trigonometry
paragraphs: The angle setting applies to sin, cos and tan inputs and to the returned angles from asin, acos and atan. In Degrees, sin(30) is 0.5. In Radians, sin(pi/6) is also 0.5. The number 30 in radian mode represents a different angle.
Use pi for π and e for Euler’s number. Explicit multiplication, such as 2*pi or 3*(4+5), makes expressions clear and avoids relying on implied multiplication conventions.

sections.title: Reproduce a short set of scientific calculations
paragraphs: Enter sqrt(81)+2^4 to obtain 25. Enter log(1000) for 3 because log is base 10 here, and ln(e^2) for approximately 2 because ln is the natural logarithm. Parentheses delimit function arguments and keep complex fractions unambiguous.

table.caption: Expressions and their intended conventions

sections.title: Keep roots, powers and inverse functions distinct
paragraphs: sqrt(9) returns the principal square root 3. Solving x² = 9 is a different task with solutions ±3. Likewise, asin(0.5) returns a principal angle, not every angle whose sine is 0.5. Trigonometric identities can generate additional solutions when solving an equation.

A negative base raised to a fractional exponent may be outside the supported real-number evaluation. For a real odd root such as the cube root of −8, use the Nth Root Calculator. Exponents in this expression interface must follow its displayed literal-exponent limits.

links.label: Calculate a real odd root of a negative number

sections.title: Use saved answers carefully and preserve input precision
paragraphs: Ans can reuse the last successful answer in a later expression. For a sequence of dependent steps, this avoids manually copying a rounded display. Reset clears answer and memory state; a new expression using Ans requires a prior successful answer.

Calculations return finite real numbers, not symbolic proofs or complex-number algebra. Rejecting log(0), dividing by zero or a non-real result is different from obtaining a large valid number. Check the function domain and grouping before changing the formula.

links.label: OpenStax: logarithmic function domains and bases

basic-calculator.description: Calculate arithmetic expressions with parentheses and standard operation order, using explicit multiplication and readable results.

faqs.question: Are operations evaluated strictly from left to right?
faqs.answer: No. Parentheses and functions are evaluated first, followed by powers, multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction.

faqs.question: How do parentheses change an arithmetic result?
faqs.answer: They group operations to be performed first. For example, 2 * (3 + 4) gives 14, while 2 * 3 + 4 gives 10.

faqs.question: How do I calculate a percentage in an expression?
faqs.answer: Multiply by the percentage divided by 100. For 15% of 80, enter 80*15/100; for a 15% reduction, enter 80*(1-15/100).

faqs.question: What does Ans refer to?
faqs.answer: Ans refers to the most recent successful calculator answer. Calculate once before using it, and use Reset to clear stored calculation state.

faqs.question: Does the calculator choose the correct financial formula for me?
faqs.answer: No. It evaluates the expression entered. You must decide which amounts, timing rules and grouping match the intended calculation.

sections.title: Making everyday arithmetic unambiguous
paragraphs: The basic calculator evaluates the expression you enter using its supported operators and order of operations. Use parentheses when a subtotal should be calculated first, such as a combined price before a division. Keep track of units outside the expression so that unlike quantities are not added accidentally. Rounding a displayed answer does not necessarily mean the original inputs were equally precise.

sections.title: Write the arithmetic you mean with explicit parentheses
paragraphs: Enter a complete numerical expression using +, −, *, / and parentheses, then select Calculate. Multiplication and division are evaluated before addition and subtraction. Use an explicit multiplication sign between a number and parentheses, such as 4*(6+2).

For a total with several components, group the terms before applying a shared multiplier. The calculator evaluates the expression; it does not infer whether a fee, discount or tax belongs inside a particular group.

sections.title: Check a practical total in two different forms
paragraphs: Suppose three items cost 12 each and two items cost 7 each. Enter 3*12+2*7 to get 50. Adding a fee of 5 gives 55. If every item instead receives a 10% discount before that fixed fee, enter (3*12+2*7)*0.9+5 to get 50.
Writing (3*12+2*7+5)*0.9 would also discount the fee and return 49.5. The difference is in the chosen grouping, not a rounding discrepancy.

table.caption: The same numbers can describe different totals

sections.title: Reuse a successful answer without rewriting it
paragraphs: After calculating a valid result, Ans refers to that stored answer. For example, calculate 50 and then enter Ans/4 to obtain 12.5. Memory controls provide a separate running value where available in the keypad.
Clear removes the current expression, while Reset clears the calculator state, including answer and memory. Use a fresh calculation if you are unsure whether Ans refers to the number you intend.

sections.title: Recognize the limits of ordinary numeric evaluation
paragraphs: A denominator of zero and an expression without a finite real result are rejected. Use parentheses around a negative number before applying an even power when the sign is part of the base: (−3)^2 differs from −3^2.

For exact integer operations with very large inputs or controlled decimal precision, use the Big Number Calculator. Additional displayed digits in an ordinary arithmetic result should not be treated as greater measurement accuracy.

links.label: Calculate with large integers or decimal precision

big-number-calculator.description: Work with exact integer operations, bounded high-precision decimals and mathematical expressions, choosing the mode suited to the numbers.

faqs.question: Which mode should I use for precise decimal arithmetic?
faqs.answer: Use Decimal arithmetic & precision for the supported basic operations and choose the displayed decimal places, up to 100.

faqs.question: Are all modes unlimited exact arithmetic?
faqs.answer: No. Exact integer operations, higher-precision decimal operations and ordinary expressions have different capabilities and explicit size or precision limits.

faqs.question: Why does −17 modulo 5 give 3?
faqs.answer: This mode chooses a nonnegative remainder relative to the absolute divisor: −17 = −4×5 + 3. Other tools may use a signed remainder convention.

faqs.question: Can a decimal result display 1/7 exactly?
faqs.answer: No finite decimal can represent its infinite repeat exactly. Use the Fraction Calculator if the rational value itself must remain exact.

faqs.question: What is the factorial of zero?
faqs.answer: It is 1. The exact-integer mode supports factorials of nonnegative integers within its stated range.

sections.title: Choosing integer or decimal precision
paragraphs: Very large integers and decimal expressions can require different arithmetic methods. Use exact integer operations when all inputs and the requested operation fit that mode. For decimal work, review the precision setting and the displayed limitations. A long result is not automatically an exact result, particularly when division creates a repeating decimal or the selected expression uses an approximate function.

sections.title: Choose exact integer work or decimal precision explicitly
paragraphs: Calculate an expression uses a 64-significant-digit big-number context for arithmetic expressions. Exact integer operations uses integer arithmetic for GCD, LCM, modulo and factorial. Decimal arithmetic & precision lets you choose the number of decimal places in its output.

These modes solve different precision problems. A long expression result is not a claim of unlimited precision, while the exact-integer mode preserves its supported integer result without conversion through ordinary floating-point numbers.

sections.title: Check a calculation beyond ordinary integer precision
paragraphs: Enter 9007199254740993+2 in the expression mode to obtain 9007199254740995. The starting integer is beyond the range in which every consecutive integer can be represented by ordinary JavaScript Number arithmetic. The big-number context retains these entered digits for this calculation.
For a decimal example, select division with A=1, B=7 and 6 decimal places. The output is 0.142857. It is a rounded display of a repeating decimal, not an exact terminating representation.

table.caption: Precision tasks and the matching mode

sections.title: Interpret modulo and factorial conventions
paragraphs: Modulo returns a nonnegative remainder relative to the magnitude of the divisor. For example, −17 modulo 5 gives 3 because −17 = (−4) × 5 + 3. This differs from a signed remainder convention used by some programming languages. A zero divisor is invalid.
Factorial uses the first integer only. It supports nonnegative integers through 1,000, including 0! = 1. Factorial is a product of positive integers, not repeated addition or exponentiation.

links.label: Explore counting with permutations and combinations

sections.title: Distinguish significant digits from decimal places
paragraphs: Six decimal places means six digits after the decimal point; six significant digits counts meaningful digits from the first nonzero digit. Those controls can produce different rounded representations of a large or tiny number. Preserve the unrounded input until the final reporting step.

Expression length and exponent limits keep computation bounded. Scientific notation is useful for entering scale, but it does not remove precision limits. When an exact rational value such as 1/7 is required, keep the fraction rather than a finite decimal.

links.label: Keep a rational result as a fraction

big-number-calculator.seoTitle: Big Number Calculator: Integer & Decimal Arithmetic

fraction-calculator.description: Add, subtract, multiply, divide, simplify and compare fractions, with mixed-number and decimal input support.

faqs.question: Can I enter a mixed number such as one and a half?
faqs.answer: Yes. Enter 1 1/2. Fraction and supported decimal inputs are interpreted as rational values for the selected operation.

faqs.question: Why is comparing fractions better than rounding them first?
faqs.answer: Cross multiplication compares the rational values directly. Rounding both to decimals can hide a small difference.

faqs.question: Why is 0.333 not simplified to 1/3?
faqs.answer: The input is a finite decimal equal to 333/1000. One-third has an infinite repeating expansion, so enter 1/3 to preserve that exact value.

faqs.question: Why can the fraction be exact while the decimal is approximate?
faqs.answer: Integer numerator-denominator arithmetic can preserve a rational result exactly. A finite decimal display cannot show every digit of a repeating expansion.

faqs.question: Can I divide by a zero fraction?
faqs.answer: No. A fraction such as 0/5 equals zero, and dividing by it is undefined just as dividing by 0 is undefined.

sections.title: Working with equivalent fractions
paragraphs: A fraction represents a numerator relative to a nonzero denominator. Simplifying changes the written form without changing that value. Use comparison mode when you need to order fractions, and arithmetic mode when combining them. For addition and subtraction, the denominators describe the unit being counted, so adding numerators and denominators independently does not produce the correct sum.

sections.title: Enter fractions, mixed numbers or finite decimals directly
paragraphs: Choose arithmetic, simplification or comparison. Write a fraction as 3/8, a mixed number as 2 1/4, or a finite decimal as 0.375. A denominator cannot be zero. For a negative mixed number, −1 1/2 means the whole quantity −1.5.

The simplified fraction preserves an exact rational value for the text entered. Its decimal display can be approximate when the decimal expansion repeats; use the fraction when the exact value matters.

sections.title: Work through addition and division with the same two fractions
paragraphs: For 2/5 + 3/10, change 2/5 to 4/10 and add the numerators to get 7/10. For 2/5 ÷ 3/10, multiply by the reciprocal: 2/5 × 10/3 = 4/3. The mixed-number form of that quotient is 1 1/3.

table.caption: Four operations on 2/5 and 3/10

sections.title: Reduce and compare without losing information to rounding
paragraphs: Simplifying 42/56 divides numerator and denominator by their greatest common factor, 14, giving 3/4. This changes the notation without changing the value. To compare 7/12 and 5/8, compare 7 × 8 = 56 with 5 × 12 = 60, so 7/12 is smaller.

For negative fractions, signs must be preserved during comparison; a larger absolute numerator does not necessarily mean a larger signed value. The calculator normalizes denominator signs before carrying out the exact comparison.

sections.title: Recognize the difference between a decimal input and a repeating fraction
paragraphs: Entering 0.333 represents exactly 333/1000, not exactly 1/3. A typed finite decimal cannot contain an implied infinite repeat. Enter 1/3 when that is the intended value.
A mixed number also differs from multiplication: 2 1/4 means 2 + 1/4. Do not enter expressions such as 2*(1/4) in a fraction input; use a supported number representation or the expression calculator.

links.label: OpenStax: fraction simplification, multiplication and division

fraction-calculator.seoTitle: Fraction Calculator: Add, Subtract, Simplify & Compare

ratio-calculator.description: Simplify ratios with whole numbers, decimals, or fractions and see exact steps. Find a missing proportion term or scale both quantities up or down.

faqs.question: Can I enter decimals or fractions directly?
faqs.answer: Yes. In Simplify ratio, enter each quantity as a whole number, decimal, or integer fraction such as 1/2. Both 1.5:2.25 and 1/2:3/4 simplify to 2:3. The breakdown shows how common denominators and the greatest common factor produce the answer.

faqs.question: Does scaling a ratio change the relationship between its parts?
faqs.answer: No. Multiplying or dividing both parts by the same nonzero factor preserves their proportion.

faqs.question: Why can some proportions not be solved uniquely?
faqs.answer: A zero denominator is invalid, and some combinations reduce to an identity with infinitely many possible values rather than one answer.

faqs.question: Can a ratio contain zero or negative quantities?
faqs.answer: Simplify ratio preserves signs and allows one zero term: 0:5 becomes 0:1, and −12:18 becomes −2:3. Both terms cannot be zero. Proportion solving separately requires nonzero denominators and enough information for one unique answer.

sections.title: Keeping the order of a ratio consistent
paragraphs: A 2:3 mixture contains 5 parts in total. To make 20 units of mixture, each part is 20 ÷ 5 = 4 units, so the two ingredients need 8 and 12 units. The first ingredient is 2/5 of the total, not 2/3: 2/3 compares the ingredients with each other. Keep their order consistent when scaling or solving a proportion, and convert measurements to compatible units before comparing them.

ratio-calculator.seoTitle: Ratio Calculator: Simplify Ratios & Solve Proportions

quadratic-formula-calculator.description: Solve quadratic equations, inspect the discriminant and find real or complex roots, with linear handling when the quadratic term is zero.

faqs.question: What does the discriminant tell me?
faqs.answer: A positive discriminant gives two real roots, zero gives a repeated real root, and a negative value gives complex roots.

faqs.question: What happens if the coefficient of x squared is zero?
faqs.answer: The equation is no longer quadratic. The calculator treats the remaining expression as a linear or degenerate equation.

faqs.question: What should I enter when the equation has no x term?
faqs.answer: Enter b=0. Keep the coefficients of x² and the constant term, including their signs.

faqs.question: What does a negative discriminant mean?
faqs.answer: There are no real roots, but there is a pair of complex-conjugate roots. This calculator displays that pair using i.

faqs.question: Does the order of Root 1 and Root 2 matter?
faqs.answer: No. Both solve the equation; their order is an output convention, not an ascending numerical sort.

sections.title: Reading the roots of a quadratic equation
paragraphs: Write the equation in the standard quadratic form before entering its coefficients, including any negative signs and a zero coefficient for a missing linear term. The roots are the input values where the expression equals zero. The discriminant helps explain whether the roots are distinct, repeated, or non-real under the supported output. A zero leading coefficient describes a different type of equation.

sections.title: Put the equation into ax² + bx + c = 0 first
paragraphs: Enter the coefficients with their signs after moving every term to the same side. For 2x² + 3x = 2, enter a=2, b=3 and c=−2. A missing linear or constant term is entered as zero.
The quadratic formula is x = [−b ± √(b² − 4ac)] ÷ (2a). Its discriminant, b² − 4ac, determines whether there are two distinct real roots, one repeated real root or a complex-conjugate pair.

sections.title: Verify both roots by substitution
paragraphs: For 2x² + 3x − 2 = 0, the discriminant is 9 + 16 = 25. The formula gives (−3 ± 5)/4, so the roots are 0.5 and −2. Substituting either value back makes the polynomial zero.

table.caption: Checking the roots of 2x² + 3x − 2

sections.title: Use the discriminant to interpret the number of solutions
paragraphs: A positive discriminant gives two distinct real roots. A zero discriminant gives the same real root twice, as in x² − 6x + 9 = 0 with x=3. A negative discriminant gives no real roots, but this calculator shows complex roots; x² + 4 = 0 gives ±2i.
Root 1 and Root 2 are output labels, not a promise that the first root is numerically smaller. Compare their values or substitute them instead of relying on display order.

sections.title: Handle zero leading coefficients and rounded input
paragraphs: When a=0, the equation is linear rather than quadratic. With b nonzero, its solution is −c/b. If a and b are both zero, c=0 makes every real number a solution, while nonzero c gives no solution.

Very small changes in coefficients can alter roots near a repeated-root boundary. Treat a result based on rounded measurements as an approximation, and verify the original equation rather than assuming every printed digit is meaningful.

links.label: OpenStax: quadratic equations and the quadratic formula

quadratic-formula-calculator.seoTitle: Quadratic Formula Calculator: Real & Complex Roots

exponent-calculator.description: Calculate a number raised to a power, including negative and fractional exponents. See the result and the limits for real-number calculations.

faqs.question: What does a negative exponent mean?
faqs.answer: For a nonzero base, a negative exponent takes the reciprocal of the corresponding positive power; for example, 2^−3 is 1/8.

faqs.question: Will a fractional power of a negative base return a complex value?
faqs.answer: No. This mode is restricted to supported real-number results and does not calculate complex powers.

faqs.question: Why is a negative base sometimes positive after exponentiation?
faqs.answer: An even whole-number power pairs negative factors, producing a positive result. An odd whole-number power leaves a negative result.

faqs.question: Can I use a decimal exponent to calculate a root?
faqs.answer: For positive bases, a fractional exponent represents a root-and-power operation. For a negative base and an odd root, use the Root Calculator to state the integer index explicitly.

faqs.question: Can I add exponents when adding powers?
faqs.answer: No. Exponents add when multiplying powers with the same base, not when adding their values. For example, 2³ + 2⁴ = 24.

sections.title: Distinguishing a base from its exponent
paragraphs: The base is the quantity being raised to a power, while the exponent controls the operation. Parentheses matter when the base is negative: a negative base raised to a power is different from negating an already computed power. Check the supported real-number domain for fractional exponents. Very large powers can also exceed the precision or range of the selected numerical method.

sections.title: Interpret a power before entering its base and exponent
paragraphs: A positive whole-number exponent counts repeated factors: 3⁴ = 3 × 3 × 3 × 3. Enter the signed base and exponent in their separate fields. This calculator evaluates one power; use the Scientific Calculator for a longer expression containing several operations.
For a nonzero base, a zero exponent gives 1 and a negative exponent takes a reciprocal. The exponent changes the operation, so 3⁴ is not 3 × 4.

sections.title: Compare whole, negative and fractional exponents
paragraphs: With base 2 and exponent −3, the result is 1/2³ = 1/8 = 0.125. With base 9 and exponent 0.5, the result is the principal square root 3. A negative base raised to an even whole-number exponent is positive; an odd whole-number exponent preserves a negative sign.

table.caption: Powers with distinct meanings

sections.title: Use exponent rules only when their conditions hold
paragraphs: Multiplying powers with the same base adds their exponents: 2³ × 2⁴ = 2⁷ = 128. Raising a power to another power multiplies whole-number exponents: (2³)² = 2⁶ = 64. Adding two powers does not follow either rule: 2³ + 2⁴ = 24.

With real fractional exponents, signs and domains need care. Entering a rounded decimal approximation to 1/3 for a negative base is not a reliable way to request a real cube root; use the dedicated root index instead.

sections.title: Recognize undefined or out-of-range power results
paragraphs: Zero raised to a negative exponent would require division by zero. Negative bases with unsupported fractional exponents do not produce a finite real result here. Extremely large powers can also exceed ordinary numeric range.
The evaluator returns 1 for 0⁰ as a computational convention. That does not settle a mathematical limit involving an indeterminate form; define the context before interpreting that input.

exponent-calculator.seoTitle: Exponent Calculator: Positive, Negative & Fractional Powers

root-calculator.description: Find square roots, cube roots and other integer-index roots, including supported real odd roots of negative numbers.

faqs.question: Can a negative number have a real root?
faqs.answer: It has real odd roots, such as the cube root of −8 being −2. Even roots of negative values are not real.

faqs.question: Does the calculator list every complex root?
faqs.answer: No. This mode returns the supported real root rather than the full set of complex roots.

faqs.question: Why does the square root return only the positive answer?
faqs.answer: The square-root symbol denotes the nonnegative principal root. Solving x² = a can produce both signs, which is a different task.

faqs.question: What does index 1 do?
faqs.answer: It returns the radicand unchanged because x¹ = x.

faqs.question: Why does squaring the displayed result not exactly recover the input?
faqs.answer: The root may be irrational and its displayed decimal rounded. Use the underlying precision rather than a shortened display when checking subsequent calculations.

sections.title: Understanding the root index and input value
paragraphs: The root index specifies which power would reproduce the entered value. A square root and a cube root therefore answer different questions about the same number. Review the real-number restrictions when the input is negative or the index is not a whole number. The calculator's root result should not be confused with listing every possible solution of a polynomial equation.

sections.title: Enter the radicand and an integer root index
paragraphs: The nth root asks which number raised to the integer n gives the input value. The input value is the radicand, and the index must be a whole number from 1 to 1,000 in this tool. Index 2 requests a square root; index 3 requests a cube root.
For a nonnegative radicand, this tool returns the nonnegative principal root. For a negative radicand, an odd index can produce a negative real root, while an even index cannot produce a real result.

sections.title: Verify a root by raising it back to its index
paragraphs: The fourth root of 81 is 3 because 3⁴ = 81. The cube root of −125 is −5 because (−5)³ = −125. The square root of 0.0625 is 0.25 because 0.25² = 0.0625.

table.caption: Checking a root against its defining power

sections.title: Distinguish evaluating a root from solving an equation
paragraphs: √25 denotes the principal square root 5. The equation x² = 25 has two real solutions, +5 and −5. This calculator evaluates the root function, so it does not list every solution to an equation involving an even power.

A root can also undo a geometric power: the cube root of 64 cubic units is an edge length of 4 units for a cube. Taking the square root of area only gives a side directly when the geometry is a square.

links.label: Calculate a cube volume or edge-related scenario
Solve a quadratic equation with two possible roots

sections.title: Interpret irrational roots and rounded checks
paragraphs: Many roots, such as √2, have nonterminating decimal expansions. A displayed approximation squared back may differ slightly from the original number because the display was rounded. Keep adequate precision during intermediate work.
A negative number with an even index belongs to complex-number mathematics, which this real-root tool does not calculate. Rejecting that input does not mean the radicand has no complex roots.

root-calculator.seoTitle: Root Calculator: Square, Cube & nth Roots

log-calculator.description: Calculate logarithms in a valid positive base, or solve for a missing argument or base from a known logarithm.

faqs.question: Why can the logarithm base not equal one?
faqs.answer: Every power of one is one, so base one cannot provide the one-to-one relationship required for a logarithm.

faqs.question: How do I solve for the argument from a logarithm?
faqs.answer: If log base b of x equals y, then x = b^y. The base must be positive and different from one.

faqs.question: Can a logarithm be negative?
faqs.answer: Yes. For a base above 1, a positive argument below 1 has a negative logarithm; log₁₀(0.001) = −3.

faqs.question: What is the logarithm of 1?
faqs.answer: It is 0 for every valid base, because b⁰ = 1.

faqs.question: Is log(a + b) equal to log(a) + log(b)?
faqs.answer: No. The sum of two logarithms of positive arguments equals the logarithm of their product, using the same valid base. There is no corresponding rule that splits the logarithm of a sum.

sections.title: Choosing the logarithm base
paragraphs: A logarithm asks which exponent gives the entered argument for a chosen base. Changing the base changes the result, even though the argument stays the same. Use the missing-base or missing-argument mode only when those are the unknown quantities in your problem. Check the real logarithm domain before calculating; not every combination of signs and base values is valid.

sections.title: Read a logarithm as a missing exponent
paragraphs: log_b(x) = y means bʸ = x. Enter a positive argument x and a positive base b other than 1. A base of 10 gives a common logarithm; a base of e gives a natural logarithm. The change-of-base formula is log_b(x) = ln(x) ÷ ln(b).
A logarithm may be negative even though its argument must be positive. For a base greater than 1, arguments between 0 and 1 produce negative logarithms.

sections.title: Work backward from powers to logarithms
paragraphs: Because 2⁶ = 64, log₂(64) = 6. Because 10⁻³ = 0.001, log₁₀(0.001) = −3. Any valid base raised to zero equals 1, so log_b(1) = 0.

table.caption: Equivalent exponential and logarithmic statements

sections.title: Solve for an argument or a base with the inverse mode
paragraphs: If log₃(x) = 4, the missing argument is x = 3⁴ = 81. If log_b(81) = 4, the missing base is b = 81^(1/4) = 3. Choose Solve base or argument, then select which quantity is unknown.
Not every inverse input determines a unique answer. For example, log_b(1) = 0 holds for every valid base, so argument 1 and logarithm value 0 cannot identify one base.

sections.title: Avoid treating logarithms as ordinary multiplication
paragraphs: For positive arguments with a valid common base, log(xy) = log(x) + log(y), but log(x + y) does not equal that sum. A base must remain the same across an identity.

Zero and negative real arguments are invalid in this real-logarithm tool. Close-to-one bases can make results very sensitive to input rounding because ln(b) is near zero; retain enough digits in the supplied base.

log-calculator.seoTitle: Log Calculator: Custom Bases & Natural Logarithms

half-life-calculator.description: Model exponential decay, solve for remaining or initial quantity and elapsed time, or convert half-life and decay constants.

faqs.question: Is half-life the same as mean lifetime?
faqs.answer: No. Half-life is ln(2) divided by the decay constant; mean lifetime is one divided by that constant.

faqs.question: Which units should I use for time?
faqs.answer: Use the same unit for elapsed time and half-life. The decay constant then has the reciprocal of that time unit.

faqs.question: Does a substance disappear after two half-lives?
faqs.answer: No. One quarter remains after two half-lives, one eighth after three, and so on under the constant-rate model.

faqs.question: Can this determine when a medication is safe to take again?
faqs.answer: No. An isolated exponential calculation does not establish dosing, clinical effect, interactions or safety for a person.

faqs.question: Does the starting amount change the half-life?
faqs.answer: In the constant exponential-decay model used here, half-life is independent of starting amount. Doubling the initial quantity doubles the remaining quantity at each time without changing its remaining percentage.

sections.title: Matching the decay model to the question
paragraphs: The half-life calculator uses an exponential-decay model with a constant rate. Choose remaining quantity, initial quantity, elapsed time, or half-life according to what is unknown. Keep the time unit consistent across the inputs. The mathematical model does not establish the actual half-life of a substance or account for additional production, changing conditions, or multiple interacting decay processes.

sections.title: State a constant-rate exponential decay model
paragraphs: The model is N(t) = N₀ × 2^(−t/T), where N₀ is the initial quantity and T is its half-life. Each elapsed half-life removes half of what remains, not half of the original quantity. Use the same time unit for elapsed time and half-life.

Choose Remaining quantity for a forward calculation, Find half-life for a known decrease over time, or the inverse mode for the initial quantity or elapsed time. These are algebraic versions of one model, not different physical mechanisms.

sections.title: Track repeated halves with a numerical example
paragraphs: Start with 160 units and a half-life of 6 hours. At 6 hours, 80 units remain; at 12 hours, 40 remain; at 18 hours, 20 remain. The final amount is 12.5% of the starting amount, so 140 units have decayed under the model.

table.caption: Decay of 160 units with a six-hour half-life

sections.title: Connect half-life, decay constant and mean lifetime
paragraphs: The equivalent exponential form is N(t) = N₀e^(−λt). Half-life is ln(2)/λ, while mean lifetime is 1/λ. They are related but not equal: with half-life 6 hours, λ is approximately 0.115525 per hour and mean lifetime approximately 8.65617 hours.
The Convert decay constants mode keeps this distinction explicit. If the time unit changes from hours to minutes, the numerical decay constant must change to reciprocal minutes as well.

sections.title: Know when a fitted half-life does not describe the process
paragraphs: The formula assumes a constant fractional decay rate and no additional input. A mixture of components with different decay rates, replenishment or a changing environment may not follow one half-life. A zero remaining amount after finite time also cannot identify a finite half-life in this ideal exponential model.

Do not turn the remaining-quantity calculation into a personalized medication schedule or a claim about environmental safety. Such decisions require a validated model and domain-specific information beyond an entered half-life.

half-life-calculator.seoTitle: Half-Life Calculator: Decay, Time & Remaining Quantity

lcm-calculator.description: Find the least common multiple of whole numbers and use it to identify a shared repeating interval or denominator.

faqs.question: How does the least common multiple differ from the greatest common factor?
faqs.answer: The LCM is a shared multiple of the numbers. The GCF is a number that divides all of them.

faqs.question: What is the LCM of 6 and 8?
faqs.answer: It is 24: the smallest positive integer divisible by both 6 and 8.

faqs.question: Is multiplying the inputs always the least common multiple?
faqs.answer: No. Their product is a common multiple, but shared factors can make the least one smaller. For 12 and 18, the product is 216 while the LCM is 36.

faqs.question: How does LCM help add fractions?
faqs.answer: Use it as the least common denominator, then rewrite each fraction with that denominator before adding numerators.

faqs.question: Can LCM find when repeating events meet?
faqs.answer: Yes when the intervals are integer quantities in one unit and the events start together. Different starting offsets require additional reasoning.

faqs.question: Why does a list containing zero return zero?
faqs.answer: That is the tool’s computational convention for LCM. It does not identify a positive common multiple or a practical repeat interval.

sections.title: When to use the least common multiple
paragraphs: The least common multiple is useful when you need the smallest positive quantity that is a multiple of every entered whole number. It differs from a greatest common factor, which looks for a shared divisor. For fraction problems, an LCM can help identify a common denominator. Check that inputs represent whole-number quantities before applying the result to a repeating schedule or grouping problem.

sections.title: Find the first shared positive multiple for nonzero integers
paragraphs: The least common multiple is the smallest positive integer divisible by every nonzero input. Enter whole numbers separated by commas, spaces or line breaks. For two positive integers a and b, LCM(a,b)=a×b/GCF(a,b).

Multiplying the inputs always gives a common multiple, but usually not the least one when they share factors. For several inputs, apply the operation across the whole list rather than comparing only the first pair.

sections.title: Use an LCM to find the next shared interval
paragraphs: If two events repeat every 12 and 18 minutes and begin together, their next shared occurrence is after 36 minutes. Their GCF is 6, so 12×18÷6=36. This assumes the same starting time; different offsets require another scheduling calculation.

table.caption: Multiples leading to the first common interval

sections.title: Build a least common denominator for fractions
paragraphs: For denominators 8 and 12, the LCM is 24. Thus 5/8 becomes 15/24 and 7/12 becomes 14/24, making their sum 29/24. A denominator of 96 would also work but would need more simplification.
Using prime exponents, 8=2³ and 12=2²×3. Keep the greatest required exponent of each prime: 2³×3=24. The GCF instead keeps only shared primes at their smaller exponents.

sections.title: Interpret zeros and large outputs
paragraphs: The calculator returns 0 if any input is zero, following the common computational LCM convention. Do not interpret this as a positive repeat interval, since zero has no positive multiples. Signs are ignored when forming the nonnegative result.

LCMs can grow quickly even from moderate inputs. This mode rejects an output beyond its exact safe-integer range instead of presenting an inexact integer as exact. For larger supported integer tasks, use Big Number Calculator’s LCM operation.

gcf-calculator.description: Find the greatest common factor of a set of whole numbers using the Euclidean greatest-common-divisor relationship.

faqs.question: How can GCF help simplify a fraction?
faqs.answer: Divide the numerator and denominator by their greatest common factor. For 18/24, dividing both by 6 gives 3/4.

faqs.question: Is greatest common divisor different from greatest common factor?
faqs.answer: No. GCD and GCF are two names for the same whole-number relationship.

faqs.question: Must coprime numbers both be prime?
faqs.answer: No. They only need to share no positive factor above 1. For example, 8 and 15 are composite but coprime.

faqs.question: What does a zero input do?
faqs.answer: For a nonzero a, GCF(a,0)=|a|. An all-zero input returns 0 by this tool’s convention.

faqs.question: Must the GCF be one of the input numbers?
faqs.answer: No. The GCF of 18 and 30 is 6, even though 6 is not an input. It must divide every input, not equal one of them.

sections.title: Using a greatest common factor
paragraphs: The greatest common factor identifies the largest shared positive divisor of the entered whole numbers. It is useful for simplifying ratios and fractions or finding the largest equal grouping size. A common multiple answers a different question and can be much larger than the inputs. Review how the tool handles zeros and signs before interpreting an edge case.

sections.title: Use GCF, GCD and HCF as names for the same operation
paragraphs: The greatest common factor, greatest common divisor and highest common factor are the largest positive integer dividing every input without a remainder. Enter a list of whole numbers, keeping each number separate.
GCF is useful when reducing fractions or splitting integer quantities into the largest shared grouping. It differs from LCM, which finds a common multiple rather than a divisor.

sections.title: Reduce a fraction by its greatest common factor
paragraphs: For 84 and 126, the GCF is 42. Dividing numerator and denominator of 84/126 by 42 gives 2/3. The value of the fraction stays the same because both parts are divided by the same nonzero quantity.

table.caption: Using GCF 42 to simplify 84/126

sections.title: Verify the result with Euclid’s remainder method
paragraphs: Divide 126 by 84 to obtain remainder 42. Then divide 84 by 42 to obtain remainder 0. The last nonzero remainder, 42, is the greatest common factor. This avoids listing every factor of large inputs.
For more than two numbers, combine the operation sequentially: GCF(84,126,210) = GCF(42,210) = 42. The final answer must divide every input, not merely the first two.

links.label: Inspect an integer quotient and remainder

sections.title: Handle coprime inputs, signs and zeros consistently
paragraphs: Numbers with GCF 1 are coprime; they need not both be prime. For example, 8 and 15 share no factor above 1. Changing an input’s sign does not change the nonnegative GCF returned here.
GCF(a,0)=|a| for nonzero a. This tool uses 0 for an all-zero GCF input as a computational convention; it should not be interpreted as the greatest positive divisor of zero.

common-factor-calculator.description: List the positive factors shared by all entered whole numbers and identify their greatest common factor.

faqs.question: How are common factors related to the GCF?
faqs.answer: Every common positive factor divides the greatest common factor. Listing the divisors of the GCF identifies the shared factors.

faqs.question: What are the common factors of 12 and 18?
faqs.answer: They are 1, 2, 3 and 6. The greatest common factor is 6.

faqs.question: Is 1 always a common factor?
faqs.answer: Yes for integer inputs when a finite common-factor list exists. A result containing only 1 means the numbers have no larger shared positive divisor.

faqs.question: Can I include zero in the list?
faqs.answer: A zero alongside nonzero integers does not change their positive common divisors. An all-zero list has infinitely many divisors and is rejected.

faqs.question: Why did adding another number shorten the list?
faqs.answer: A factor must divide every input. The new number can exclude candidates that divided the previous numbers.

sections.title: Reading the complete list of common factors
paragraphs: Common factors are whole-number divisors shared by the entered values. The largest item has a special role as the greatest common factor, but smaller factors may be useful when choosing a grouping size. Check the original values when verifying the list: each reported factor should divide every relevant input without a remainder. Common factors should not be confused with common multiples.

sections.title: Find every positive divisor shared by the whole list
paragraphs: Enter two or more integers separated by commas, spaces or line breaks. A common factor must divide every entered integer without a remainder. The result is a list, not only its largest member.

Conceptually, first find the greatest common factor and then list all positive factors of that value. Adding another input can remove shared factors but cannot introduce a positive common factor that failed to divide an earlier input.

sections.title: Check the shared factors of 18, 30 and 42
paragraphs: The factors common to all three numbers are 1, 2, 3 and 6. Although 9 divides 18, it does not divide 30 or 42. Although 5 divides 30, it does not divide the other two. Testing every input is what distinguishes a common-factor list from one number’s factors.

table.caption: Candidates tested against 18, 30 and 42

sections.title: Use common factors to compare valid grouping sizes
paragraphs: Imagine 18 red, 30 blue and 42 green counters, with every group required to contain the same composition and no leftovers. One, two, three or six identical groups are possible; six is the largest count. With six groups, each contains 3 red, 5 blue and 7 green counters.

That interpretation uses a count of groups. If the problem instead asks for the largest equal item size or a repeat interval, identify the units before deciding whether GCF or LCM is the right operation.

links.label: Return only the greatest common factor

sections.title: Understand zero and negative-input conventions
paragraphs: Signs do not change the positive divisor list: −18 and 18 have the same positive divisors. Every nonzero integer divides 0, so adding a zero to a list with nonzero integers does not remove their common factors.

If every input is zero, there are infinitely many positive common divisors and no finite list to show. The calculator rejects that case. Entries must still be whole numbers within the stated numeric limits.

common-factor-calculator.seoTitle: Common Factor Calculator: Shared Factors of Whole Numbers

factor-calculator.description: List all positive factors of a whole number and count its divisors. Enter an integer up to one trillion and check which numbers divide it without a remainder.

faqs.question: Does this calculator show all factors or only prime factors?
faqs.answer: It lists all positive factors and the factor count. For 12, the list is 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12. Use the Prime Factorization Calculator to express a number as a product of primes.

faqs.question: Why is the input limited to one trillion?
faqs.answer: This implementation uses bounded trial division. The limit keeps the calculation responsive rather than implying that larger integers lack factors.

faqs.question: Are negative factors included?
faqs.answer: No. This page lists positive divisors. Each positive divisor also has a negative counterpart when considering signed factor pairs.

faqs.question: Why is 1 not prime?
faqs.answer: A prime must have exactly two distinct positive factors. The number 1 has only one.

faqs.question: Why does a perfect square have an odd factor count?
faqs.answer: Its square root pairs with itself and is listed once; all other factors form distinct pairs.

sections.title: Reading a positive-factor list
paragraphs: A positive factor divides the entered integer without a remainder. For 12, both 2 and 6 are factors because 2 × 6 = 12; 1 and the number itself also belong in the list. The calculator reports all positive divisors and their count, rather than a prime decomposition. A prime number has exactly two positive factors, while 1 has one positive factor. Use the separate prime-factorization tool when you need the product of primes.

sections.title: List the positive divisors of one integer
paragraphs: A factor divides an integer with no remainder. Enter a positive whole number; this tool lists its positive factors in ascending order and gives their count. The range is 1 through 1,000,000,000,000.

Factors are finite for a positive integer. Multiples continue indefinitely, so a factor list is not a list such as n, 2n, 3n. Negative factor pairs exist mathematically but are not included in this positive-factor output.

sections.title: Use factor pairs to check that no divisor is missing
paragraphs: For 84, the positive factor pairs are 1×84, 2×42, 3×28, 4×21, 6×14 and 7×12. Listing both members of each pair gives twelve factors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 12, 14, 21, 28, 42 and 84.

table.caption: Factor pairs for 84

sections.title: Recognize prime numbers and perfect squares from their factors
paragraphs: A prime has exactly two positive factors, 1 and itself. The number 1 has only one positive factor and is not prime. A perfect square has an unpaired middle factor equal to its square root: the factor 6 appears once in the list for 36 even though 6×6 is a pair.
This makes the count of positive factors odd for a perfect square and even for a nonsquare positive integer. Do not double-count the square-root factor when checking a manual list.

sections.title: Choose factorization or common-factor tools for a different task
paragraphs: A factor list contains composite divisors as well as prime divisors. Prime factorization instead writes a product of primes, such as 84 = 2² × 3 × 7. For divisors shared by several integers, calculate common factors or their greatest common factor.

These tools all describe integer divisibility. Decimal measurements should not be rounded to integers just to force them into a factorization problem unless that rounding is part of the intended task.

links.label: Write a product of prime factors
Find factors shared by several numbers

factor-calculator.seoTitle: Factor Calculator: All Positive Factors & Factor Count

prime-factorization-calculator.description: Express a positive integer as a product of prime factors, including repeated factors. Supports whole numbers up to one trillion.

faqs.question: How are repeated prime factors shown mathematically?
faqs.answer: Repeated factors can be written as powers. For example, 72 = 2^3 × 3^2.

faqs.question: Does the number 1 have a prime factorization?
faqs.answer: No. One is neither prime nor a product of primes; it has no prime factors.

faqs.question: Can this factor an algebraic polynomial?
faqs.answer: No. It factors a positive integer into prime integers. Polynomial factorization is a different operation.

faqs.question: How can I check a prime factorization?
faqs.answer: Multiply all returned factors, including repeated ones. Their product must equal the entered integer.

faqs.question: Can I factor a negative number or a decimal here?
faqs.answer: This tool accepts positive whole numbers within its displayed limit. For a negative integer, a factor of −1 can be handled separately, but the input itself must be positive.

sections.title: Reading repeated prime factors
paragraphs: The calculator displays prime factors as a multiplication product. For 72, the result is 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3. You can write the same product as 2³ × 3²: the exponent counts how many times a prime repeats. Multiplying the displayed factors reconstructs the original integer. One has no prime factors. To list every positive divisor rather than only the prime factors, use the Factor Calculator.

sections.title: Break an integer into prime factors until no composite factor remains
paragraphs: Enter a positive integer and read its factorization as multiplication. A prime number has only 1 and itself as positive divisors. Composite factors must be split further: 12 = 3×4 is a factorization, but its prime factorization is 2×2×3.
Finflo lists repeated prime factors separately, making multiplicities visible. You can combine repetitions into exponent notation when writing the result elsewhere.

sections.title: Work through the factorization of 840
paragraphs: Repeated division gives 840 ÷ 2 = 420, then 210, then 105. Continue with 105 ÷ 3 = 35, 35 ÷ 5 = 7 and 7 ÷ 7 = 1. The product is 2×2×2×3×5×7, or 2³×3×5×7.

table.caption: Successive prime divisions of 840

sections.title: Use the exponents to recover useful divisibility information
paragraphs: The factorization 840 = 2³×3¹×5¹×7¹ has (3+1)(1+1)(1+1)(1+1)=32 positive divisors. For a greatest common factor, take only shared primes with their smaller exponents. For a least common multiple, take every required prime with its larger exponent.
This explains why GCF and LCM are different constructions. A prime that occurs in only one input belongs in the LCM but not the GCF.

sections.title: Interpret 1, primes and the supported range
paragraphs: The number 1 has no prime factors; it is the empty-product boundary case, not a prime. Entering a prime returns that same prime as its factorization. This tool accepts integers through 10¹² and does not factor decimals, negative values or symbolic polynomials.

Multiplying the returned factors reconstructs the original integer and provides a useful independent check. A factor list requires an additional combination step, so use the Factor Calculator when you need every divisor.

prime-factorization-calculator.seoTitle: Prime Factorization Calculator: Prime Factors of a Number

long-division-calculator.description: Divide whole numbers and see the quotient, remainder and digit-by-digit long division. Check your answer with divisor × quotient + remainder.

faqs.question: How can I check a quotient and remainder?
faqs.answer: Multiply the divisor by the quotient and add the remainder. The result should equal the original dividend.

faqs.question: What does the steps mode show?
faqs.answer: It shows each partial dividend, quotient digit, multiplication and subtraction, followed by the resulting remainder.

faqs.question: What does the remainder mean?
faqs.answer: It is the part left after making the maximum number of complete groups. It must be nonnegative and smaller than the positive divisor.

faqs.question: Is 17 remainder 6 the same as 17.6?
faqs.answer: No. For division by 7, it means 17 + 6/7, approximately 17.8571. The divisor determines the fractional part.

faqs.question: Can I enter a decimal dividend or divisor?
faqs.answer: These modes accept nonnegative whole-number dividends and positive whole-number divisors. For decimal division, use the Basic or Big Number Calculator, or first transform the problem by scaling both operands consistently.

sections.title: Interpreting a quotient and remainder
paragraphs: Integer division separates the result into a whole-number quotient and a remainder, while decimal division expresses the same relationship as a decimal value where supported. Keep the dividend and divisor in the correct order. A useful check is to multiply the divisor by the quotient and add the remainder. The step-by-step mode is intended to make that division process easier to follow.

sections.title: Interpret integer quotient and remainder together
paragraphs: For a nonnegative dividend a and positive divisor b, the result satisfies a=bq+r with 0≤r<b. The quotient q counts complete groups and r is the amount left over. The standard mode also returns a decimal quotient.

Use Integer division steps to see each brought-down digit, partial dividend, quotient digit, subtraction and remainder. That mode preserves supported large integer inputs as integers rather than converting them into a decimal approximation.

sections.title: Follow 238 divided by 7 digit by digit
paragraphs: Seven does not fit into the first digit 2, so use 23. Three sevens make 21, leaving 2. Bring down 8 to get 28; four sevens make 28, leaving zero. The quotient is 34, checked by 7×34=238.

table.caption: Long-division steps for 238 ÷ 7

sections.title: Convert a remainder into a fraction or decimal when appropriate
paragraphs: For 125÷7, the integer quotient is 17 and the remainder is 6. This can be written 17 + 6/7, approximately 17.857142857. A remainder of 6 is not a decimal digit to append as 17.6.
The appropriate answer depends on the task: 125 objects in groups of 7 make 17 complete groups with 6 left, while a length of 125 units divided into 7 equal parts can use the fractional quotient.

links.label: Keep a quotient as an exact fraction

sections.title: Check zero cases and the supported sign convention
paragraphs: A zero dividend divided by a positive divisor gives quotient 0 and remainder 0. A divisor of zero is undefined. This long-division interface uses nonnegative dividends and positive divisors, so it does not silently choose among competing signed-remainder conventions.

Always verify the reconstruction dividend = divisor×quotient + remainder. If the remainder is as large as the divisor, another complete division step is still possible and the quotient is not finished.

long-division-calculator.seoTitle: Long Division Calculator: Steps, Quotient & Remainder

rounding-calculator.description: Round a number to decimal places, significant figures or a chosen increment. Choose how halfway values round and compare the result with your input.

faqs.question: How do I round to the nearest tenth or hundredth?
faqs.answer: In Round a number, select Decimal places and enter 1 for tenths or 2 for hundredths. For example, 12.346 becomes 12.3 or 12.35, respectively.

faqs.question: How do I round to the nearest 10 or 100?
faqs.answer: Select Increment & rounding rule, set the increment to 10 or 100, and choose the rounding direction. With nearest rounding, 154 becomes 150 at increment 10.

faqs.question: Are decimal places and significant figures the same?
faqs.answer: No. Decimal places count positions after the decimal point; significant figures count meaningful digits from the first nonzero digit.

faqs.question: Why might two rounding rules disagree at a halfway value?
faqs.answer: Tie rules choose different directions. The increment mode names the selected behavior explicitly so that halfway cases can be interpreted correctly.

faqs.question: Can I round to the nearest quarter or eighth?
faqs.answer: Yes. Use Increment & rounding rule with 0.25 or 1/8. The result is a multiple of that increment.

faqs.question: Can rounding twice change the answer?
faqs.answer: Yes. For example, 1.2449 rounds directly to 1.24 at two decimal places, but rounding through 1.245 first can give 1.25.

faqs.question: Does round up always mean away from zero?
faqs.answer: No. Toward positive infinity and away from zero differ for negative values. This tool names each direction explicitly.

sections.title: How to round to the nearest whole number, tenth or hundredth
paragraphs: Choose Round a number, enter your number and select Decimal places. Use 0 for the nearest whole number, 1 for tenths and 2 for hundredths. This mode rounds to the nearest value; an exact halfway value rounds away from zero.

For the nearest 10, 100 or another multiple, select Increment & rounding rule and enter that increment. An increment of 0.05 rounds to five-cent steps; it is different from keeping two decimal places.

table.caption: Rounding examples using the nearest value, with halfway cases rounded away from zero.

links.label: Choose an increment and rounding rule

sections.title: Significant figures and negative numbers
paragraphs: Significant figures start at the first nonzero digit. For example, 0.004567 rounded to 3 significant figures is 0.00457; rounding the same number to 3 decimal places gives 0.005. Select the matching method before entering the digit count.

For negative values, rounding toward positive infinity and rounding away from zero are different. At increment 1, -2.5 rounds to -2 using ties toward positive infinity, but to -3 using ties away from zero. Ties to even gives 2 for 2.5 and 4 for 3.5. The increment mode names each rule explicitly.
Keep full intermediate precision when possible. Rounding each step can produce a different final answer from rounding once at the end.

sections.title: Compare tie rules using the same positive and negative values
paragraphs: A tie occurs exactly halfway between two allowed results. At increment 1, both 2.5 and −2.5 are ties. The chosen direction matters; the phrase round up can ambiguously mean toward positive infinity or away from zero. Select the explicitly named rule instead.

table.caption: Halfway values under three rounding rules

sections.title: Round to a measurement increment rather than a decimal display
paragraphs: At an increment of 0.25, 2.37 rounds to 2.25 under nearest rounding because it is closer to 2.25 than 2.50. This differs from rounding to two decimal places, which leaves 2.37 unchanged. Fractional increments such as 1/8 are also accepted.

The selected increment defines allowed results k×increment for integer k. It does not define an offset grid: if your measuring system starts at a nonzero reference, account for that offset separately before rounding.

sections.title: Avoid rounding twice when the final precision is known
paragraphs: At half-away rounding, 1.2449 rounded directly to two decimal places is 1.24. Rounding it first to three places gives 1.245, which then rounds to 1.25 at two places. The extra intermediate step changes the answer.

Preserve full available values during arithmetic and round once at the reporting stage unless a governing rule explicitly requires intermediate rounding. Decimal arithmetic addresses representation at decimal ties; it does not infer a measurement’s uncertainty or a required reporting standard.

rounding-calculator.seoTitle: Rounding Calculator: Decimal Places & Significant Figures
