scientific-notation-calculator.description: Convert numbers to scientific notation or back to decimals. Add, subtract, multiply and divide using coefficients and powers of ten.

faqs.question: What does E mean in scientific notation?
faqs.answer: E means multiply by a power of ten. For example, 3.2e5 means 3.2 × 10^5, or 320000, and 3.2e-5 means 0.000032.

faqs.question: Can I convert scientific notation to an ordinary decimal?
faqs.answer: Yes. Enter a value such as 7.2e-4 or 7.2 × 10^-4 in the converter. The Decimal form result is 0.00072.

faqs.question: What makes scientific notation normalized?
faqs.answer: For a nonzero number, the coefficient's magnitude is at least 1 and below 10, with the scale represented by an integer power of ten.

faqs.question: Do square and square-root operations use both input values?
faqs.answer: No. They use only the first value. Power uses a whole-number exponent within the mode's stated bounds.

faqs.question: Can I add coefficients when the exponents differ?
faqs.answer: First express both numbers using the same power of ten. For example, 4.2×10⁵ + 3.5×10⁴ becomes (4.2+0.35)×10⁵.

faqs.question: Does a negative exponent make a number negative?
faqs.answer: No. It indicates a reciprocal power of ten. The sign of the coefficient determines whether the number itself is negative.

faqs.question: How does engineering notation differ from scientific notation?
faqs.answer: Its exponent is divisible by three and its coefficient can have one, two or three digits before the decimal point.

sections.title: Convert scientific notation to decimal form and back
paragraphs: Enter a number in ordinary decimal form, such as 579.5, or enter scientific notation as 5.795e2 or 5.795 × 10^2. The converter returns both scientific notation and decimal form. In E notation, e means “times ten raised to”; it is not the mathematical constant e.
For a nonzero value, normalized scientific notation has one nonzero digit before the decimal point. A positive exponent moves the decimal point to the right; a negative exponent moves it to the left.

table.caption: Equivalent forms of the same numbers; conversion alone does not round the input.

sections.title: Calculate with scientific notation
paragraphs: Use Scientific notation arithmetic to add, subtract, multiply or divide two numbers. Square and square root use only the first number. Power uses the second input as a whole-number exponent.

For multiplication, multiply the coefficients and add the exponents: (2 × 10^3) × (3 × 10^4) = 6 × 10^7. For division, divide the coefficients and subtract the exponents. For addition and subtraction, first align the powers of ten.

Significant digits control the arithmetic result: 999.9 at 3 significant digits becomes 1.00e3. Engineering notation uses an exponent divisible by three and keeps a nonzero coefficient’s magnitude from 1 to below 1000. Rounding can therefore change the engineering exponent. The Decimal result expands the rounded value without E notation.

links.label: Compare decimal places and significant figures

sections.title: Align exponents before adding numbers of different sizes
paragraphs: To add 4.2×10⁵ and 3.5×10⁴, rewrite the second as 0.35×10⁵. The sum is 4.55×10⁵, or 455000. Adding the coefficients while leaving unrelated exponents unchanged would mix different scales.
In arithmetic mode, enter 4.2e5 and 3.5e4, choose addition and request at least three significant digits to reproduce 4.55e5.

table.caption: Arithmetic with powers of ten

sections.title: Use engineering notation when groups of three powers are useful
paragraphs: Engineering notation restricts the exponent to a multiple of three. Thus 0.00047 is 4.7×10⁻⁴ in scientific notation but 470×10⁻⁶ in engineering notation. Both represent the same value.

The engineering coefficient can have up to three digits before the decimal point, while normalized scientific notation has one. This formatting convention can align with powers used by SI prefixes, but the calculator does not attach or convert a physical unit.

sections.title: Keep precision and the sign of the exponent separate
paragraphs: A negative exponent describes a scale below one; it does not make the number negative. For example, 3e−4 is positive 0.0003, while −3e4 is negative −30000. The coefficient sign and exponent sign perform different jobs.

Conversion preserves the entered numerical value; the arithmetic mode’s significant-digit setting rounds its result. Neither operation establishes how many digits were actually measured. Keep unit and measurement-uncertainty information alongside the number.

links.label: OpenStax: scientific notation and exponent rules

binary-calculator.description: Perform exact binary integer arithmetic and convert signed integers between base 2 and decimal without floating-point conversion.

faqs.question: Should I include a 0b prefix with a binary input?
faqs.answer: No. Enter the binary digits directly. The selected mode already establishes the base.

faqs.question: Does binary division return a repeating fractional expansion?
faqs.answer: No. The arithmetic mode returns an integer quotient and remainder rather than a fractional binary expansion.

faqs.question: What happens to leading zeros?
faqs.answer: They do not change the integer value. The result is not padded to a chosen bit width.

faqs.question: Does the calculator use two’s-complement signed integers?
faqs.answer: No. A leading minus sign denotes an ordinary signed integer. Fixed-width encodings and overflow rules are separate tasks.

faqs.question: How can I check a binary sum in decimal?
faqs.answer: The arithmetic result includes its decimal value. For example, 101101₂ + 111₂ is 110100₂, corresponding to 45 + 7 = 52.

sections.title: Distinguishing binary values from decimal values
paragraphs: Binary notation uses a different place-value base from ordinary decimal notation. The same written sequence of digits can therefore represent a different amount depending on the chosen base. Select conversion mode when changing notation and arithmetic mode when operating on binary inputs. Keep leading zeros only when a fixed bit width is relevant to your separate application.

sections.title: Read binary digits as powers of two
paragraphs: Binary uses only 0 and 1. From right to left, the place values are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and so on. Enter the digits without a 0b prefix in the arithmetic fields. A leading minus sign represents an ordinary signed integer.
Arithmetic operates on whole-number values rather than fixed-width machine registers. Leading zeros do not request an 8-bit, 16-bit or two’s-complement interpretation.

sections.title: Check binary addition through decimal values
paragraphs: The binary number 101101 equals 32+8+4+1=45. The number 111 equals 7. Adding them gives decimal 52, written 110100 in binary. Both the base-2 result and decimal result help check whether the intended base was used.

table.caption: Place values in binary 101101

sections.title: Use the conversion mode for a number in a different base
paragraphs: Select Convert decimal and binary, then choose whether the supplied number is decimal or binary. Decimal 45 converts to binary 101101. Entering 45 into a binary arithmetic field is invalid because digits 4 and 5 do not exist in base 2.
The conversion uses integer arithmetic. This tool does not parse binary fractions such as 0.101, apply a bit-width overflow rule or execute bitwise AND/OR operations.

links.label: Convert a decimal integer to binary

sections.title: Interpret quotient and remainder without assuming a fractional expansion
paragraphs: Binary integer division of 1101 by 11 corresponds to 13÷3: the quotient is 100 and remainder 1, meaning 4 remainder 1 in decimal. A fractional binary expansion is not generated by this operation.

For negative inputs, integer division truncates toward zero and the remainder follows the dividend’s sign. If a programming task requires a particular fixed-width encoding, supply and apply that rule separately.

hex-calculator.description: Calculate exact hexadecimal integer operations and convert signed values between base 16 and decimal, using digits 0–9 and A–F.

faqs.question: Are uppercase and lowercase hexadecimal letters different?
faqs.answer: No. A–F and a–f represent the same digits. Enter the digits without a base prefix.

faqs.question: Why does hexadecimal division show a remainder?
faqs.answer: The integer arithmetic mode separates the quotient and remainder instead of producing a fractional hexadecimal result.

faqs.question: What do A through F mean?
faqs.answer: They are hexadecimal digits representing decimal 10 through 15. For example, F is 15 and 10 is 16 in base 16.

faqs.question: Does 10 mean ten in hexadecimal arithmetic?
faqs.answer: No. It means 1×16+0, or decimal 16. Use the conversion mode when your original input is decimal.

faqs.question: Can I paste a 0x prefix?
faqs.answer: Enter the hexadecimal digits without the prefix. The selected field or mode already identifies the base.

faqs.question: Will a result wrap at FF or FFFF?
faqs.answer: No. These are integer operations without an implied 8-bit or 16-bit width. Apply any required machine-width convention separately.

sections.title: Working with hexadecimal place values
paragraphs: Hexadecimal notation uses digits and letter symbols to represent values in a base larger than decimal. Check the input mode before pasting a number, because a string containing only digits can still have different values in different bases. Conversion changes representation rather than quantity. Arithmetic results follow the supported number model, not every fixed-width overflow rule used by programming languages.

sections.title: Interpret hexadecimal place values and letter digits
paragraphs: Hexadecimal is base 16, with digits 0–9 and A–F representing values 10–15. Place values increase as 1, 16, 256 and 4096 from right to left. Enter values without a 0x prefix in the arithmetic fields; uppercase and lowercase letters are accepted.
A leading minus sign denotes an ordinary negative integer. The calculator does not infer a signed machine word from a leading hexadecimal F or preserve a chosen byte width.

sections.title: Verify a hexadecimal sum using decimal arithmetic
paragraphs: The hexadecimal value 2A equals 2×16+10=42. Adding hexadecimal 15, which is decimal 21, gives decimal 63 or hexadecimal 3F. The decimal output makes this interpretation visible.

table.caption: Converting and adding 2A and 15

sections.title: Separate hexadecimal arithmetic from decimal conversion
paragraphs: In Arithmetic, both inputs are hexadecimal: 10 therefore means decimal 16. In Convert decimal and hexadecimal, select the input base explicitly. Decimal 255 converts to FF, while hexadecimal 255 converts to decimal 597.

This distinction is useful when copying identifiers from code or a device display. Remove prefixes or separators according to the field’s format instead of assuming that every numeric-looking string is decimal.

sections.title: Know what the result does not encode
paragraphs: Integer division of FF by 10 gives quotient F and remainder F: decimal 255=16×15+15. No hexadecimal fractional expansion is produced. Signed division truncates toward zero rather than defining a fixed-width processor instruction.

Hex values may encode colors, bytes or addresses in other contexts, but this calculator performs integer arithmetic. It does not interpret byte order, wrap an overflowed word, convert a character encoding or validate an address range.

number-sequence-calculator.description: Generate arithmetic, geometric and Fibonacci sequences or find a selected term and series sum with explicit index conventions.

faqs.question: Does the first term always have index one?
faqs.answer: Arithmetic and geometric sequences start at index one. Fibonacci uses F0 = 0 and F1 = 1.

faqs.question: Do first-term and difference inputs change the Fibonacci sequence?
faqs.answer: No. Fibonacci uses its fixed starting values and recurrence. Those controls apply to the other sequence types.

faqs.question: Can the calculator find a unique next number from any list?
faqs.answer: No. A finite list can fit many rules. Select an arithmetic, geometric or Fibonacci model based on the stated problem.

faqs.question: What does Step mean in geometric mode?
faqs.answer: It is the multiplier, or common ratio. In arithmetic mode the same role is an added common difference.

faqs.question: Why is the first displayed Fibonacci value zero?
faqs.answer: This calculator uses F₀=0 and F₁=1. The generated list begins at F₀, while a requested nth Fibonacci term uses its explicit index.

faqs.question: Can I find the tenth term without listing all ten?
faqs.answer: Yes. Nth term and series sum returns the requested term and cumulative sum directly within its supported limits.

sections.title: Identifying the sequence model before extending it
paragraphs: A sequence calculator can extend only the pattern described by the selected model and inputs. Several different rules can fit a short list of terms, so an apparent pattern is not proof of a unique continuation. Distinguish the value of a particular term from the sum of several terms. Check the starting index and common difference or ratio when comparing results.

sections.title: Choose a rule rather than guessing from a short pattern
paragraphs: Arithmetic sequences add a constant difference; geometric sequences multiply by a constant ratio. The Fibonacci option follows its stated starting values and recurrence. Select the model and enter its parameters rather than expecting the tool to infer a unique rule from a few observations.
Many formulas can match the same finite prefix and then diverge. A sequence model should come from the problem’s definition or an explicit assumption, not merely a visual resemblance.

sections.title: Compare arithmetic and geometric progressions
paragraphs: Starting from 5 with difference 3 gives 5, 8, 11, 14, totaling 38 over four terms. Starting from 3 with ratio 2 gives 3, 6, 12, 24, totaling 45. The same Step field represents a difference or a ratio depending on the selected type.

table.caption: Four-term examples under two different rules

sections.title: Use the nth-term mode without generating a long list
paragraphs: For an arithmetic sequence, aₙ=a₁+(n−1)d and Sₙ=n(a₁+aₙ)/2. With first term 5, difference 3 and index 10, the term is 32 and the sum through that term is 185.

For a geometric sequence with ratio r other than 1, Sₙ=a₁(1−rⁿ)/(1−r). When r=1, every term is the first term and the sum is n×a₁. The calculator handles that special case rather than dividing by zero.

links.label: Find a distant term and its partial sum

sections.title: Keep Fibonacci indexing separate from list position
paragraphs: The Fibonacci convention here is F₀=0 and F₁=1, followed by Fₙ=Fₙ₋₁+Fₙ₋₂. In the generated list, the first displayed item is F₀. In nth-term mode, index 10 means F₁₀=55. Arithmetic and geometric indexing starts at 1 instead.

The Fibonacci mode does not use an entered first term or step as custom starting values. Very large requested sequences and powers are bounded; a selected rule can also grow beyond ordinary finite numeric range.

number-sequence-calculator.seoTitle: Number Sequence Calculator: Arithmetic, Geometric & Fibonacci

permutation-and-combination-calculator.description: Count ordered selections and unordered groups of distinct objects without replacement, using permutation and combination formulas.

faqs.question: When should I use a permutation instead of a combination?
faqs.answer: Use permutations when order matters. Use combinations when the same selected objects form one group regardless of their order.

faqs.question: Can the same object be selected more than once?
faqs.answer: Not in this model. It assumes distinct objects sampled without replacement, so the selection size cannot exceed the available count.

faqs.question: Why is choosing zero items counted as one possibility?
faqs.answer: There is exactly one empty selection. This convention gives C(n,0)=P(n,0)=1.

faqs.question: Why is the permutation count larger?
faqs.answer: It distinguishes the r! possible orders within each unordered selection. Thus P(n,r)=C(n,r)×r!.

faqs.question: Does the formula handle identical objects?
faqs.answer: The nPr and nCr formulas here treat the n available items as distinct. Arrangements with repeated indistinguishable objects need a different counting formula.

sections.title: Deciding whether order matters
paragraphs: Choosing 3 people from 5 for an unordered team gives 5! ÷ (3! × 2!) = 10 combinations. Assigning 3 different positions to people from the same group gives 5 × 4 × 3 = 60 permutations, because changing the order changes the assignment. Both calculations assume distinct people and no repeated selection. Decide whether positions matter before choosing the result; the number of outcomes alone does not establish that every outcome is equally likely.

sections.title: Decide whether rearranging a selection changes the outcome
paragraphs: Choose n distinct available items and r items to select without replacement. A combination counts an unordered selection; a permutation counts an ordered arrangement. Finflo returns both so the distinction remains visible.
If choosing Alice, Ben and Chen is the same team regardless of listing order, use combinations. If those people fill different first, second and third positions, use permutations.

sections.title: Count teams and ordered positions from five people
paragraphs: Selecting three people from five produces C(5,3)=5!/(3!2!)=10 teams. Assigning three ordered positions produces P(5,3)=5!/2!=60 arrangements. Each three-person team has 3!=6 orderings, explaining why 10×6=60.

table.caption: Five distinct people, three selected

sections.title: Check replacement and repeated-item assumptions
paragraphs: These formulas assume that the same item cannot be selected again. If each of three positions can independently use any of five symbols, repetition is allowed and the count is 5³=125 instead. Identical objects also require accounting for repeated arrangements.
Do not use the permutation count for strings with repeated letters without adjusting for multiplicities. The simple n and r interface cannot infer whether two listed choices represent distinct items.

sections.title: Interpret zero selections and numerical limits
paragraphs: There is one way to select nothing, so both C(n,0) and P(n,0) equal 1. Selecting all n items gives one unordered set but n! ordered arrangements. The selected count r cannot exceed n under the no-replacement model.

Inputs are bounded to keep factorial calculations finite. Large returned counts can exceed the range where every integer is represented exactly by ordinary numerical arithmetic; do not treat the final digit of a huge displayed count as a certified exact combinatorial integer.

permutation-and-combination-calculator.seoTitle: Permutation & Combination Calculator: nPr and nCr

random-number-generator.description: Generate random whole numbers or fixed-precision decimals within bounds, with unique-value and sorting options using exact sampling.

faqs.question: Are the minimum and maximum included?
faqs.answer: Integer bounds are inclusive. Decimal mode samples the permitted fixed-precision grid within the bounds, so an endpoint must lie on that grid.

faqs.question: Why can a request for unique values be rejected?
faqs.answer: The requested count cannot exceed the number of permitted values in the range or decimal grid. Output-size limits also apply.

faqs.question: Can I generate unique decimal values?
faqs.answer: Yes. Decimal mode samples a fixed grid at the selected number of decimal places, and uniqueness applies to those grid values.

faqs.question: Does sorting make the selection less random?
faqs.answer: Sorting rearranges the already selected values for display. It changes their order, not which values were drawn.

faqs.question: Can I set a seed to reproduce the same output?
faqs.answer: No. This interface uses browser cryptographic random values and does not expose a seed. Save the generated list if you need to reuse that exact selection.

sections.title: Checking range and repetition settings
paragraphs: Choose the minimum, maximum, and number of results according to the sample you need. Check whether endpoints are included and whether repeated values are allowed in the selected options. A random sample can contain clusters or repeats without indicating an error. Keep the generator's stated limitations in mind before using output for a security-sensitive or formally regulated drawing.

sections.title: Set the range, precision and duplicate rule before generating
paragraphs: Choose whole numbers or a fixed decimal grid, enter the inclusive minimum and maximum, and select how many results to generate. Allow duplicates samples with replacement; Unique values samples without replacement. Sorting changes presentation after selection, not the sampling rule.
The tool uses cryptographic random bytes and rejection sampling. Editing an input does not generate a new result; select Calculate when the requested settings are ready.

sections.title: Count the available decimal values before requesting unique results
paragraphs: From 1.00 through 1.03 at two decimal places, the available grid contains four values: 1.00, 1.01, 1.02 and 1.03. Requesting all four uniquely and sorting ascending must return that complete list, although their original generation order can vary.
The bounds themselves need not lie on the grid. At two decimal places, bounds 1.004 and 1.026 contain 1.01 and 1.02; they do not make 1.004 an eligible output.

table.caption: Fixed precision defines the actual sample space

sections.title: Understand independence and uniqueness as different requirements
paragraphs: With duplicates allowed, consecutive draws may repeat; a recent value is not automatically excluded. Without duplicates, each selected value is removed from the available set for that request, so the draws cannot be independent in the same way.

A short sample can contain streaks or uneven frequencies without proving that the method is biased. Conversely, merely looking well mixed is not evidence that a random source is suitable for a particular regulated process.

sections.title: Use random outputs in the right context
paragraphs: Bounds support large signed integers and fixed precision subject to the displayed output-size limits. An impossible unique request is rejected when fewer eligible grid points exist than the requested count. A range with no grid point at the chosen precision is also invalid.

This interface does not provide a reproducible seed, a public audit trail, a lottery certification or a password policy. Use the Password Generator when character rules are needed, and record the original unsorted draw if order matters to an experiment.

random-number-generator.seoTitle: Random Number Generator: Ranges, Decimals & No Repeats

z-score-calculator.description: Standardize a value as a z-score, explore normal tail probabilities or recover a boundary from a known normal probability.

faqs.question: Does calculating a z-score prove the data are normal?
faqs.answer: No. Standardization uses a mean and standard deviation. Interpreting the result as a normal percentile adds a normal-distribution assumption.

faqs.question: Should a probability of 95% be entered as 95 or 0.95?
faqs.answer: Enter 0.95 in probability fields. Those modes use probabilities from 0 to 1 rather than percentages.

faqs.question: What does a z-score of −2 mean?
faqs.answer: The value lies two reference standard deviations below the mean. Its normal percentile is a separate interpretation that assumes a normal distribution.

faqs.question: Can a z-score be larger than 3?
faqs.answer: Yes. Standard scores are not restricted to a fixed range. A large magnitude indicates a value far from the chosen mean in standard-deviation units; it does not by itself prove a data error.

faqs.question: Why does a central 95% probability return both signs?
faqs.answer: The central interval has a lower and upper boundary around zero, approximately −1.96 and +1.96. A central area determines the boundary magnitude rather than a unique signed cutoff.

faqs.question: Can I use the standard deviation of individual values for a test of a sample mean?
faqs.answer: A mean test usually standardizes by the standard error of the mean, not by individual-value spread. Choose the test and its reference distribution before interpreting a resulting probability.

sections.title: Relating a value to its mean and spread
paragraphs: A z-score expresses how far a value is from the entered mean in standard-deviation units. Its sign shows the direction of that difference. A probability interpretation additionally relies on the selected distribution assumption; standardizing a value does not by itself make the data normally distributed. Use the interval or inverse mode only when that is the probability question you intend to answer.

sections.title: Standardize a measurement using a compatible reference
paragraphs: Enter the observed value, reference mean and a positive standard deviation measured in the same units. The calculation z = (x − mean) ÷ standard deviation removes the unit and expresses the difference as a number of standard deviations.

A positive result is above the mean, a negative result is below it and zero is exactly at the mean. A standard deviation of zero cannot be used because it would require division by zero. Choose a reference population that actually answers the comparison you intend to make.

sections.title: Worked example: convert a score into a standard score
paragraphs: For a value of 85, mean 70 and standard deviation 10, z = (85 − 70) ÷ 10 = 1.5. That value is 1.5 standard deviations above the reference mean. Under a normal-distribution model, approximately 93.3193% of values fall below it and 6.6807% fall above it.

The standardization step needs only the mean and positive spread; the percentile step adds the normal model. A skewed dataset can have the same mean and standard deviation while assigning a different percentile to 85.

table.caption: One value, two distinct interpretations

sections.title: Select the probability region before using the inverse mode
paragraphs: Normal probabilities & inverse accepts a z-score or a probability below, above, centrally around zero, outside symmetric boundaries, or between the mean and |z|. Probability inputs are fractions: enter 0.975 for 97.5%. A left probability of 0.975 corresponds to z ≈ 1.959964.

A central probability of 0.95 describes the interval from approximately −1.959964 to +1.959964. It determines a magnitude and two signs, not a single one-sided cutoff. The mean-to-boundary probability is at most 0.5 because it covers only half of the symmetric distribution.

links.label: Use normal tail and inverse calculations

sections.title: Calculate between-boundary probabilities without adding tails
paragraphs: Use Probability between two z-scores for a bounded region. Between −1 and +1, the standard normal probability is approximately 0.682689, or 68.2689%. This is the upper cumulative probability minus the lower cumulative probability.

For an individual measurement, use the reference standard deviation in z. For a test about a sample mean, the denominator is a standard error under the applicable test assumptions, and a t distribution may be needed when population spread is estimated. Standardizing an individual observation and testing a population mean are different tasks.

links.label: Convert a test statistic into a p-value

z-score-calculator.seoTitle: Z-Score Calculator: Standard Scores & Normal Probabilities

sample-size-calculator.description: Estimate a survey proportion's sample size or margin of error, with confidence, expected proportion and finite-population assumptions.

faqs.question: Why is the required sample size rounded up?
faqs.answer: A fraction of a participant cannot be sampled. Rounding up preserves the minimum count required by the stated approximation.

faqs.question: Does the calculation account for nonresponse or clustered sampling?
faqs.answer: No. It assumes random independent sampling. Nonresponse and complex survey designs may require a larger planned sample.

faqs.question: Why use 50% when I do not know the expected proportion?
faqs.answer: The product p(1 − p) is largest at p = 0.5. Within this approximation, that gives the largest required sample for the selected confidence and margin.

faqs.question: What does a 5-percentage-point margin mean?
faqs.answer: An estimate of 40% with a 5-point margin spans 35% to 45%. It is not a relative 5% margin of 38% to 42%.

faqs.question: What should I enter as the population size?
faqs.answer: Enter the total number of eligible members in the finite population you want to describe, when the sampling assumptions support the correction. Enter 0 for the unlimited-population approximation.

faqs.question: Can I use this result to plan a randomized experiment?
faqs.answer: It is a precision calculation for one population proportion. An experiment usually needs a power analysis with an effect size, significance level, allocation and other design assumptions.

sections.title: Planning precision before collecting data
paragraphs: With 95% confidence, a 50% expected proportion, a 5-percentage-point margin of error, and unlimited population, the normal approximation requires 385 observations after rounding up. Halving the margin to 2.5 percentage points increases the requirement to 1,537, roughly four times as many. The 50% proportion gives the largest p(1−p) when no better estimate is available. This count assumes random independent sampling; it does not correct selection bias or include extra invitations needed for nonresponse.

sections.title: Set the margin in percentage points and choose a planning proportion
paragraphs: A margin of 5 percentage points around a 40% estimate means approximately 35% to 45%, not a 5% relative change around 40%. Enter 5 in the margin field. Confidence and expected proportion also use their displayed percent units.

When the proportion is unknown, 50% gives the largest p(1 − p) and the largest sample requirement for these inputs. A smaller planning proportion may reduce the count, but it should reflect credible prior information rather than a desire for a smaller sample.

sections.title: Compare an unlimited population with a finite sampling frame
paragraphs: At 95% confidence, a 5-point margin and a 50% planning proportion, the unlimited-population calculation gives n₀ ≈ 384.146 and rounds up to 385. If the complete eligible population contains 1,000 distinct members and sampling is without replacement, the finite-population correction gives about 277.741 and rounds up to 278.

Enter 0 when using the unlimited-population assumption. A finite population means the full group the estimate describes, not the number invited or the number who already responded. The correction assumes the sample is drawn from that defined population.

table.caption: Sample planning with the same confidence, margin and proportion

sections.title: Work backward from a completed sample to its margin
paragraphs: Choose Find margin of error to supply the sample size instead. With 400 observations, 95% confidence, an estimated proportion of 50% and unlimited population, the normal approximation gives a margin of approximately 4.8999 percentage points.

The calculation uses z × √[p(1 − p)/n]. For sampling without replacement from a finite population, it also multiplies by √[(N − n)/(N − 1)]. A census eliminates this modeled sampling variance, but not measurement error, coverage problems or missing answers.

links.label: Estimate margin from a sample count
OpenStax: proportion precision and sample planning

sections.title: Separate required responses from invitations and research design
paragraphs: The required count refers to usable observations. If 385 complete responses are required and the anticipated response rate is 70%, 385 ÷ 0.70 = 550 invitations is a basic planning estimate. The calculator does not add this adjustment, and a larger invitation count does not guarantee that respondents represent nonrespondents.

The normal proportion approximation is least dependable with very small samples or proportions close to 0 or 1. Cluster sampling, survey weights, unequal selection probabilities and correlated responses need design-specific methods. This page estimates precision for a proportion; it does not conduct power analysis for a treatment comparison or calculate a required sample for a mean.

sample-size-calculator.seoTitle: Sample Size Calculator: Surveys & Margin of Error

confidence-interval-calculator.description: Estimate a confidence interval for a mean using Student t or normal z assumptions, sample size and standard deviation.

faqs.question: When should I use Student t instead of normal z?
faqs.answer: Use Student t when the standard deviation is estimated from the sample; the z method assumes a known population standard deviation.

faqs.question: Is the interval a range containing most individual observations?
faqs.answer: No. It describes uncertainty in the estimated mean under the model, rather than a prediction range for individual values.

faqs.question: Should I enter standard deviation or standard error?
faqs.answer: Enter the standard deviation of individual observations. The calculator obtains standard error by dividing that input by the square root of the sample size.

faqs.question: Does 95% confidence mean a 95% probability for this fixed population mean?
faqs.answer: In the frequentist interpretation used here, the coverage rate belongs to the repeated-sampling procedure. The fixed mean is either inside or outside the interval computed from one sample.

faqs.question: Why does 99% confidence produce a wider interval than 95%?
faqs.answer: A higher confidence level requires a larger critical value. With the same mean, spread and sample size, that increases the margin on both sides.

faqs.question: Can I use this page for a survey percentage?
faqs.answer: This page calculates an interval for a mean using standard deviation. Proportions use a different sampling variance and may need a Wilson, exact or another suitable proportion interval.

sections.title: Interpreting a mean confidence interval
paragraphs: With a sample mean of 100, known population standard deviation of 15, and sample size of 100, the standard error is 15 ÷ √100 = 1.5. A 95% normal-z interval is approximately 100 ± 1.96 × 1.5, or 97.06 to 102.94. If the standard deviation is estimated from the sample, select Student t instead. The interval estimates the population mean; it is not a range containing 95% of individual observations. Its coverage relies on the sampling and distribution assumptions.

sections.title: Match the method to the standard deviation you actually know
paragraphs: Enter the sample mean, the standard deviation of individual observations and the sample size. Select Student t when the standard deviation is estimated from that sample; the calculator uses n − 1 degrees of freedom. Select Normal z when a population standard deviation is known independently. A large sample alone does not turn an estimated standard deviation into a known population value.

Do not enter an already calculated standard error in the standard-deviation field. The calculator divides the supplied standard deviation by √n, so entering a standard error would divide by √n a second time.

sections.title: Follow a complete 95% interval calculation
paragraphs: Suppose the mean is 100, the known population standard deviation is 12 and n = 36. The standard error is 12 ÷ 6 = 2. Choose Normal z and 95% confidence. The critical value is approximately 1.959964, so the margin is 3.919928 and the interval runs from about 96.0801 to 103.9199.

If 12 is instead a sample standard deviation, choose Student t. With 35 degrees of freedom, its larger critical value makes the interval a little wider. This reflects uncertainty in estimating the population spread.

table.caption: Normal-z interval with mean 100, standard deviation 12 and 36 observations

sections.title: Interpret confidence as a property of the procedure
paragraphs: A 95% confidence procedure is designed so that 95% of intervals from repeated samples cover the fixed population mean, under its assumptions. After one sample is observed, the computed interval either covers that mean or it does not.

This is not the interval containing 95% of individual observations. For the known-normal example above, individual values have standard deviation 12, while the estimated mean has standard error 2. Distribution coverage and uncertainty about a mean answer different questions.

links.label: Calculate coverage for individual normal observations
NIST: confidence limits for a mean

sections.title: Understand which changes narrow or widen the interval
paragraphs: Holding the other inputs fixed, increasing confidence widens the interval and increasing sample size narrows it. In the Normal-z calculation, quadrupling n halves the margin because √n doubles. Increasing standard deviation increases the margin in direct proportion.

The assumptions still matter: independent observations and a suitable sampling design are needed, and the usual t procedure is exact for a normal population. Large-sample approximations depend on the distribution; severe skew, outliers or dependence can make a simple mean interval unreliable. This page does not calculate a proportion interval, a paired difference or a two-sample comparison.

confidence-interval-calculator.seoTitle: Confidence Interval Calculator: Mean, t & z Intervals

p-value-calculator.description: Find tail probabilities from z, t, chi-square or F statistics, with required degrees of freedom and normal inverse-probability options.

faqs.question: Is a p-value the probability that the null hypothesis is true?
faqs.answer: No. It measures how extreme the statistic is under the specified null distribution and tail definition.

faqs.question: Why do degrees of freedom matter?
faqs.answer: They determine the shape of t, chi-square and F distributions. Using the wrong degrees of freedom changes the resulting probability.

faqs.question: Do I enter raw measurements or a test statistic?
faqs.answer: Enter the statistic from the chosen test. The page evaluates its reference distribution; it does not derive a t, chi-square or F statistic from a dataset.

faqs.question: Why are there two degrees-of-freedom fields for F?
faqs.answer: An F distribution has numerator and denominator degrees of freedom. Enter them in the order used by the test; swapping them changes the probability.

faqs.question: Can I always double the right-tail probability for a two-sided test?
faqs.answer: No. For symmetric z and t tests, use twice the smaller tail. Chi-square and F tests require the rejection rule appropriate to that particular test.

faqs.question: Does p greater than 0.05 prove that there is no effect?
faqs.answer: No. It may reflect a small effect, substantial uncertainty, limited sample size or other features of the study. Establishing equivalence requires an appropriate equivalence procedure and prespecified bounds.

sections.title: Matching a p-value to the test direction
paragraphs: Select the test direction and distribution assumptions that match the question being tested. One-sided and two-sided probabilities can differ for the same standardized statistic. A p-value describes evidence under the specified null model; it is not the probability that a hypothesis is true or a measure of practical importance. Interpret it alongside the effect size and study design.

sections.title: Start with a test statistic and its null distribution
paragraphs: This calculator converts a supplied statistic into tail probabilities. It does not calculate the statistic from raw observations or choose the test for you. Choose Standard normal for a z statistic, Student t for a t statistic, Chi-square for a nonnegative chi-square statistic, or F for a nonnegative F statistic.

Student t and chi-square need the appropriate degrees of freedom; F needs numerator and denominator degrees of freedom in the correct order. Those values come from the test design. For example, a one-sample t test normally uses n − 1 degrees of freedom, while a Welch two-sample test can have noninteger degrees of freedom.

sections.title: Worked example: three probabilities for the same z statistic
paragraphs: Select Standard normal and enter a statistic of 2. The probability above 2 is about 0.0227501; the probability below 2 is about 0.9772499. A two-sided test of a symmetric normal null distribution includes both equally extreme tails, giving approximately 0.0455003.

Use the probability that matches the alternative hypothesis specified before examining the result. Switching from a two-sided question to a one-sided question after seeing the sign changes the testing procedure.

table.caption: Tail choices for z = 2

sections.title: Keep the sign, the tail and the distribution together
paragraphs: A negative z or t statistic can provide evidence for a left-sided alternative and little evidence for a right-sided one. The two-sided z/t result is twice the smaller tail probability because those distributions are symmetric.

Chi-square and F distributions are not symmetric around zero. The page therefore reports their left and right tails without inventing a universal two-sided result. Goodness-of-fit, variance and other tests use different rejection rules; use the tail definition of the actual test.

links.label: NIST: t-test assumptions, degrees of freedom and alternatives

sections.title: Report what the probability can and cannot establish
paragraphs: A small p-value indicates that the observed statistic, or one more extreme in the chosen direction, is unusual under the null model. It does not measure the chance that the null hypothesis is true, the size of the effect or whether the effect matters in practice.

Report the effect estimate, an appropriate interval, the study design and the number of analyses considered. A nonsignificant result does not establish equivalence, and repeating many tests creates additional opportunities for a small p-value. This calculator does not apply a multiple-testing adjustment.

links.label: Calculate a confidence interval for a mean
Inspect normal tail and inverse probabilities

probability-calculator.description: Explore event unions and intersections, solve independent-event constraints, model repeated trials or calculate normal probabilities.

faqs.question: When can I multiply two event probabilities?
faqs.answer: Multiplication gives the intersection directly when the events are independent. Dependent events require appropriate joint or conditional information.

faqs.question: Why can the independent-event solver return two solutions?
faqs.answer: Some aggregate constraints fit two labeled event pairs. Redundant constraints can also leave infinitely many possibilities rather than a unique pair.

faqs.question: Should I enter a probability as 0.4 or 40?
faqs.answer: Use 0.4 for a 40% event probability in the event and repeated-trial modes. In Normal probability to boundary, the Tail probability field is labeled %, so use 40 for 40%. Match the field label rather than using one convention for every mode.

faqs.question: Does “A or B” include the outcome where both happen?
faqs.answer: Yes. The union includes A alone, B alone and their intersection. The exactly-one result excludes the intersection.

faqs.question: Are mutually exclusive events independent?
faqs.answer: Not when both have positive probability. If one occurs, the other cannot occur, so their intersection is zero rather than the positive product of their probabilities.

faqs.question: How do I calculate the probability of at least one success?
faqs.answer: For independent trials with a fixed probability p, subtract the probability of no successes from 1: 1 − (1 − p)^n. With p = 0.2 and n = 3, the result is 0.488.

faqs.question: Is the normal coverage table a confidence interval for the mean?
faqs.answer: No. It shows central intervals of the assumed distribution of individual observations. An interval for an estimated mean uses its sampling uncertainty, including sample size.

sections.title: Checking dependence and event definitions
paragraphs: For independent events with probabilities 0.4 and 0.3, the chance of both is 0.4 × 0.3 = 0.12. The chance of at least one is 0.4 + 0.3 − 0.12 = 0.58, because outcomes where both happen must not be counted twice. Independence is an assumption, not something established by entering two probabilities. If the events are dependent, use their actual intersection or conditional information rather than the independent-event shortcut. Event and repeated-trial probability inputs use decimals from 0 to 1. The Normal probability to boundary mode instead labels its input as a percentage, so enter 97.5 for 97.5%.

sections.title: Distinguish both, either and exactly one
paragraphs: For events A and B, “A or B” is inclusive: it includes outcomes where both occur. “Exactly one” excludes those shared outcomes. “Neither” is the complement of the inclusive union. Define the events before selecting a formula.

If P(A) = 0.6 and P(B) = 0.25 and the events are independent, both occur with probability 0.15. Their union is 0.6 + 0.25 − 0.15 = 0.70. Neither has probability 0.30, and exactly one has probability 0.55.

table.caption: Independent events with P(A) = 0.6 and P(B) = 0.25

sections.title: Use a known intersection when independence does not apply
paragraphs: With the same marginal probabilities, suppose the measured intersection is 0.20 instead. Select Known intersection and enter that value. The union becomes 0.65, neither becomes 0.35 and exactly one becomes 0.45. The independent formula would answer a different model.

An intersection cannot exceed either event probability or fall below max(0, P(A) + P(B) − 1). Mutually exclusive positive-probability events have zero intersection and are not independent. A conditional probability, such as P(B given A), is also not the same input as the intersection; convert it using P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B given A).

sections.title: Calculate repeated-trial events through their complements
paragraphs: In Repeated independent trials, suppose each A trial succeeds with probability 0.2 and there are 3 A trials. All three successes have probability 0.2³ = 0.008. No successes have probability 0.8³ = 0.512, so at least one has probability 1 − 0.512 = 0.488.

Each group assumes a fixed success probability and independence across trials. Multiplying the A and B group outcomes also assumes the groups are independent. The page returns all, none and at-least-one events; it does not return a complete binomial table for every possible success count.

sections.title: Separate normal coverage from a confidence interval
paragraphs: In Normal distribution probability, enter mean 100, standard deviation 15, lower bound 85 and upper bound 115. These are one standard deviation on either side of the mean, covering approximately 0.682689 of a normal distribution, or 68.2689%. The output is a probability for individual observations under that model.

Use -inf or inf for an unbounded end. Normal probability to boundary works in reverse: a left-tail probability of 97.5%, mean 100 and standard deviation 15 gives a boundary near 129.3995. This mode labels its probability input as %, whereas event and repeated-trial inputs use fractions from 0 to 1.

links.label: Calculate uncertainty around an estimated mean

sections.title: Check whether two independent-event constraints determine a solution
paragraphs: In Solve independent-event probabilities, enter P(A) = 0.4 and P(A and B) = 0.12. Independence gives P(B) = 0.12 ÷ 0.4 = 0.3. The calculator then fills out the remaining event probabilities.

Two aggregate inputs can leave two labeled solutions because exchanging A and B preserves those aggregates. Redundant constraints may leave infinitely many possibilities, while inconsistent constraints have none. A returned pair is a solution under the independence assumption, not evidence that real observations are independent.

probability-calculator.seoTitle: Probability Calculator: Events, Trials & Normal Distribution

slope-calculator.description: Find slope and a line equation from two points, or determine endpoints from a point, distance and direction.

faqs.question: What does an undefined slope mean?
faqs.answer: A vertical line has no finite slope because its horizontal change is zero. Identical points do not determine a unique line.

faqs.question: Does a slope and distance identify only one endpoint?
faqs.answer: No. A slope allows two opposite directions from the starting point. A directed angle selects a particular direction.

faqs.question: Does switching the order of the two points change the slope?
faqs.answer: No, provided both coordinate differences are reversed together. Both signs change and cancel in the ratio.

faqs.question: Is a 75% grade a 75-degree angle?
faqs.answer: No. A 75% grade is slope 0.75, with angle arctan(0.75), about 36.87°.

faqs.question: What is the slope of a horizontal line?
faqs.answer: For two distinct points with equal y coordinates, the rise is zero and the slope is 0. This differs from a vertical line, whose horizontal change is zero and slope is undefined.

sections.title: Reading slope from coordinate changes
paragraphs: Slope compares the vertical change with the horizontal change between two points. Keep the point order consistent in both differences. A vertical line has no finite slope under this ratio, while a horizontal line has zero slope. In direction-based mode, check the angle convention and distance input before comparing coordinates with a slope obtained from two known points.

sections.title: Calculate rise over run in a consistent coordinate order
paragraphs: For two distinct points, slope is (y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁). Subtract coordinates in the same order in numerator and denominator. Reversing both differences leaves the slope unchanged; reversing only one changes its sign incorrectly.
Slope is a ratio of vertical units to horizontal units. It is dimensionless only when those units are comparable. On a graph of distance versus time, for example, the slope has units of speed.

sections.title: Find a line from the points (2,3) and (6,11)
paragraphs: The rise is 11−3=8 and the run is 6−2=4, so the slope is 2. Substituting the first point into y=mx+b gives 3=2×2+b, hence b=−1 and the equation is y=2x−1. The distance between the points is √(4²+8²)=√80≈8.94427.

table.caption: Two-point line calculation

sections.title: Distinguish vertical, horizontal and coincident points
paragraphs: If the x coordinates match and the y coordinates differ, the line is vertical and its slope is undefined. Its equation is x=constant, not y=mx+b. If the y coordinates match, the slope is zero and the line is horizontal.
Identical points do not specify one unique line, so they are rejected. An undefined slope for a vertical line should not be replaced with zero or an arbitrary very large number.

sections.title: Use distance and direction carefully when finding an endpoint
paragraphs: The Point, distance & direction mode calculates an endpoint from a starting point, length and angle or slope. A slope alone specifies a line but leaves two opposite travel directions; the tool reports both endpoints in that case.
An inclination angle describes direction, while percent grade equals 100×rise/run. A slope of 0.75 corresponds to a 75% grade and an angle arctan(0.75), approximately 36.8699°, not 75°.

links.label: Find an endpoint from distance and direction

slope-calculator.seoTitle: Slope Calculator: Two Points, Line Equation & Endpoints

distance-calculator.description: Calculate coordinate distance or spherical great-circle distance from decimal or degree-minute-second latitude and longitude.

faqs.question: Is great-circle distance the same as driving distance?
faqs.answer: No. It estimates the shortest surface arc on a spherical Earth, without roads, terrain or route restrictions.

faqs.question: How do I enter southern or western DMS coordinates?
faqs.answer: Type a nonnegative degree magnitude followed by minutes, seconds and the hemisphere letter. For example, enter 33 52 08 S for a southern latitude. Use W for a western longitude; the hemisphere letter supplies the sign.

faqs.question: Can I calculate a two-dimensional distance?
faqs.answer: Yes. Enter the x and y coordinates and leave both z coordinates at zero.

faqs.question: Can I enter latitude and longitude as x and y?
faqs.answer: Use the geographic modes for latitude and longitude. Those angular coordinates are not Cartesian lengths.

faqs.question: What does changing the Earth radius do?
faqs.answer: It scales the modeled arc length directly while leaving the angular separation unchanged. The default is a spherical approximation, not a detailed ellipsoidal model.

sections.title: Choosing planar or geographic distance
paragraphs: Coordinate distance treats points in the selected mathematical space, while great-circle distance models locations on a curved Earth. Use latitude and longitude fields only with the geographic mode, and check signs and angle units. A geographic straight-line estimate is different from a road route. For travel mileage along roads, use the separate driving-route calculator and review its provider result.

sections.title: Choose coordinate distance or distance along a spherical Earth
paragraphs: Coordinate distance uses √[(Δx)²+(Δy)²+(Δz)²] in a Cartesian system. Leave both z coordinates at zero for a flat two-dimensional calculation. Great-circle distance instead interprets latitude and longitude on a sphere.
Do not treat latitude and longitude in degrees as ordinary x and y lengths. Geographic degrees describe angles, and the distance represented by a longitude difference depends on latitude.

sections.title: Work through a three-dimensional coordinate example
paragraphs: Between (1,2,3) and (4,6,15), the differences are 3, 4 and 12. The straight-line distance is √(9+16+144)=√169=13 units. This is the direct segment, not the total length of a path along three perpendicular axes.

table.caption: Coordinate differences for a 13-unit segment

sections.title: Interpret the Earth-radius assumption and coordinate format
paragraphs: The great-circle model uses the entered sphere radius, initially 6,371 km. A quarter-circle from latitude 0°, longitude 0° to latitude 0°, longitude 90° is πR/2, approximately 10,007.54 km at that radius. It is a spherical reference, not an ellipsoidal survey result.

The DMS mode accepts degrees, minutes and seconds with directional letters, such as 40 30 0 N. Decimal degrees instead encode that coordinate as 40.5. Keep latitude and longitude in their correct fields and use the stated sign or hemisphere convention.

links.label: Enter geographic coordinates in degrees, minutes and seconds

sections.title: Separate geometric distance from a travel route
paragraphs: A great-circle arc does not follow roads, shipping lanes, air-traffic restrictions or terrain. Driving distance and travel time therefore need route information, while Cartesian distance needs a suitable coordinate system and common length units.

The geographic model does not include altitude changes. Its precision is limited by the chosen Earth model and coordinate accuracy; additional decimal places in the output do not turn it into a property survey.

links.label: Estimate a road journey with routing inputs

pythagorean-theorem-calculator.description: Find a right triangle's hypotenuse from two perpendicular legs, or recover one leg from the hypotenuse and the other leg.

faqs.question: Can I use this formula for any triangle?
faqs.answer: No. The equation a² + b² = c² applies when the legs meet at a right angle.

faqs.question: Why must the hypotenuse be longer than the known leg?
faqs.answer: The missing leg uses the square root of c² − a². A nonpositive difference cannot form a nondegenerate right triangle.

faqs.question: Which side is the hypotenuse?
faqs.answer: It is the side opposite the right angle and is the longest side of a nondegenerate right triangle.

faqs.question: How do I find the diagonal of a rectangle?
faqs.answer: Use its perpendicular length and width as the two legs. For 8 and 15, the diagonal is 17 in the same length unit.

faqs.question: Does scaling a 3–4–5 triangle preserve its right angle?
faqs.answer: Yes. Multiplying all three sides by the same positive factor preserves a² + b² = c². For example, 6² + 8² = 10².

sections.title: Identifying the hypotenuse correctly
paragraphs: The Pythagorean theorem applies to a right triangle. The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle and is the longest side, so it cannot be interchanged with a leg when choosing the unknown. Use consistent length units for all sides. A valid arithmetic result does not establish that a measured triangle actually has a right angle.

sections.title: Identify the right angle and the side opposite it
paragraphs: The Pythagorean theorem applies to a right triangle: a²+b²=c², where c is the hypotenuse opposite the 90° angle. The two remaining sides are legs. Select Find hypotenuse when both legs are known, or Find a leg when the hypotenuse and one leg are known.
All side lengths must use the same unit. Convert them first if necessary. The hypotenuse must exceed either leg; the calculator rejects a known leg that is at least as long as the hypotenuse.

sections.title: Calculate a diagonal and then reverse the calculation
paragraphs: For perpendicular lengths 8 and 15, the diagonal is √(8²+15²)=√289=17. If the diagonal 17 and leg 8 are known instead, the other leg is √(17²−8²)=√225=15.

table.caption: Forward and reverse calculations for an 8–15–17 triangle
rows: Other leg when the known leg is 8
Other leg when the known leg is 15

sections.title: Apply the theorem to rectangular geometry without adding lengths
paragraphs: The diagonal of an 8-by-15 rectangle is 17, not 23. The sum 23 follows two edges, while 17 is the straight diagonal between the opposite corners. That geometric distinction matters for screens, plans and coordinate distances.
For a three-dimensional rectangular box, combine three perpendicular dimensions: d=√(a²+b²+c²). The Coordinate Distance Calculator accepts three coordinates when that is the actual problem.

sections.title: Check the right-triangle assumption before using the answer
paragraphs: For three measured sides, use the longest as the candidate hypotenuse and compare its square with the sum of the other squares. An exact equality characterizes a right triangle in ideal geometry; measurements may agree only within their uncertainties.
For a triangle with a different included angle, use the law of cosines rather than forcing the Pythagorean relationship. The Triangle Calculator has separate modes for known sides and angles.

pythagorean-theorem-calculator.seoTitle: Pythagorean Theorem Calculator: Hypotenuse or Missing Leg

right-triangle-calculator.description: Solve a right triangle from supported pairs of known measurements, returning sides, angles, area and possible alternate solutions.

faqs.question: Why can a known pair produce more than one solution?
faqs.answer: Some measurements do not distinguish the two labeled legs or angles. The solver displays each admissible labeled solution.

faqs.question: Can I enter angles in radians?
faqs.answer: Yes. Select radians for angular inputs. Calculated angles are displayed in degrees, and all lengths must follow the stated unit convention.

faqs.question: Is the altitude to the hypotenuse the same as a leg?
faqs.answer: No. It is perpendicular to the hypotenuse from the right-angle vertex. Its length is ab/c.

faqs.question: Can two acute angles determine all side lengths?
faqs.answer: No. They determine the shape but leave the overall scale unknown. At least one suitable length or area measurement is needed.

faqs.question: What unit should I use when one input is area?
faqs.answer: Use the square of the length unit used elsewhere. If side lengths are meters, the area must be in square meters.

sections.title: Solving a right triangle from known quantities
paragraphs: Choose the pair of known quantities supported by the mode, such as two sides or a side and an acute angle. Label the hypotenuse and legs carefully before entering values. The right-angle assumption supplies information that a general triangle problem does not have. Review the resulting side lengths and angle units together to check that the solution matches the diagram you intended.

sections.title: Choose the two measurements you actually know
paragraphs: Two legs is the most direct mode when a and b are given. Any two known quantities supports combinations involving legs, hypotenuse, altitude to the hypotenuse, area, perimeter and acute angles. Enter the First known value and Second known value in the order shown by the selected pair.
Two acute angles alone determine shape but not size, so a length or area is needed to establish scale. Angular inputs can use degrees or radians; returned angle labels specify degrees.

sections.title: Check the complete 5–12–13 right triangle
paragraphs: Enter legs 5 and 12. The hypotenuse is 13, area is 5×12/2=30 and perimeter is 30. Angle A opposite leg a=5 is approximately 22.6199°, while B is approximately 67.3801°. Their sum is 90°.

table.caption: Measurements of a right triangle with legs 5 and 12

sections.title: Distinguish a leg from the altitude to the hypotenuse
paragraphs: Both legs meet at the right angle. The altitude to the hypotenuse instead runs from that right-angle vertex perpendicular to the sloping hypotenuse. Its length is h=ab/c, not either leg length.

For the 5–12–13 example, choosing Hypotenuse c + Area with values 13 and 30 allows the same geometric triangle with a and b swapped. Two labeled solutions can therefore describe different side assignments rather than two different overall shapes.

links.label: Solve from another pair of known quantities

sections.title: Check units and feasibility before reading derived values
paragraphs: A length input uses the shared length unit; an area input uses its square. Entering 30 square feet with a hypotenuse measured in meters would describe inconsistent geometry unless the quantities are converted first.

Not every pair of positive numbers can form a right triangle. A hypotenuse shorter than a leg, an acute angle outside 0°–90°, or an impossible area for the given hypotenuse must be rejected rather than treated as a valid shape.

right-triangle-calculator.seoTitle: Right Triangle Calculator: Sides, Angles & Area

triangle-calculator.description: Solve SSS, SAS, ASA or ambiguous SSA triangles, with angles, area and derived measurements such as altitudes, medians and radii.

faqs.question: Why can the SSA case have two triangles?
faqs.answer: A non-included angle can match two supplementary angle candidates. Only candidates with valid positive remaining angles form solutions.

faqs.question: What condition must three side lengths satisfy?
faqs.answer: Every side must be shorter than the sum of the other two. Equality would form a degenerate straight-line shape.

faqs.question: What is the difference between SAS and SSA?
faqs.answer: In SAS, the known angle lies between the two known sides. In SSA, it is opposite one of them; that case can produce zero, one or two triangles.

faqs.question: Why do sides 3, 4 and 7 fail?
faqs.answer: The shorter sides add to exactly the longest side, so the shape collapses to a line. A nondegenerate triangle requires a strict inequality.

faqs.question: Can three angles give the area?
faqs.answer: No. Angles determine shape but not scale. A side length or other suitable size measurement is needed.

faqs.question: Are the returned center coordinates map coordinates?
faqs.answer: No. They use the calculator’s mathematical placement of the vertices. They do not specify a location or orientation on Earth.

sections.title: Choosing a triangle-solving case
paragraphs: Three sides, two sides with an included angle, and two angles with a side provide different starting information. Select the matching case rather than placing an unrelated measurement in an available field. A side-side-angle problem can have ambiguous solutions, which is why the selected method matters. Check whether the entered values can form a triangle before interpreting its area or angles.

sections.title: Match the solver to SSS, SAS, ASA/AAS or SSA data
paragraphs: Three sides uses SSS. Two sides & included angle uses SAS, where the angle lies between those sides. Two angles & side uses a side a opposite angle A together with angles A and B. Two sides & a non-included angle uses SSA and may have multiple solutions.
A side label is tied to its opposite angle: side a faces A, b faces B and c faces C. Choose degrees or radians for angular inputs. The calculated angular outputs are labeled in degrees.

sections.title: Work a three-side example with Heron’s formula
paragraphs: For sides 5, 5 and 6, the semiperimeter is s=(5+5+6)/2=8. Heron’s formula gives area √[8(8−5)(8−5)(8−6)]=√144=12 square units. The perimeter is 16 and the height to the base of length 6 is 2×12/6=4.

table.caption: A 5–5–6 isosceles triangle

sections.title: Understand why SSA can produce two triangles
paragraphs: With a=10, b=12 and A=30°, the sine rule gives sin(B)=12×sin(30°)/10=0.6. Both B≈36.8699° and B≈143.1301° can leave a positive third angle. They produce different triangles, so retaining only the principal inverse-sine angle would miss a valid solution.

The solver checks candidate angles and reports every valid solution within its supported precision. If the sine ratio exceeds 1 or the remaining angle is not positive, the measurements cannot form the proposed triangle.

sections.title: Validate dimensions and interpret the coordinate-based results
paragraphs: For SSS, the two shorter sides must sum to more than the longest side. Equality is a collapsed line with zero area, not a triangle. Three angles without any length cannot determine an absolute area or perimeter.

Additional centers and geometric measures use the stated reference coordinates A=(0,0), B=(c,0), with C above the x-axis. These are coordinates of the mathematical model, not a geolocation or a surveyed orientation. Lengths share a unit and areas use its square.

triangle-calculator.seoTitle: Triangle Calculator: Solve SSS, SAS, ASA & SSA

circle-calculator.description: Find a circle's radius, diameter, circumference and area from any one of those measurements using consistent length units.

faqs.question: How do radius and diameter differ?
faqs.answer: The diameter is twice the radius. A radius runs from the center to the edge; a diameter crosses the circle through its center.

faqs.question: Why does the area use square units?
faqs.answer: Area measures two-dimensional coverage. If radius is measured in centimeters, πr² is measured in square centimeters.

faqs.question: Can I start with the area instead of the radius?
faqs.answer: Yes. Select area as the known quantity. The calculator uses r=√(A/π) and then finds the other dimensions.

faqs.question: Why does confusing diameter and radius change area fourfold?
faqs.answer: The diameter is twice the radius, and area depends on radius squared. Doubling the radius multiplies area by four.

faqs.question: Is circumference the perimeter of a circle?
faqs.answer: Yes. Circumference is the full distance around the circle’s boundary.

faqs.question: Do circle results all use the same unit?
faqs.answer: Linear dimensions use the chosen implicit length unit, while area uses its square. Keep that distinction when entering a known area.

sections.title: Distinguishing radius, diameter, and circumference
paragraphs: The radius runs from the center to the circle, while the diameter spans the circle through its center. Circumference measures the boundary and area measures the enclosed region. Mixing those quantities can produce a plausible-looking number with the wrong meaning. Keep length units consistent and remember that area uses squared units rather than the original length unit.

sections.title: Choose the measurement you know before entering its value
paragraphs: Select radius, diameter, circumference or area as the known quantity. The tool first obtains the radius, then calculates the other measurements using d=2r, C=2πr and A=πr². Supply a positive value.

Use one consistent length unit for radius, diameter and circumference. If the supplied quantity is area, its unit must be the square of the intended length unit. For example, entering area in square centimeters returns linear dimensions in centimeters.

sections.title: Reconstruct a circle from its diameter
paragraphs: For a diameter of 14 cm, the radius is 7 cm. Circumference is 14π ≈ 43.9823 cm and area is 49π ≈ 153.9380 cm². Selecting diameter rather than radius is essential: entering 14 as the radius would double the circumference and quadruple the area.

table.caption: A circle with diameter 14 cm

sections.title: Use the inverse relationship for a known area or circumference
paragraphs: If the area is known, r=√(A/π). If the circumference is known, r=C/(2π). Dividing area by π alone gives r², not r. A circumference is a length around the boundary, not the distance across the circle.

For a semicircle, half the full-circle area gives the curved region’s area, but its complete perimeter includes the diameter as well as the half-circumference. Keep the geometry of the requested quantity explicit.

sections.title: Check how a change in radius scales the result
paragraphs: Multiplying radius by k multiplies circumference by k and area by k². A 10% larger radius therefore gives 10% more circumference but 21% more area. This explains why an apparently small diameter error can materially change a covering estimate.
The circle model assumes a perfect circular boundary. An ellipse needs two semi-axes, and an irregular outline requires another method. Extra digits in π do not compensate for uncertain measurements.

circle-calculator.seoTitle: Circle Calculator: Radius, Diameter, Area & Circumference

area-calculator.description: Use this area calculator for rectangles, circles and more. Mix units and get results in ft², m² or acres.

faqs.question: How do I calculate area in square feet?
faqs.answer: Choose the shape and set Area unit to Square feet. For a rectangle measured in feet, multiply length by width: 12 ft × 10 ft = 120 ft². You can also enter inches, meters, or mixed units; the calculator converts each dimension before finding the area.

faqs.question: How do I calculate circle area from a diameter?
faqs.answer: Divide the diameter by 2, then enter that value as the radius in Circle mode. For a diameter of 10 m, the radius is 5 m and the area is π × 5² ≈ 78.54 m². Using the diameter as the radius makes the answer four times too large.

faqs.question: Is a triangle's height the same as its sloping side?
faqs.answer: Usually not. The height is the perpendicular distance from the opposite vertex to the line containing the base. If you only know the three side lengths, choose Triangle from three sides instead of using a sloping side as the height.

faqs.question: Can I calculate land area from four side lengths?
faqs.answer: Not for an arbitrary quadrilateral. The same four side lengths can enclose different areas as the angles change. A known rectangle needs length and width; a trapezoid needs both parallel bases and perpendicular height. Otherwise, obtain additional measurements such as a diagonal that divides the plot into two triangles.

faqs.question: How do I convert square feet to acres or square meters to hectares?
faqs.answer: Divide square feet by 43,560 to get acres, or square meters by 10,000 to get hectares. For example, 30,000 ft² is approximately 0.688705 acres and 9,600 m² is 0.96 hectares. You can choose Acres or Hectares as the result unit directly.

faqs.question: How do I enter feet and inches?
faqs.answer: Use decimal feet or convert the entire measurement to inches. For 5 ft 6 in, enter 5.5 with Feet selected or 66 with Inches selected. Entering 5.6 feet means 5 feet 7.2 inches, so it changes the area.

sections.title: Selecting the shape that matches the measurement
paragraphs: Area formulas depend on the shape and on whether a height is perpendicular to the relevant base. Choose the matching shape before entering measurements. For an irregular region, calculate suitable pieces separately rather than forcing it into an unrelated formula. Check the output's squared unit and avoid treating a side length or perimeter as an area input.

area-calculator.seoTitle: Area Calculator: Rectangle, Circle, Triangle & More

volume-calculator.description: Calculate volume for 11 shapes in cubic units. See which measurements to use for a tank’s capacity, a tapered planter, or the material in a pipe wall.

faqs.question: How do I find the radius if I can only measure around a cylinder?
faqs.answer: Wrap a tape once around the cylinder and divide that circumference by 2π. A can measuring 31.4 cm around has an outside radius of about 5 cm. To find what it holds, use the inside radius or subtract the wall thickness from the outside radius.

faqs.question: Can I mix feet, inches, and meters?
faqs.answer: Yes. Set the unit beside each dimension. If one side measures 5 ft 6 in, enter 5.5 feet or 66 inches. Those 6 inches are half a foot.

faqs.question: How do I find the volume of an irregular stone?
faqs.answer: For a stone that sinks and does not absorb water, use water displacement. Read the level in a graduated cylinder at eye level. Lower the stone until it is fully covered and release any trapped bubbles. A rise from 75 mL to 93 mL gives a stone volume of 18 mL, or 18 cm³.

faqs.question: Which gallon should I use for tank capacity?
faqs.answer: A US liquid gallon is about 3.785 L. An imperial gallon is about 4.546 L. If a tank label just says “gal,” check which gallon the manufacturer uses before comparing capacities.

faqs.question: Does capsule length include the rounded ends?
faqs.answer: The Cylinder length input includes only the straight section. The total end-to-end length is that straight length plus twice the radius. The calculator adds the volume of both hemispherical ends automatically.

faqs.question: How deep will a known volume of water be in a rectangular tray?
faqs.answer: Divide the water volume by the inside base area. A tray measuring 40 cm by 25 cm inside has a base area of 1,000 cm². Pour in 12 L (12,000 cm³) and the water will be 12 cm deep, provided the sides are vertical and tall enough.

sections.title: Matching dimensions to a solid shape
paragraphs: Select a solid and use its diagram to identify radius, perpendicular height, and semi-axes. Each dimension can use its own unit; the calculator converts the lengths before applying the formula. Choose Volume unit to return cubic feet, cubic meters, or another supported cubic unit. For capacity, use inside measurements. Wall thickness and openings need a mode or separate calculation that accounts for them.

volume-calculator.seoTitle: Volume Calculator for 11 Shapes | Box, Cylinder & Sphere

surface-area-calculator.description: Calculate surface area for 11 solids with labeled diagrams and mixed units. Compare formulas, worked examples, and which faces or bases each result includes.

faqs.question: What is the difference between surface area and volume?
faqs.answer: Surface area measures a solid’s faces and curved surfaces in square units. Volume measures the space inside it in cubic units. A cube with edges of 3 m has surface area 54 m² and volume 27 m³.

faqs.question: Does the cylinder result include both circular ends?
faqs.answer: Yes. Total cylinder area is 2πr² + 2πrh. For an open-top cylinder, subtract one base area, πr². For only the curved side, use 2πrh.

faqs.question: Can I use mixed measurement units?
faqs.answer: Yes. Choose each dimension’s unit and a square output unit. A prism 2 ft × 12 in × 6 in has surface area 7 ft². The calculator converts the dimensions before adding the faces.

faqs.question: Does spherical-cap surface area include the flat base?
faqs.answer: Yes. Total area is the curved area 2πrh plus the flat base area π(2rh − h²). The alternate cap mode lists the curved area and total area separately, along with cap height and volume.

faqs.question: Is the ellipsoid surface-area result exact?
faqs.answer: No. The engine uses the stated Knud Thomsen approximation with exponent 1.6075; ellipsoid volume uses a separate exact formula.

faqs.question: Which surfaces are counted for a hollow cylinder?
faqs.answer: The total includes the outer curved wall, inner curved wall, and both flat ring-shaped ends. If you need only the outside wall, calculate 2πrh using the outer radius and height.

sections.title: Checking which surfaces are included
paragraphs: Surface area adds the modeled exposed faces of a solid, rather than measuring the space inside it. Review the selected shape's formula to see whether bases, ends, or inner surfaces are included. This matters for tasks such as covering a container or comparing an open and closed shape. The output uses squared units, even though the object itself has volume.

surface-area-calculator.seoTitle: Surface Area Calculator: Sphere, Cylinder, Cone & More

matrix-calculator.description: Add, subtract, multiply, scale, transpose and raise matrices to integer powers, or calculate determinants and inverses up to 10 by 10.

faqs.question: When can two matrices be multiplied?
faqs.answer: The number of columns in A must equal the number of rows in B. The result uses row-by-column dot products.

faqs.question: Which matrices have an inverse?
faqs.answer: A matrix must be square and nonsingular. A zero determinant means no inverse exists, while nearly singular matrices can be numerically sensitive.

faqs.question: Why can I not add a 2×3 matrix to a 3×2 matrix?
faqs.answer: Addition pairs corresponding entries, so both row counts and column counts must match exactly.

faqs.question: What size is the result of a 2×3 times a 3×4 matrix?
faqs.answer: It is 2×4. The matching inner dimensions are summed over; the outer dimensions determine the result.

faqs.question: Is matrix multiplication performed entry by entry?
faqs.answer: No. Each output entry is a row-by-column dot product. Entrywise multiplication is a different operation.

faqs.question: Can I transpose a rectangular matrix?
faqs.answer: Yes. Transpose exchanges rows and columns and does not require a square matrix. A 2×3 matrix becomes a 3×2 matrix.

sections.title: Checking matrix dimensions before an operation
paragraphs: Matrix operations have different dimension requirements. Addition needs matching shapes, while multiplication matches the first matrix's column count with the second matrix's row count. Reversing multiplication can change the result or make the operation undefined. For an inverse or determinant, review the square-matrix requirements and singularity limitations. Check row order and separators when entering the values.

sections.title: Match matrix dimensions to the selected operation
